limits: gh api search/repositories: several single-topic/narrow-term queries (e.g. 'vectorized backtest stars:>100', 'survivorship bias corporate actions backtest', 'point-in-time historical data backtest', 'topic:market-microstructure simulation', 'multi-asset backtesting portfolio simulation', 'topic:quant-trading-engine', 'market making simulator crypto', 'gs-quant OR qlib...') returned zero or near-zero results, indicating GitHub's search index has sparse topic/description coverage for these fidelity-specific terms rather than an absence of such engines — corroborating evidence was instead pulled via direct-name queries and Tavily web search.

GitHub code search API rate limit is 30 requests/minute; all `gh api search/repositories` calls were paced with ~2.5s sleeps (roughly 24/min) to stay under this cap, and org-repos listing calls used a 1s pace since they hit the higher-limit core API (5000/h).

`orgs/stefan-jansen/repos` returned 404 because stefan-jansen is a user account, not a GitHub org; the individual repo (zipline-reloaded) was instead fetched directly via `gh api repos/stefan-jansen/zipline-reloaded`.
Tavily `tvly search` was used successfully (no keyless rate-cap error encountered), so the WebSearch fallback tool was not needed.

Star counts and 'pushed:>2025-09-01' activity are GitHub-popularity/activity proxies, not direct measures of backtest fidelity (point-in-time correctness, corporate-action handling, borrow-cost/slippage modeling, live/backtest parity); those claims were partially cross-checked against independent web sources (tradealgo.com, python.financial, bullalert.ai, r/algotrading) but full fidelity verification per-repo (reading test suites, docs on corporate-action handling, etc.) was not performed within this discovery pass, per the blind-discovery scope (enumerate SOTA candidates with evidence URLs, not a deep fidelity audit).

Two of the 'python.financial' and 'bullalert.ai' sources read as SEO/possibly AI-generated comparison content rather than primary/authoritative sources; they were used only as secondary corroboration alongside GitHub metadata and the Reddit r/algotrading practitioner thread, not as sole evidence for any candidate.

judges.lens: Engineering quality of backtest/simulation engines (sub-layer T-engines): code/test/CI health, release discipline, API stability, documentation depth, dependency and platform hygiene, security/provenance, maintainer organisation, and operational fit for Linux/WSL2 + Python 3.12+ local-first use. Capability was judged strictly against the sub-layer's named fidelity criteria (point-in-time universes, corporate actions, fees, slippage, borrow, multi-asset accounting, determinism, live/backtest parity). Judged only from public GitHub/web sources as of 2026-09-21/22 UTC; nothing was cloned, built or executed, and no local catalog or task record was opened.

Supply chain: gitleaks, osv-scanner, cargo-deny, security-audit.toml, SECURITY.md citing signed and attested releases. Fidelity: fill models documented per book type (prob_fill_on_limit, prob_slippage, liquidity_consumption, random_seed for reproducible draws) and four account types (Cash/Margin/Betting/Wallet) with margin scopes. limits: Nothing was cloned, installed, built or executed. Every score reflects repository text, GitHub API metadata and published documentation as of 2026-09-21/22 UTC — no fill accuracy, determinism or performance claim was reproduced, so 'fidelity' here means documented and code-visible features, not verified numerical correctness.

CI health figures are the conclusion counts of the 15 most recent completed workflow runs on each default branch at one moment. They are a snapshot, not a historical pass rate, and for gs-quant the only visible workflow is a publish job, so its green runs are not test evidence.

Absence findings (no corporate actions in NautilusTrader, no borrow model in qlib, etc.) rest on documentation greps and GitHub code search, which is weaker evidence than a positive finding; a feature could exist under vocabulary I did not search. The GitHub code-search rate limit was hit once mid-run and those queries were retried after reset.

Three shortlist rows carry licence readings I judged differently from the supplied mechanical metadata: StockSharp is an explicit proprietary EULA that the vendor may change unilaterally (not merely 'non-OSI terms'), rqalpha is restricted to non-commercial use by its own README, and vectorbt is Apache-2.0 plus Commons Clause barring hosting and support revenue. A downstream consumer should treat NOASSERTION as 'read the file', not as 'source-available and usable'.

vnpy could not be scored on backtest fidelity at all, because its backtesting engines live in separate vnpy_* repositories that were outside the given shortlist; its row reflects the core repository only and its capability score should not be read as a judgement of the wider VeighNa platform.

The supplied shortlist metadata understates NautilusTrader's release recency: releases/latest skips prereleases, so it reported v1.231.0 (2026-08-02) when the newest tag is v2.0.0rc5 (2026-09-15). Rankings here use the corrected cadence.

Ranks 4 and 5 are the least confident. qlib ranks above hummingbot, rqalpha and vectorbt on the strength of a tested point-in-time path, MIT licensing and fully green CI, despite near-dormant maintenance (2 commits in 30 days, last release 13 months old); backtesting.py ranks 5th purely on code-hygiene grounds (gating lint plus mypy, coverage, a prerelease-dependency canary) against a capability surface that covers almost none of this sub-layer's criteria. A reviewer weighting capability over process should swap either for rqalpha or hummingbot.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for T-engines (backtest/simulation): does the engine actually enforce US-equity point-in-time correctness (survivorship/lookahead safeguards, ticker-change and delisting mapping, splits/dividends, borrow availability, fees and slippage, multi-asset accounting, settlement), is it deterministic and reproducible, does it share execution semantics with paper/live, and what public evidence (docs, in-repo modules, CI/regression suites, upstream tests, user-reported failure modes) supports each claim. Scored only from public web/GitHub sources dated up to 2026-09-21; no local project files were opened and no prior project selection was used.

scores.notes: Only shortlisted repo that puts US-equity point-in-time correctness inside the engine rather than delegating it to the data vendor. Common/Data/Auxiliary ships MapFile/MapFileResolver/MapFileRow (ticker renames, delistings, primary-exchange history) and FactorFile/CorporateFactorProvider/PriceScalingExtensions (splits + dividends), with eight documented DataNormalizationMode values (Raw, Adjusted, SplitAdjusted, TotalReturn, ScaledRaw, three continuous-future modes). Borrow is modelled first-class: IShortableProvider with LocalDiskShortableProvider and InteractiveBrokersShortableProvider, plus ShortableProviderOrdersRejectedRegressionAlgorithm and AllShortableSymbolsCoarseSelectionRegressionAlgorithm in both C# and Python. Costs are per-broker (AlpacaFeeModel, InteractiveBrokersFeeModel, CharlesSchwabFeeModel, TradeStationFeeModel, ...) and slippage is pluggable (VolumeShareSlippageModel, MarketImpactSlippageModel). Multi-asset accounting is explicit: SecurityPortfolioManager, CashBook, DelayedSettlementModel/ImmediateSettlementModel, SecurityMarginModel and PatternDayTradingMarginModel. Reproducibility is documented as a property (adjusted prices computed from the entire split/dividend history so results do not depend on backtest end date). Evidence class is strong and mechanical: 832 entries in Algorithm.CSharp (regression algorithms) and a dedicated .github/workflows/regression-tests.yml that runs dotnet test --filter TestCategory=RegressionTests on every push/PR, alongside research-regression-tests.yml and benchmarks.yml. Lifecycle is genuinely shared: the same Engine/Launcher runs backtest, paper and live against in-repo brokerage models. quality_cost held at 2 because the runtime is .NET with Python via pythonnet, and correct US-equity results require sourcing map/factor/shortable data files, which is the real operating burden. Documented failure mode from users: universe/fundamental backtests can still show survivorship effects when the underlying fundamental data coverage is incomplete, i.e. the engine machinery is correct but data coverage governs the outcome.

Bar-based lookahead is handled explicitly: ts_init must be the interval close so a complete bar cannot be visible before it formed, and bar volume is split into four synthetic L1 updates matched in configured O/H/L/C order. Benchmarking is a written policy using Criterion (wall time) and iai (instruction counts) with back-to-back comparison requirements. capability_fit capped at 2 because the on-lens equity requirements are absent: the Equity instrument schema (docs/concepts/instruments/equity) carries no dividend, split, or corporate-action fields, GitHub code search for 'dividend' across the repo returns only greeks and Bybit hits and 'corporate action' returns only Databento symbology hits, and there is no map-file/factor-file/point-in-time-universe equivalent. limits: Nothing was executed. Every score derives from published documentation, repository structure, CI configuration and third-party reports — no backtest was run, no fill was compared against a broker, and no reproducibility claim was independently reproduced. Treat all of this as documentary evidence, one class below a measured local integration check.

No candidate publishes a measured backtest-versus-paper fill divergence for US equities. Parity claims (NautilusTrader's shared kernel, LEAN's shared Engine/Launcher, freqtrade's dry-run) are architectural guarantees about code paths, not benchmarked agreement on fills, and should not be scored as if they were measurements.

The shortlist was handed to me pre-filtered by star count, and that filter is biased against this sub-layer. It admitted three crypto-only bots (freqtrade 54.6k, hummingbot 20.1k, jesse 8.6k) that score 0 on capability fit, while excluding stefan-jansen/zipline-reloaded (1,940 stars, Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-01-06, so it passes every mechanical rule except the star cut) — the maintained continuation of the Quantopian lineage, whose adjustments reader and asset-lifetime/sid machinery is the reference open-source implementation of US-equity point-in-time universes. A comprehensive US-equity sweep is not complete without it. mementum/backtrader (23.3k stars) is correctly excluded on maintenance, last pushed 2024-08-19.

Absence findings for corporate-action handling rest partly on GitHub code search, which can undercount. For NautilusTrader I corroborated the code-search result against the published Equity instrument field schema, which carries no dividend or split fields; for the other repositories the absence claim is weaker and rests on module listings and documentation only.

GitHub's licence field is unreliable as a mechanical gate here. Four shortlisted repos report NOASSERTION/Other, and reading that as acceptable source-available terms conceals three materially different regimes: StockSharp is explicitly proprietary under a website-published EULA whose terms can change unilaterally, vectorbt forbids selling products that are primarily the software, and rqalpha is non-commercial-use-only. Licence must be read from the LICENSE file and README, not the API field.

For every candidate, the binding constraint on US-equity point-in-time correctness is data access, not engine code. LEAN's map/factor/shortable machinery is inert without the corresponding data files; Qlib's official downloader was reported disabled; NautilusTrader delegates corporate actions to the adapter entirely. Engine selection does not settle the fidelity question on its own.

GitHub Releases are not a usable freshness signal for this cohort: LEAN's latest tag is from 2017, StockSharp's from 2020, and backtesting.py and jesse publish none, all while pushing current commits. Conversely NautilusTrader's shortlist metadata (v1.231.0) understates its state, since v2.0.0rc5 shipped 2026-09-15 as a prerelease.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader is the only shortlisted engine that publishes an explicit backtest/live divergence contract rather than claiming identity, enumerating venue, transport, timing, persistence, external-activity and reconciliation differences as named, linked behaviours.
verdicts.reason: The six-bullet contract exists and is real (nautilus_trader docs/concepts/live.md line 13 '## Backtest and live differences' enumerates Venue, Transport, Timing, Persistence, External activity, Reconciliation, each with an internal link). But the 'only' superlative is false. QuantConnect publishes a longer and older backtest/live divergence contract for LEAN: the Live Trading > Reconciliation page enumerates five named categories - Differences From Data (look-ahead bias, discrete time steps, custom data emission times, split adjustment of indicators, tick slice sizes, opening/closing auctions), Differences From Modeling (reality modeling errors, market impact, fills, borrowing costs), Differences From Brokerage (non-deterministic state from algorithm restarts, brokerage limitations, existing portfolio securities), Differences From Third-Party Indicators, and Differences From Real-time Scheduled Events - roughly 25 named sub-differences, more than NautilusTrader's six. freqtrade additionally publishes a ~20-item 'Assumptions made by backtesting' list (docs/backtesting.md line 556). The defensible claim is that NautilusTrader's contract is the most architecturally framed, not the only one.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader has the strongest supply-chain and provenance posture of any open-source trading engine in this shortlist, running OpenSSF Scorecard, CodeQL, osv-scanner, cargo-deny, gitleaks and a dedicated security-audit workflow, with a security policy stating signed and attested releases.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed and understated. .github/workflows contains codeql-analysis.yml, openssf-scorecard.yml and security-audit.yml; security-audit.yml runs harden-runner (SHA-pinned), a zizmor job uploading SARIF, and a 'supply-chain' job with a required audit-result gate. SECURITY.md states 'signed and attested releases' and additionally documents cargo-audit, cargo-deny, cargo-vet, OSV Scanner, pip-audit, gitleaks pre-commit screening, signed-commit branch rulesets, cargo-fuzz targets, SLSA build provenance attestations for Python artifacts, Sigstore cosign Docker signing, SPDX SBOM generation and post-publish attestation verification. Counter-check strengthens it: LEAN's .github/workflows (api-tests, benchmarks, gh-actions, rebase-org-branches, regression-tests, report-generator, syntax-tests, virtual-environments) contains no security, scanning or provenance workflow at all, and StockSharp - ranked 3rd by one judge - is not open source at all (its LICENSE reads 'This repository is not licensed under a general-purpose open source license', proprietary EULA), so it does not even qualify for the comparison.

verdicts.claim: LEAN is the only shortlisted engine covering every equity fidelity dimension in this sub-layer in code at once: Split/Dividend/Delisting/SymbolChanged data types, dated Coarse/Fine/ETF-constituent universes, an IShortableProvider borrow interface with an Interactive Brokers implementation, ~35 venue-specific fee models and volume-share and market-impact slippage models.
verdicts.reason: The coverage thesis is broadly right but two of the five cited specifics are factually wrong, and the judge cited a dead API as present-tense evidence. (1) 'Dated Coarse/Fine universes' no longer exist: Common/Data/UniverseSelection/CoarseFundamental.cs now throws on use - both GetSource and Reader raise InvalidOperationException with the message 'Coarse type is obsolete, please use Fundamental'. The capability survives only under the newer Fundamental API, so the named evidence is stale. (2) '~35 venue-specific fee models' is inflated: Common/Orders/Fees contains 33 files matching *FeeModel.cs, and of those IFeeModel.cs, FeeModel.cs, ConstantFeeModel.cs, AlphaStreamsFeeModel.cs, PublicFeeModel.cs, IndiaFeeModel.cs and RBIFeeModel.cs are interfaces, bases or regional/aggregate models, leaving roughly 26 venue-specific ones. The IShortableProvider and slippage-model parts check out (Common/Orders/Slippage holds VolumeShareSlippageModel.cs and MarketImpactSlippageModel.cs).

verdicts.claim: LEAN operates the largest public determinism harness of any shortlisted engine, with 444 files in Algorithm.Python replayed by Tests/RegressionTests.cs against per-algorithm expected statistics in dedicated regression and research-regression CI workflows.
verdicts.reason: Both the number and the mechanism are wrong. Algorithm.Python contains 444 directory entries but only 435 .py files, so 444 is a raw listing count, not an algorithm count. More importantly RegressionTests.cs (6203 bytes) does not enumerate or replay Algorithm.Python at all: GetLocalRegressionTestParameters calls GetRegressionTestParameters<IRegressionAlgorithmDefinition, ..., BasicTemplateAlgorithm>(canRunLocally: true), which reflects over typeof(J).Assembly.GetTypes() - the Algorithm.CSharp assembly - and then fans out per language via instance.Languages, filtered by instance.CanRunLocally. Python cases are therefore derived from C# definition classes, of which only 294 files in Algorithm.CSharp reference Language.Python (out of 826 .cs files). The fixture is also tagged Category("TravisExclude"). The regression-tests.yml and research-regression-tests.yml workflows do exist, and the harness is genuinely large, but the quantitative evidence as stated does not survive inspection of the cited file.

verdicts.claim: freqtrade is the only shortlisted project that ships first-class look-ahead and recursive bias-detection commands alongside a published list of its own backtest assumptions, including that fills ignore slippage inside the candle and that intra-candle path is always biased.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed on every element. docs/ contains both lookahead-analysis.md (7801 bytes) and recursive-analysis.md as first-class command documentation. docs/backtesting.md line 556 '## Assumptions made by backtesting' publishes ~20 named assumptions, including verbatim 'All orders are filled at the requested price (no slippage) as long as the price is within the candle's high/low range', 'Low happens before high for stoploss', and 'Stoploss is evaluated before ROI within one candle'; line 623 states backtesting 'can never be perfect, and will always be biased in one way or the other'. No other shortlisted engine (NautilusTrader, LEAN, qlib, vectorbt, backtesting.py, StockSharp) ships an equivalent bias-detection command. Scope caveat that does not refute the claim: freqtrade is crypto/exchange-oriented and has no equity corporate-action, borrow or point-in-time universe machinery, so its uniqueness here is orthogonal to the US-equity fidelity criteria.

verdicts.claim: LEAN is the only engine in this shortlist that implements US-equity point-in-time correctness inside the engine itself, shipping map files for ticker changes and delistings alongside factor files for splits and dividends, exposed through eight documented data-normalization modes.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed. Common/Data/Auxiliary ships MapFile.cs, MapFileRow.cs, MapFileResolver.cs, LocalDiskMapFileProvider.cs, LocalZipMapFileProvider.cs alongside FactorFile.cs, CorporateFactorProvider.cs, CorporateFactorRow.cs, IFactorProvider.cs and PriceScalingExtensions.cs - ticker-change/delisting mapping and split/dividend factors as first-class engine components. The DataNormalizationMode enum in Common/Global.cs has exactly eight members: Raw, Adjusted, SplitAdjusted, TotalReturn, ForwardPanamaCanal, BackwardsPanamaCanal, BackwardsRatio, ScaledRaw. Qualification worth recording: only five of the eight (Raw, Adjusted, SplitAdjusted, TotalReturn, ScaledRaw) apply to equities; the three Panama/Ratio modes are continuous-futures modes, so '(eight) exposed' overstates the equity-specific surface. A material operational caveat the claim omits: the map/factor/shortable data files are data-licensed, and the open-source repository ships only sample data, so the code path is free while the point-in-time data behind it is not.

verdicts.claim: LEAN is the only shortlisted engine with a first-class short-borrow availability model, providing IShortableProvider with an InteractiveBrokersShortableProvider implementation and paired C#/Python regression algorithms that assert short orders are rejected when borrow is unavailable.
verdicts.reason: Fully confirmed, element by element. Common/Interfaces/IShortableProvider.cs (2395 bytes) exists; Common/Data/Shortable/ contains InteractiveBrokersShortableProvider.cs, LocalDiskShortableProvider.cs, NullShortableProvider.cs and ShortableProviderPythonWrapper.cs; the paired rejection tests exist in both languages as Algorithm.CSharp/ShortableProviderOrdersRejectedRegressionAlgorithm.cs and Algorithm.Python/ShortableProviderOrdersRejectedRegressionAlgorithm.py, with further pairs CustomShortableProviderRegressionAlgorithm and AllShortableSymbolsCoarseSelectionRegressionAlgorithm; fixture borrow data ships under Data/equity/usa/shortable/testbrokerage/symbols/. No counter-example found: no other shortlisted engine exposes a borrow-availability interface. This was the single best-supported capability claim from either judge.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader has the most structurally enforced research-to-live parity of any open-source engine reviewed: BacktestEngine and LiveNode are both built on one NautilusKernel sharing messaging, data, risk, execution, portfolio and cache, and the backtest is documented as deterministic and single-threaded with k-way-merged timestamp-ordered replay, so runs are replayable event-for-event.
verdicts.reason: The mechanism is confirmed, though not by the source the judge cited (a company marketing blog post, the weakest evidence class offered in either judge's set). The primary source is docs/concepts/architecture.md: line 158 states 'Backtest, sandbox, and live systems share the NautilusKernel struct from the nautilus-system crate. The kernel owns the common cache, portfolio, engines, trader, clock, and messaging'; line 574 lists 'system: The kernel shared by backtest, sandbox, and live'; line 467 confirms 'the core consumes and dispatches messages on a single thread'. docs/concepts/backtesting/apis-and-runs.md line 42 confirms streams are ordered 'by replay timestamp' and merged 'chronologically during the run' (the words 'k-way' are the judge's, not the docs'). Two qualifications the claim glosses: determinism is conditional, since fill models draw randomly and the docs instruct 'Set random_seed when a run must reproduce the model's random draws'; and NautilusTrader's own live.md states the live runner 'does not define one global FIFO order', so event-for-event replay is a backtest property, not a live-parity guarantee.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader documents the most explicit open-source bar-execution lookahead safeguard - each bar's ts_init must represent the interval close so a complete bar cannot become visible before it formed - combined with eleven named fill models and a seedable slippage draw for reproducibility.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed precisely, including the count. docs/concepts/backtesting/bar-execution.md line 13 states each bar's initialization timestamp (ts_init) must represent the interval close, lines 19-20 give the two conventions (ts_init = ts_event at close, ts_init = ts_event + interval_ns at open), and lines 121-124 carry an explicit warning block 'Next-bar-open fills and look-ahead' noting that using the current bar's open from its on_bar callback would introduce look-ahead. docs/concepts/backtesting/fill-models.md '## Available models' lists exactly eleven: DefaultFillModel, BestPriceFillModel, OneTickSlippageFillModel, ProbabilisticFillModel, TwoTierFillModel, ThreeTierFillModel, LimitOrderPartialFillModel, SizeAwareFillModel, CompetitionAwareFillModel, VolumeSensitiveFillModel, MarketHoursFillModel; line 21 states 'Set random_seed when a run must reproduce the model's random draws'. Minor documented gap the claim omits: the same file notes Python bindings do not expose state setters for VolumeSensitiveFillModel or MarketHoursFillModel.

verdicts.claim: Microsoft Qlib is the only shortlisted repository with a dedicated point-in-time database for financial-report data, targeting fundamental-data lookahead (report availability date versus period date), which is the bias axis every price-level backtest engine in this shortlist leaves unaddressed.
verdicts.reason: The first half is supportable - docs/advanced/PIT.rst (7298 bytes) exists and Qlib is the only shortlisted repo with a purpose-built PIT store keyed on report period. The distinguishing second half is false. LEAN addresses exactly that axis in code: Common/Data/Fundamental/Generated/ ships FinancialStatementsFileDate.cs, EarningReportsFileDate.cs, BalanceSheetFileDate.cs and CashFlowFileDate.cs, whose XML summary reads 'Specific date on which a company released its filing to the public' - i.e. report availability date exposed separately from the reporting period, which is precisely the fundamental-data lookahead axis. QuantConnect's reconciliation documentation also names look-ahead bias explicitly as a documented difference category. So 'every price-level backtest engine in this shortlist leaves (it) unaddressed' is refuted by the top-ranked engine in the same shortlist.

survivors: NautilusTrader has the strongest supply-chain and provenance posture of any open-source trading engine in this shortlist (OpenSSF Scorecard, CodeQL, zizmor, cargo-deny/vet/audit, OSV Scanner, pip-audit, gitleaks, dedicated security-audit workflow with a required audit-result gate, SLSA provenance attestations, Sigstore cosign signing, SPDX SBOM) - strengthened, since LEAN ships no security workflow at all and StockSharp is not open source.

freqtrade is the only shortlisted project shipping first-class look-ahead and recursive bias-detection commands alongside a published list of its own backtest assumptions, including that fills ignore slippage inside the candle and that intra-candle path is always biased.

LEAN is the only engine in this shortlist implementing US-equity point-in-time correctness inside the engine itself, shipping map files for ticker changes and delistings alongside factor files for splits and dividends, exposed through eight DataNormalizationMode members (qualification: only five apply to equities; the point-in-time data behind the code path is separately licensed).

LEAN is the only shortlisted engine with a first-class short-borrow availability model: IShortableProvider, InteractiveBrokersShortableProvider, and paired C#/Python ShortableProviderOrdersRejectedRegressionAlgorithm tests asserting short-order rejection when borrow is unavailable. (Best-supported capability claim in the whole set.)

NautilusTrader has the most structurally enforced research-to-live parity of the engines reviewed: backtest, sandbox and live share one NautilusKernel owning cache, portfolio, engines, trader, clock and messaging, with a single-threaded core and timestamp-ordered merged replay (qualifications: determinism requires random_seed; the live runner explicitly does not define one global FIFO order; the judge's cited source was a marketing blog, not the docs).

NautilusTrader documents an explicit bar-execution lookahead safeguard (ts_init must represent the interval close, plus a named next-bar-open look-ahead warning) combined with exactly eleven named fill models and a seedable random draw.

better_alternatives_found.name: zipline-reloaded
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Absent from both judges' rankings despite being the most US-equity-native open-source event-driven engine after LEAN, and the only maintained descendant of Quantopian Zipline. It encodes several of this sub-layer's named fidelity criteria structurally rather than as data conventions: the asset database (src/zipline/assets: asset_writer.py, asset_db_schema.py, _assets.pyx) stores per-security start_date/end_date/auto_close_date lifetimes and sid-to-symbol mappings over time, which makes point-in-time universes and delisting handling a property of the asset layer rather than of the user's data; adjustment writers apply splits, dividends and mergers at read time. Apache-2.0, so cleaner licensing than backtesting.py (AGPL-3.0), vectorbt (NOASSERTION) or StockSharp (proprietary EULA). Honest caveats that keep it below LEAN and NautilusTrader: 1940 stars, last push 2026-01-06 (roughly 8.5 months stale as of 2026-09-21) with 44 open issues, no borrow/shortable model, no live trading path at all - so zero live/backtest parity - and no security or provenance CI. It belongs in the shortlist as the reference for equity asset-lifetime modelling, not as a destination.

better_alternatives_found.name: hftbacktest
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Absent from both rankings although it targets the highest-fidelity end of this sub-layer more directly than any ranked engine except NautilusTrader. Its own description states it 'accounts for limit orders, queue positions, and latencies, utilizing full tick data for trades and order books (Level-2 and Level-3)' - queue-position modelling and explicit feed/order latency models are fidelity dimensions that LEAN, qlib, vectorbt and backtesting.py do not model at all, and it ships a live trading bot sharing the backtest strategy interface, which is the same live/backtest parity argument made for NautilusTrader. Rust core with Python bindings, MIT licensed (cleaner than StockSharp, vectorbt or backtesting.py), 4746 stars. Caveats that stop it displacing the top two: last push 2025-12-23, about nine months stale as of 2026-09-21; it is crypto/derivatives-oriented with Binance and Bybit examples, so it has no corporate actions, no point-in-time equity universes, no borrow model and no multi-asset equity accounting. Relevant as the microstructure-fidelity benchmark to compare execution simulation against, not as a US-equity destination.

better_alternatives_found.name: pybroker
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Absent from both rankings and the most actively maintained Python equity-research backtester found outside the shortlist (3544 stars, pushed 2026-09-21, same day as LEAN and NautilusTrader). Its differentiator against every ranked engine is statistical validity tooling rather than execution fidelity: built-in walk-forward analysis with anchored/unanchored windows and bootstrapped confidence intervals and drawdown significance testing, which addresses overfitting - a research-validity axis the sub-layer's fidelity criteria do not cover and which neither judge scored. Flagged with a clear reservation: GitHub reports its license as NOASSERTION rather than a recognised OSI identifier, which needs legal review before adoption, and it has no borrow model, no map/factor-file corporate-action machinery and no live execution path, so it is a complement to a fidelity engine, not a replacement. Also surfaced but rejected during the same sweep: backtrader (23301 stars but last push 2024-08-19, effectively abandoned), StockSharp (10786 stars, ranked 3rd by one judge, but its LICENSE states 'This repository is not licensed under a general-purpose open source license' - proprietary EULA, which should disqualify it from an open-source shortlist), and backtesting.py (AGPL-3.0, a copyleft risk for any derived proprietary research stack).

limits: No GitHub API rate limits were hit: core remained at 5000/5000 remaining and search 30/30 remaining throughout (search API was not used; only repos/{owner}/{repo}, repos/.../releases/latest and repos/.../contents endpoints were called).

commands_run (231) is a reconstructed estimate, not an exact log: 60 repo-metadata calls + 60 releases/latest calls + 60 contents-root calls + 51 conditional repos/.../contents/.github/workflows calls (made only when a .github directory was present in the root listing) is the deterministic minimum; exact per-repo counts were not separately persisted.

has_tests/has_ci detection is a cheap heuristic (root-listing dir names + presence of a non-empty .github/workflows dir), not a manual audit of actual test coverage or CI health; one repo (quickfixj/quickfixj, an abandoned 1-star SVN mirror) returned 'unknown' for both because its contents listing was effectively empty.

License field is GitHub's automated SPDX detector (license.spdx_id), not a manual read of each repo's LICENSE file. Several well-known, actively-maintained, clearly-relevant repositories (StockSharp, the entire QuickFIX/QuickFIX-J/QuickFIX-Go/QuickFIX/n family, vectorbt, OpenBB, ricequant/rqalpha, edtechre/pybroker) were mechanically dropped only because GitHub reports NOASSERTION/none for their license, which can reflect a non-standard LICENSE format or dual/custom terms rather than an actual absence of licensing terms; this is flagged as a known mechanical-detection artifact per the user's bias-check request, not a manual confirmation that these projects are unlicensed.

The brief's 4 mechanical rules (not archived / recency / license / relevance) alone still left 32 of 60 candidates passing, well above the 'at most 12' cap. No tiebreak rule was specified in the brief, so stars-descending (a mechanical, non-subjective proxy already present in the required gh api fields) was applied as the cutoff among rule-passing candidates; this tiebreak choice, not a 5th mechanical filter, is why several rule-passing equities/IBKR-specific repos (ib_async, alpaca-py, ib-gateway-docker, alpaca-trade-api-js/go, schwab-py, AmpyFin, lumibot, investing-algorithm-framework, tfrmma OMS, uberdeveloper omspy) did not make the final 12 despite passing every stated rule.

Relevance was judged narrowly and literally against the sub-layer title ('Auto/live trading runtimes and broker integration ... live nodes, broker adapters, OMS, execution algorithms, pre-trade risk, reconciliation, paper-trading, rate handling'): pure backtest-only libraries (backtesting.py, vectorbt row not evaluated for relevance since it was already license-dropped, zipline-reloaded), market-data-only clients (polygon wrapper), and curated meta-lists/awesome-lists (awesome-systematic-trading, best-of-algorithmic-trading) were dropped on relevance even though several passed the other 3 rules, since they are not themselves runtimes/adapters/OMS components.

kungfu-systems/kungfu was flagged in the input candidate list as repurposed away from trading; the live gh api description ('Your agents don't hand off the work... across Codex, Claude, OpenCode...') independently confirms it is now an agent-orchestration project, not a trading runtime, so it was dropped on relevance despite passing the other 3 rules.

Per the BLINDNESS RULE, no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> was opened and no prior project selection (e.g. NautilusTrader/IBKR/Alpaca as 'the' destination) was used to weight or exclude any candidate; all filtering above used only gh api-derived facts (stars, pushed_at, archived, license, releases, contents) and the sub-layer's own stated relevance criteria.

tavily CLI was not invoked because the supplied CANDIDATES list already covered independent web/GitHub/awesome-list discovery modalities per the brief; all verification work here was the required per-candidate gh api mechanical pass, not additional discovery.

judges.lens: Engineering quality applied to the T-runtimes sub-layer (US-equities auto/live trading runtimes and broker integration). I gated every score on sub-layer fit first — a repository that cannot reach a US-equities broker cannot be a US-equities runtime however well engineered it is — then judged code/test/CI health, release discipline, API stability, documentation depth, dependency and platform hygiene (Linux/WSL2, Python 3.12+, local-first), security/provenance, and maintainer organisation. All evidence is public GitHub API/raw-file and public API output read on 2026-09-21; I opened no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> and used no project-internal selection. Scores are per-repository only; I computed no averages or aggregates.

scores.notes: Strongest sub-layer fit in the set. crates/adapters holds an in-core interactive_brokers adapter (Data/Execution per ADAPTERS.md) plus databento (US equities/futures data); crates/execution/src contains dedicated reconciliation/, order_manager/, order_emulator/, matching_engine/, protection.rs and trailing.rs; crates/risk/src has engine/ and sizing.rs; crates/live/src has node/, execution/ and fuzz/. Pre-trade risk, OMS, execution algorithms, sandbox matching and reconciliation are therefore all in-core rather than bolted on. python/pyproject.toml declares requires-python >=3.12,<3.15 and classifiers for 3.12/3.13/3.14 — the only shortlisted Python runtime that targets 3.12+ as its floor. License is LGPL-3.0-only with license-files declared. Test tree is segmented (tests/{unit,integration,acceptance,memleak,persistence,strategies}) and CI is 11 workflows including openssf-scorecard.yml, security-audit.yml, codeql-analysis.yml, nightly-tests.yml and performance.yml; test.yml pins every action to a full SHA and runs step-security/harden-runner with an egress-block policy. Supply-chain artefacts present at root: deny.toml, osv-scanner.toml, .gitleaks.toml, .supply-chain/, SECURITY.md, AI_POLICY.md. Live OpenSSF Scorecard 8.5 (scanned 2026-09-19, scorecard v5.5.0). 100+ commits on develop in the trailing 90 days; v2.0.0rc5 released 2026-09-15 with rc6 already in-tree. quality_cost is 2, not 3, for one measured reason: the v2 release-candidate line carries a long Breaking Changes block per rc (RELEASES.md rc6 lists ~12 breaking API changes including ParquetDataCatalog signature changes and ExecutionEngine::register_client routing changes), so API stability is currently a real adoption cost, compounded by a Rust/maturin toolchain. Docs are deep: docs/concepts (37 entries incl. execution/, live.md, portfolio.md, accounting.md) and docs/integrations (19 per-venue pages). Notably, reconciliation is not just present but enforced — rc6 changed live node startup to fail when in-scope nonzero venue positions remain unrecovered, and bounds reconciliation_startup_delay_secs at 86,400s.

ThetaGang is the most thoroughly tested IBKR-native live trading runtime in the set relative to its size, with 33 pytest modules covering order execution, IBKR wiring, trades, portfolio management, exchange hours and the connection watchdog, on a fully locked uv/ruff/alembic toolchain supporting Python 3.11 through 3.14.

limits: Shortlist coverage is incomplete for this sub-layer: probing GitHub directly surfaced at least four US-equities-relevant runtimes absent from the twelve — Lumiwealth/lumibot (2,079 stars, GPL-3.0, pushed 2026-09-21), StockSharp/StockSharp (10,786 stars, .NET, pushed 2026-09-19), ib-api-reloaded/ib_async (1,742 stars, BSD-2-Clause, the IBKR client that both thetagang and pysystemtrade depend on) and alpacahq/alpaca-py (1,526 stars, the official Alpaca SDK). Six of the twelve shortlisted repositories cannot reach any US-equities venue at all, so the mechanical star-ranked shortlist is biased toward crypto by construction.

I executed nothing: no repository was cloned, installed, built or run, and no paper or live order was placed. Every score rests on repository text, file-tree structure and GitHub/OpenSSF API metadata read on 2026-09-21. Runtime correctness, fill quality, latency, rate-limit behaviour and reconciliation-after-disconnect are therefore unmeasured for all twelve.

Test presence was judged from directory listings and workflow definitions, not from coverage reports or CI run results. I did not query recent workflow-run outcomes, so 'has CI' does not mean 'CI is green', and file counts are a proxy for depth, not a measure of it. This cuts both ways in my scores: vnpy's listed test directory turned out to contain only factor-research tests, while ccxt and hftbacktest have tests the shortlist metadata recorded as absent.

Release cadence for QuantConnect Lean was inferred from its README's NuGet and Docker Hub links plus the org-wide same-timestamp push pattern; I did not query nuget.org or Docker Hub, so the actual published package cadence and the availability of pinnable engine versions remain unverified.

Licence assessments come from GitHub's detected SPDX field and in-repo LICENSE files only; no legal review was performed, and the Lean.Brokerages.Alpaca licence gap is reported as an observed absence of a LICENSE file (API returns license: null), not as a determination of the code's actual licensing status.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for a US-equities auto/live trading runtime: does the repository actually provide a live node, US-equities broker adapters, OMS/execution algorithms, pre-trade risk, reconciliation, paper/live parity and point-in-time correctness safeguards (survivorship-free symbol mapping, corporate-action adjustment, costs), and what upstream tests, published artefacts or documented failure modes support the claim. Every judgment below comes from public GitHub/API/doc reads dated on or before 2026-09-21 (a few pushed_at timestamps read as 2026-09-22 UTC). Asset-class mismatch is scored under capability_fit; license_deployment_fit scores licence permissiveness plus self-hostability only, so a crypto-only tool can still score well there — read the two together.

scores.notes: Deepest documented live-operations model of the twelve. docs/concepts/execution/reconciliation.md defines startup state recovery from venue reports plus continuous runtime consistency checks, with LiveNode owning an ExecutionManager that tracks retries and fill identities; docs/concepts/live.md documents external-order creation, node lifecycle, coordinated startup abort and explicit non-guarantees (the runner does not automatically throttle a feed or halt trading). Execution algorithms exist natively (docs/concepts/execution/algorithms.md, Rust TWAP with spawned-order management); crates/ contains separate risk, execution, live, portfolio and adapters crates. docs/integrations/interactive_brokers.md documents TWS/Gateway paper ports (4002/7497) versus live (4001/7496), defaults to the paper port, and supports a Dockerized gateway with TradingMode.PAPER and read_only_api. examples/live/ includes interactive_brokers, databento and a sandbox target. ADAPTERS.md codifies Official/Community/External adapter tiers and demotion. Concrete open US-equities failure modes temper quality_cost: 'Rust IB adapter: execution client venue IB never matches instrument venue SMART, so every stock order is denied locally' (2026-09-12), 'Execution callback can lose submitted client_order_id mapping and materialize duplicate reconciliation order' (2026-09-10), 'No liveness detection for subscriptions that are open but delivering no data' (2026-09-08), 'Detect duplicate live orders after modify during connectivity loss' (2026-07-24). LGPL-3.0 permits linking proprietary strategy code.

scores.notes: Excluded from the sub-layer on venue coverage, but the strongest execution-realism methodology in the shortlist and the right reference for anyone judging fill assumptions. It models feed latency, order latency and order queue position over full L2 market-by-price and L3 market-by-order feeds, and argues explicitly that a backtest of a given month must reproduce that month's live results before any further research is credible. Live deployment is the limiting factor: 'currently for Binance Futures and Bybit. (Rust-only)', and connector/src contains exactly binancefutures, binancespot and bybit — no US equities broker. Pushed 2025-12-23, release rust-v0.9.4 2025-12-10, so it is the least recently advanced of the shortlist; MIT, readthedocs documentation with tutorials.

unknowns: No US-equities or broker path exists at all; whether the dry-run abstraction could be retargeted to a broker is not established.
Corporate actions, survivorship and point-in-time equity correctness are out of scope by construction.
scores.notes: Best published-evidence profile of the twelve and zero task fit. The README badges a JOSS peer-reviewed paper (DOI 10.21105/joss.04864), codecov coverage and a CI workflow, plus a full readthedocs site — a genuinely higher evidence class than the self-documented projects here. But the supported venues are crypto spot and futures exchanges only (Binance, Bybit, Gate, HTX, Hyperliquid, Bitget, BingX…), and its parity mechanism is dry-run against an exchange, not paper-to-live broker parity. GPL-3.0. Useful as a maturity benchmark for CI and documentation practice, not as a US-equities runtime.

unknowns: The '$34 billion in trading volume across 140+ venues' figure in the README is self-reported and unaudited.
No US-equities broker path; whether the connector abstraction could carry a broker order lifecycle is not established.
scores.notes: Crypto CEX/DEX market-making framework: hummingbot/connector splits into exchange, derivative, gateway and test_support with a shared budget_checker, client_order_tracker, trading_rule and time_synchronizer — real OMS and pre-trade-check machinery, but the connector taxonomy is explicitly 'CLOB CEX / AMM DEX / CLOB DEX'. Parity is provided as per-exchange paper-trade modes (e.g. exchange=binance_paper_trade), which is a venue-simulation shim rather than an engine-level backtest-to-live path. Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-09-20, v2.16.0 2026-07-29.

unknowns: No US-equities or broker support; README scopes it as 'an advanced crypto trading framework'.
The 'without look-ahead bias' claim for multi-timeframe/multi-symbol backtesting is asserted in the README; I found no test or published study substantiating it.
No GitHub Release object exists, so version provenance rests on commits and PyPI only.
scores.notes: Clean lifecycle story in the wrong asset class: a single strategy definition runs backtest, paper and live with the same interactive charting across all three session types, plus multi-account support, spot/futures and DEX. Repo has tests/, conftest.py, codecov.yml and CI, is MIT licensed and pushed 2026-09-21 with only 16 open issues. Nothing in it addresses US-equities brokers, corporate actions or reconciliation.

unknowns: Test suite: shortlist metadata records has_tests=no and I did not verify one; CI exists.
No US-equities broker and no equity instrument model.
scores.notes: Category mismatch twice over: it is a unified market-access library, not a runtime (no engine, no strategy lifecycle, no pre-trade risk engine, no reconciliation), and its coverage is '100+ cryptocurrency exchanges and prediction markets'. Lifecycle portability scores 0 because there is no backtest or paper layer to be portable between. Provenance is excellent — MIT, v4.5.82 released 2026-09-21, multi-language bindings, an official MCP server with opt-in trading tiers and notional caps — and 693 open issues reflect surface area rather than neglect. Relevant to this sub-layer only as a reference for adapter normalisation design.

unknowns: Whether any US-equities broker adapter is planned or exists outside the broker/ tree.
Point-in-time correctness, corporate actions and survivorship are not addressed anywhere I read.
Depth of the sandbox mode (dhan_sandbox) as a parity mechanism is not established.
scores.notes: Disqualified for this sub-layer by broker geography, not by quality. Enumerating broker/ gives 36 plugins — aliceblue, angel, dhan, fyers, groww, hdfcsecurities, iifl, kotak, motilal, paytm, samco, shoonya, upstox, zerodha and so on — i.e. 35 Indian securities brokers plus Delta Exchange for crypto derivatives; the README states this composition outright. The platform layer itself is credible (unified /api/v1 contract across plugins, ZMQ-normalised WebSocket market data, semi-auto mode requiring manual approval before broker execution, a latency monitor for order round-trip times), and it is very actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-22), but there is no US broker and no US-equities evidence. AGPL-3.0 plus 318 open issues.

sota_claims.claim: Lean is the only repository in this shortlist that ships US-equities point-in-time correctness machinery in-tree — survivorship-free ticker map files and corporate-action factor files under Data/equity/usa, resolved by Common/Data/Auxiliary (MapFileResolver, CorporateFactorProvider, PriceScalingExtensions) — rather than delegating it to an external data vendor.

Lean has the broadest set of separately maintained, separately tested open-source US-equities brokerage adapters of any shortlisted engine — Interactive Brokers, Alpaca, TradeStation, Tradier, Tastytrade and Wolverine repositories in the QuantConnect organisation, all pushed on 2026-09-21, each with its own test project — plus an in-engine PaperBrokerage for the same algorithm code path.

NautilusTrader has the most thoroughly specified open-source execution-reconciliation model in this shortlist: a dedicated docs/concepts/execution/reconciliation.md defining startup state recovery from venue reports, continuous runtime consistency checks, snapshot-freshness fill corrections and command-outcome classification for unknown live results — a layer the other eleven repositories either omit or leave undocumented.

NautilusTrader's US-equities broker coverage is Interactive Brokers only as of 2026-09-21 — Alpaca exists solely as open RFC issue #3374 (created 2026-01-01, unmerged) — and its Rust IB path carries an open defect in which the execution client venue IB never matches the instrument venue SMART, denying every stock order locally (issue dated 2026-09-12); any Alpaca or Rust-IB stock claim about this engine should be treated as unproven.

hftbacktest is the shortlist's state of the art for execution-realism modelling — order queue position plus separate feed and order latency over full L2 market-by-price and L3 market-by-order feeds — but it is not a US-equities runtime: its live deployment supports only Binance Futures and Bybit (connector/src contains binancefutures, binancespot, bybit) and it was last pushed 2025-12-23.

limits: Discovery was confined to the 12 repositories handed to me by the shortlist; I did not search for additional US-equities runtime candidates, so this is not comprehensive SOTA coverage of the sub-layer. Notable classes absent from the shortlist and therefore unjudged here: broker-native SDKs (alpaca-py, alpaca-trade-api, ib_insync/ib_async, ibapi, tastytrade, schwab-py), Alpaca's own example runtimes, and Python engines such as backtrader, zipline-reloaded, lumibot or QuantRocket.

All scores rest on repository self-documentation (READMEs, docs/, directory listings, issue titles, CI workflow filenames) and GitHub API metadata. I executed no code, installed nothing, ran no upstream test suite and placed no paper order, so every 3 for 'evidence' means abundant cited upstream artefacts, never a measured result I reproduced.

For several repositories I inferred test strength from directory listings and workflow filenames rather than from a passing run or a coverage number; the shortlist's mechanical has_tests flag contradicts in-repo evidence for ccxt and nautilus_trader, and I did not resolve that contradiction.

Documented failure modes come from open GitHub issue titles only; I did not read issue bodies or check whether a fix has since landed on a development branch, so the severity and current status of the Nautilus IB defects are unverified beyond the titles and dates.

Third-party evidence gathering was thin: one Tavily search returned mostly low-quality secondary content (SEO blogs, social posts), so essentially no independent user-reported failure data or external benchmark informs these scores. Claims about backtest-to-live parity are architectural claims from upstream, not independently measured.

Corporate actions, survivorship bias and point-in-time correctness were verified affirmatively only for Lean (map/factor files). For every other repository, including NautilusTrader, these are recorded as unknown rather than absent — I did not read the accounting, instrument or data-catalog documentation that might establish them.
Licence judgments are surface readings of the declared SPDX identifier (LGPL-3.0, AGPL-3.0, GPL-3.0) and are not legal advice about linking proprietary strategy code or hosted deployment.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader is the only shortlisted repository that ships an in-core, maintainer-supported Interactive Brokers data-and-execution adapter alongside a dedicated execution-reconciliation module, a risk engine with position sizing, an order emulator and a sandbox matching engine in the same codebase.
verdicts.reason: The conjunction survives, but the cited source does not prove it and one component of it is false standalone. Verified independently: crates/adapters contains interactive_brokers and sandbox; crates/ contains risk, execution, live, portfolio, trading; docs/concepts/execution/reconciliation.md exists. Counter-evidence against the 'only in-core IBKR adapter' element taken alone: pysystemtrade also ships an in-core IBKR data-and-execution adapter (sysbrokers/IB with ib_orders.py, ib_positions.py, ib_futures_contract_price_data.py, ib_connection.py) plus sysproduction/reporting/reconcile_report.py and position sizing; it merely lacks the emulator and sandbox. vnpy core genuinely has no in-tree gateways (vnpy/ contains only alpha, chart, event, rpc, trader), and Lean's IB adapter is a separate repo, so the full conjunction holds. Material qualification the claim omits: the risk engine's pre-trade checks are the subject of open defect #4946 (2026-09-08) 'Risk engine silently skips all account-scoped pre-trade checks for broker-routed instruments' — i.e. the risk-engine component exists but is documented as not firing on broker-routed instruments, which is exactly the US-equities/SMART path.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader has the strongest measured supply-chain posture in this sub-layer, with a live OpenSSF Scorecard of 8.5 (scanned 2026-09-19) backed by full SHA-pinned GitHub Actions, step-security/harden-runner egress blocking, CodeQL, osv-scanner, cargo-deny and gitleaks in-tree.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed against primary sources and against every comparator I could measure. Scorecard API returns score 8.5, date 2026-09-19T12:38:18Z. Comparators pulled from the same API on 2026-09-21: QuantConnect/Lean 4.9, vnpy/vnpy 4.5, brndnmtthws/thetagang 4.5, Lumiwealth/lumibot 5.5, pst-group/pysystemtrade has no scorecard at all. Tooling verified in-tree: .github/workflows/build.yml and security-audit.yml pin every third-party action by full SHA (step-security/harden-runner@e14015d..., actions/checkout@3d3c42e..., astral-sh/setup-uv@20cfd1b...) and start each job with harden-runner; security-audit.yml references osv-scanner.toml, scripts/install-osv-scanner.sh, ~/.cargo/bin/cargo-deny and runs zizmor with SARIF upload to github/codeql-action; codeql-analysis.yml exists; .gitleaks.toml is at repo root. Two caveats the claim's wording glosses: the Scorecard Code-Review sub-check scores 1/10 ('Found 5/30 approved changesets'), so the maintainer-review gate is measurably weak despite the 8.5 aggregate, and Pinned-Dependencies scores 7/10 ('dependency not pinned by hash detected'), so 'full SHA-pinned' is true of GitHub Actions specifically but not of all dependencies.

verdicts.claim: QuantConnect Lean has the broadest actively-maintained US-equities brokerage surface of any shortlisted engine — Alpaca, Interactive Brokers, Tradier, TradeStation, Tastytrade and Wolverine plugins were all non-archived and pushed within the same 2026-09-21 release sweep as the engine itself.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed literally, and the 'actively maintained' part survives a harder test than the one the claim used. org:QuantConnect search returns Lean.Brokerages.{InteractiveBrokers,Alpaca,Tradier,TradeStation,Tastytrade,Wolverine} all archived=false with pushed_at 2026-09-21T23:17:40-41Z, identical to Lean's own. That identical timestamp is an automated CI sweep and by itself proves nothing, so I pulled commit histories: Alpaca (2026-09-15 deployment flag, 2026-08-24 paper-env detection, 2026-07-10 SDK bump, 2026-07-08 renamed-ticker symbol mapper), Tastytrade (2026-09-18 x2, 2026-09-16 websocket reconnect, 2026-09-15, 2026-09-10), TradeStation (2026-09-15, 2026-08-06, 2026-07-30) all show real human feature/fix work. Wolverine is the thin one: 6 commits spanning 2026-02-04 to 2026-09-15. Omission the claim should have carried: Lean.Brokerages.Alpaca, TradeStation, Tastytrade and Wolverine all report license spdx_id NONE and carry no LICENSE file in their root listing, while InteractiveBrokers and Tradier are Apache-2.0 — a deployment-licensing hole across most of the 'broadest surface'.

verdicts.claim: No shortlisted engine ships an official in-core Alpaca adapter as of 2026-09-21: NautilusTrader's Alpaca integration remains an open RFC (#3374, opened 2026-01-01, last updated 2026-05-08) and Lean's Alpaca support lives in a separate plugin repository that carries no LICENSE file.
verdicts.reason: The two sub-facts are exactly right; the blanket headline is overbroad. Confirmed: issue #3374 '[RFC] Alpaca Markets Integration' is state=open, created 2026-01-01T15:40:49Z, updated 2026-05-08T18:27:03Z, closed_at null; crates/adapters contains no alpaca directory; Lean.Brokerages.Alpaca root listing is .github/.gitignore/QuantConnect.AlpacaBrokerage{,.Tests,.sln}/README.md/alpaca.json with no LICENSE and spdx NONE. But Lean's core Apache-2.0 repository does ship in-core Alpaca support: Common/Brokerages/AlpacaBrokerageModel.cs, Common/Orders/Fees/AlpacaFeeModel.cs, Common/Orders/AlpacaOrderProperties.cs, Engine/Results/Analysis/.../AlpacaBrokerageModel/TradingOutsideRegularHoursNotSupportedAnalysis.cs, plus Tests/Common/Brokerages/AlpacaBrokerageModelTests.cs and Tests/Common/Orders/Fees/AlpacaFeeModelTests.cs. Only the connectivity layer is external. Separately, the 'no engine ships one' framing is an artifact of the shortlist, not of the sub-layer: Lumibot ships lumibot/brokers/alpaca.py in-core under GPL-3.0 alongside interactive_brokers.py, schwab.py and tradier.py.

verdicts.claim: ThetaGang is the most thoroughly tested IBKR-native live trading runtime in the set relative to its size, with 33 pytest modules covering order execution, IBKR wiring, trades, portfolio management, exchange hours and the connection watchdog, on a fully locked uv/ruff/alembic toolchain supporting Python 3.11 through 3.14.
verdicts.reason: The count is wrong and the category is wrong. tests/ contains 33 files but only 32 are test modules — the 33rd is __init__.py. The named coverage is real (test_order_execution.py, test_ibkr.py, test_trades.py, test_portfolio_manager.py, test_exchange_hours.py, test_thetagang_watchdog.py all exist), and pyproject.toml confirms requires-python '>=3.11,<3.15', alembic>=1.13, ib-async>=2.0.1 and a uv dependency-group. The substantive refutation is 'live trading runtime': pyproject.toml's own description reads 'ThetaGang is an IBKR bot for getting money' — it is a covered-call/cash-secured-put wheel strategy bot, not a general US-equities runtime. It has no broker-adapter abstraction (it calls ib-async directly), no pre-trade risk engine, no execution-reconciliation module and no paper/live parity layer, so it does not compete on this sub-layer's definition. The superlative also fails once the comparator set is widened beyond the shortlist: Lumibot is IBKR-native in-core and ships 308 test files.

verdicts.claim: Lean is the only repository in this shortlist that ships US-equities point-in-time correctness machinery in-tree — survivorship-free ticker map files and corporate-action factor files under Data/equity/usa, resolved by Common/Data/Auxiliary (MapFileResolver, CorporateFactorProvider, PriceScalingExtensions) — rather than delegating it to an external data vendor.
verdicts.reason: The code half is confirmed, the data half is false. Common/Data/Auxiliary does contain MapFile.cs, MapFileResolver.cs, LocalDiskMapFileProvider.cs, LocalZipMapFileProvider.cs, CorporateFactorProvider.cs, FactorFile.cs, PriceScalingExtensions.cs, MappingContractFactorProvider.cs — real in-tree machinery, and no other shortlisted repo has an equivalent. But Data/equity/usa/map_files holds only 26 files and Data/equity/usa/factor_files only 22, covering a handful of demo tickers (aaa.csv 30 bytes, aapl.csv, aig.csv, bac.csv, bno.csv, eem.csv, fb.1.csv 24 bytes). That is a unit-test fixture set, not a survivorship-free US-equities universe. The production map/factor dataset is not in the repository; it is obtained from QuantConnect's own data marketplace, i.e. the point-in-time data IS delegated to a vendor — exactly what the claim says Lean avoids. The claim conflates shipping the resolver with shipping the dataset.

verdicts.claim: Lean has the broadest set of separately maintained, separately tested open-source US-equities brokerage adapters of any shortlisted engine — Interactive Brokers, Alpaca, TradeStation, Tradier, Tastytrade and Wolverine repositories in the QuantConnect organisation, all pushed on 2026-09-21, each with its own test project — plus an in-engine PaperBrokerage for the same algorithm code path.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed on every element. All six repos are non-archived with pushed_at 2026-09-21T23:17:40-41Z; each carries its own test project (verified for Alpaca: QuantConnect.AlpacaBrokerage.Tests contains AlpacaBrokerageTests.cs, AlpacaBrokerageDataQueueHandlerTests.cs, AlpacaBrokerageHistoryProviderTests.cs, AlpacaBrokerageSymbolMapperTests.cs, AlpacaBrokerageFactoryTests.cs); and the in-engine paper path exists as Brokerages/Paper/PaperBrokerage.cs, PaperBrokerageFactory.cs with Tests/Brokerages/Paper/PaperBrokerageTests.cs. The one word I would strike is 'open-source': four of the six named repos (Alpaca, TradeStation, Tastytrade, Wolverine) have no LICENSE file and report spdx NONE, so they are source-available rather than licensed open source, and only InteractiveBrokers and Tradier are Apache-2.0.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader has the most thoroughly specified open-source execution-reconciliation model in this shortlist: a dedicated docs/concepts/execution/reconciliation.md defining startup state recovery from venue reports, continuous runtime consistency checks, snapshot-freshness fill corrections and command-outcome classification for unknown live results — a layer the other eleven repositories either omit or leave undocumented.
verdicts.reason: The substantive part holds; the universal quantifier is not supported by the cited source and should be softened. Confirmed: docs/concepts/execution/ contains algorithms.md, index.md, policies.md and reconciliation.md — a dedicated design document, which no comparator has. Counter-evidence I looked for and could not make stick: Lean's equivalent is code plus tests rather than a design doc (Engine/TransactionHandlers/BrokerageTransactionHandler.cs with Tests/Engine/BrokerageTransactionHandlerTests/), and pysystemtrade ships sysproduction/reporting/reconcile_report.py — so 'omit' is wrong for at least two of the eleven, but 'leave undocumented as a specified model' is fair. Note the cited source proves only that Nautilus's own file exists; the comparative half rests on my enumeration, not on that URL.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader's US-equities broker coverage is Interactive Brokers only as of 2026-09-21 — Alpaca exists solely as open RFC issue #3374 (created 2026-01-01, unmerged) — and its Rust IB path carries an open defect in which the execution client venue IB never matches the instrument venue SMART, denying every stock order locally (issue dated 2026-09-12); any Alpaca or Rust-IB stock claim about this engine should be treated as unproven.
verdicts.reason: Fully confirmed, and I found corroborating evidence the claim did not cite. crates/adapters lists architect_ax, betfair, binance, bitmex, blockchain, bybit, coinbase, databento, deribit, derive, dydx, hyperliquid, interactive_brokers, kraken, lighter, okx, polymarket, sandbox, tardis — IB is the only US-equities broker and there is no alpaca crate. Issue #3374 is state=open, closed_at null. Issue #4983 'Rust IB adapter: execution client venue `IB` never matches instrument venue `SMART`, so every stock order is denied locally' is state=open, created 2026-09-12T16:19:39Z. Additional corroboration: #4946 (open, 2026-09-08) 'Risk engine silently skips all account-scoped pre-trade checks for broker-routed instruments' and #4973 (open, 2026-09-11) '[Interactive Brokers] IneligibilityReason in contract details cannot be serialized into the cache database'. Note the earlier closed #4122 (2026-05-23) describes the same venue-mismatch class on the Python path, so this is a recurring rather than novel defect.

verdicts.claim: hftbacktest is the shortlist's state of the art for execution-realism modelling — order queue position plus separate feed and order latency over full L2 market-by-price and L3 market-by-order feeds — but it is not a US-equities runtime: its live deployment supports only Binance Futures and Bybit (connector/src contains binancefutures, binancespot, bybit) and it was last pushed 2025-12-23.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed exactly as stated. connector/src contains binancefutures, binancespot, bybit, connector.rs, main.rs, utils.rs — no equities venue of any kind. The repository API reports pushed_at 2025-12-23T15:57:58Z, archived=false, 18 open issues, MIT — so roughly nine months of no pushes as of 2026-09-21, which makes it the least-maintained repo in the set and independently disqualifies it as a live US-equities runtime regardless of its queue-position modelling quality.

survivors: NautilusTrader ships an in-core IBKR adapter alongside reconciliation, risk, order emulator and sandbox in one codebase (conjunction holds; the 'only in-core IBKR adapter' element alone is false — pysystemtrade has one too)

NautilusTrader has the strongest measured supply-chain posture in the sub-layer: OpenSSF 8.5 (2026-09-19) vs Lean 4.9, lumibot 5.5, vnpy 4.5, thetagang 4.5, pysystemtrade unscored — caveat Code-Review sub-check 1/10

Lean has the broadest actively-maintained US-equities brokerage surface among shortlisted engines (IB, Alpaca, Tradier, TradeStation, Tastytrade, Wolverine), independently confirmed by real 2026 commit histories, not just the CI push sweep

Lean's brokerage adapters are separately maintained and separately tested and Lean ships an in-engine PaperBrokerage on the same algorithm code path (strike 'open-source': 4 of 6 adapter repos have no LICENSE)

NautilusTrader has the most thoroughly specified execution-reconciliation design document in the set (docs/concepts/execution/reconciliation.md); the 'other eleven omit it' quantifier is overstated but the uniqueness of a dedicated spec holds
NautilusTrader's US-equities coverage is IBKR-only, Alpaca is an unmerged open RFC (#3374), and the Rust IB path has open defect #4983 (2026-09-12) denying every stock order locally
hftbacktest is execution-realism SOTA but is not a US-equities runtime: connectors are Binance/Bybit only and it has not been pushed since 2025-12-23

better_alternatives_found.name: Lumibot (Lumiwealth/lumibot)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Found via GitHub topic:algorithmic-trading and topic:trading-bot searches; absent from both judges' rankings yet it plausibly beats thetagang, pysystemtrade and vnpy on this sub-layer and is the only candidate that closes the exact gap both judges flagged for Nautilus and Lean. It ships every US-equities broker adapter IN-CORE under a single GPL-3.0 licence — lumibot/brokers/{alpaca.py, interactive_brokers.py, interactive_brokers_rest.py, schwab.py, tradier.py, tradovate.py, projectx.py} — so it has an official in-core Alpaca adapter (which no shortlisted engine has), both IBKR TWS and IBKR Web/REST paths, plus Schwab, which Lean's plugin set lacks entirely. It is actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-21, release v4.5.91 on 2026-09-06 on a rapid release cadence), carries 308 test files, has one backtesting/live code path via lumibot/backtesting + lumibot/traders, and scores OpenSSF 5.5 (2026-09-21) — above Lean's 4.9. Weaknesses a fair comparison must record: GPL-3.0 is more restrictive than Lean's Apache-2.0 and Nautilus's LGPL-3.0; 90 open issues; no published execution-reconciliation specification comparable to Nautilus's; no in-tree point-in-time map/factor machinery; and the very high release velocity (v4.5.88 to v4.5.91 inside three weeks) suggests weaker API stability than either ranked engine.

better_alternatives_found.name: StockSharp (evaluated and REJECTED — recorded so it is not re-proposed)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Surfaced repeatedly in topic searches as the largest multi-broker trading platform outside the rankings (10,786 stars, pushed 2026-09-19, C#, 70+ connectors including Interactive Brokers and Alpaca), which would superficially beat Lean's brokerage-surface claim. It does not qualify: its root LICENSE is not an open-source licence but a 'StockSharp Custom License Notice' stating that all source, binaries, documentation and examples are 'the proprietary property of StockSharp' and that 'This repository is not licensed under a general-purpose open source license', restricting viewing, copying, building, modifying, using and distributing. GitHub reports the licence as NOASSERTION for this reason. It therefore fails the self-hostable open-source gate that every ranked candidate meets, and no US-equities brokerage-breadth claim should be conceded to it.

GitHub code search API caps results at 1000 total per query and ranks primarily by stars, so very new/low-star SOTA strategy repos (e.g. recent single-paper reproductions) are systematically under-represented; this biases the list toward already-popular, English- and Chinese-language-dominant projects.

Search results conflate adjacent sub-layers (general trading platforms, curated awesome-lists, job-board repos) with pure strategy-research repos; candidates were manually filtered to keep only genuine strategy/validation/prediction-research relevance.
30/min GitHub search rate limit was respected via ~2.5s sleeps between calls; no rate-limit errors were hit.

GitHub code search / REST search API results for niche queries (e.g. 'awesome reinforcement learning trading', 'deflated sharpe ratio combinatorial purged cross validation') are dominated by very-low-star or auto-generated/spam-like repos (0-35 stars), reflecting the current state of GitHub's search relevance for this niche rather than a lack of real candidates; higher-quality items for those sub-areas were instead sourced from curated awesome-list entries and cross-referenced star counts.

wilsonfreitas/awesome-quant's live README currently contains a substantial number of very new, low-provenance entries (freshly created repos, some with promotional-sounding descriptions) alongside long-established projects; candidates pulled from it were filtered to those with independently verified, non-trivial star counts and recent legitimate activity via gh api, to avoid propagating list-submission bias.

georgezouq/awesome-ai-in-finance is largely stale (many entries last updated 2018-2020, dominated by small Gekko-bot and toy-RL repos) and was used mainly for historical/RL context, not as a primary source of current SOTA candidates.

Did not independently fetch a 5th/6th awesome list beyond the four named plus one GitHub-search-discovered list (LLMQuant/awesome-trading-agents); broader coverage of niche sub-areas (e.g. purely academic RL-trading benchmarks, CPCV/deflated-Sharpe standalone tooling) is thinner than the LLM-agent-trading area given time constraints.

GitHub API search rate limits were not hit (well under 30/min search, 5000/h core) but only a bounded number of search queries were run; some possible sub-layer angles (e.g. dedicated walk-forward-analysis-only repos, academic RL-trading paper-code repos beyond FinRL family) were not exhaustively enumerated.

sota_claims.claim: Among the shortlisted strategy-research repositories, machine-learning-for-trading is the only one that implements the modern strategy-validation methodology named in this sub-layer (combinatorial purged cross-validation, deflated Sharpe, walk-forward, embargo/leakage detection) as named, CI-executed tests rather than prose - in-repo code search returns 61 hits for 'deflated sharpe', 56 for 'purged' and 68 for 'walk_forward', against 0 for each in both microsoft/qlib and microsoft/RD-Agent.

Vibe-Trading has the largest executed test surface in this set (690 Python test files) and the only CI that verifies hash-locked dependencies across Linux x64, macOS ARM64 and Windows x64 in addition to a Python 3.11/3.14 pytest-with-coverage matrix, with a green run on main dated 2026-09-21.

Qlib is the most complete organisation-backed open-source factor/alpha research platform in this set, and the only one whose CI separately tests the published PyPI wheel and the source tree (test_qlib_from_pip.yml alongside test_qlib_from_source.yml and a slow variant) - though its own README now routes LLM-driven factor generation to RD-Agent, and it has shipped no release since v0.9.7 on 2025-08-15.

RD-Agent reports the strongest quantified automated-factor-research result in this set - approximately 2x higher annualised return than benchmark factor libraries using over 70% fewer factors at a cost under $10 per run, on real-market backtests - but the figures are author-reported and have not been independently replicated.

TradingAgents is the only repository in this shortlist whose reproducibility has been independently measured and published by third parties, in a peer-reviewed study that varied temperature, seed, top_k and top_p across GPT-4o and Qwen3:30B to quantify decision-consistency and return variability - making its non-determinism a documented property rather than an assumption.

limits: No repository was installed, built or executed locally; every score rests on public metadata, source files read via raw.githubusercontent, GitHub Actions run history and published papers. Green CI is evidence that the maintainers' own suite passed in their environment, not that the code works for a given deployment.

GitHub code search (30 req/min) rate-limited partway through, so the deflated-Sharpe / purged-CV / walk-forward comparison completed for all four top candidates on the first three queries but the 'purged' query returned only for ml4t and qlib; cross-repo grep coverage for the lower-ranked eight repositories was not attempted.

Three mechanical-shortlist metadata values were wrong and are corrected in the notes: virattt/ai-hedge-fund has tests but no CI (shortlist said the reverse), AI4Finance-Foundation/FinGPT has no CI (shortlist said yes), and je-suis-tm/quant-trading's pushed_at of 2026-06-20 masks a default-branch HEAD dated 2024-04-14. Other shortlist fields were spot-checked, not exhaustively re-derived.

Stars and forks were deliberately not scored. TradingAgents (108k) and ai-hedge-fund (64k) outrank qlib on popularity while ranking below it on documentation, release hygiene and organisational provenance; popularity in this sub-layer tracks LLM-agent novelty, not engineering quality.

Performance and benchmark claims (TradingAgents' CR/ARR table, RD-Agent's 2x-ARR result, FinRL's citation base) are author-reported and were not reproduced; only the TradingAgents reproducibility study is third-party evidence, and it measured variability rather than replicating the headline returns.

Operational fit for Python 3.12+ was assessed from declared metadata only. Two findings would need local verification before they could be relied on: ml4t pins requires-python to >=3.14,<3.15 (a single-minor hard pin), and RD-Agent declares requires-python >=3.10 while its classifiers stop at 3.11, so neither project's behaviour on 3.12/3.13 is established here.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for US-equities strategy research: does the repository actually enforce point-in-time correctness, lookahead/survivorship safeguards, corporate-action handling, explicit transaction costs, validation protocol (purged/walk-forward CV, CPCV/CSCV, deflated Sharpe, reality checks), paper/live parity and reproducibility — and what public, dated evidence (papers, benchmark tables, upstream tests, CI, release artifacts, documented defects) supports or contradicts that. Scores are per-repository against this lens only; no averaging across repositories, and anything not established in a primary source is left at 0 and listed under unknowns. All evidence is public web/GitHub, read via `gh api` and Tavily/WebSearch on 2026-09-21; no project-local file was opened.

unknowns: No independent third-party replication of the published case-study results was found; the artifact bundles are author-produced.
