Test engineering is genuinely good for a scraper: 22 test modules including test_price_repair.py, test_calendars.py, test_cookie_crumb_degradation.py, test_cache_noperms.py and test_download_concurrency.py - the cookie/crumb and price-repair tests are themselves evidence of recurring upstream breakage. CI includes Run Tests, Pyright, Ruff, zizmor (workflow-security scanner), Dependabot and a docs deploy; releases are frequent (1.4.1 2026-05-28 through 1.7.0 2026-08-26) and Python 3.12/3.13 are classified. The two 1s are deliberate and both stem from the upstream, not the code: the README states in bold that yfinance is not affiliated with or vetted by Yahoo, directs users to Yahoo's terms for rights to the downloaded data, and says the Yahoo finance API is intended for personal use only - so it is not a licensed data source for anything beyond research, regardless of the Apache-2.0 code licence; and it depends on an undocumented private endpoint with no versioned contract, which is the opposite of what a point-in-time equities catalog needs. Acceptable as a cross-check or prototyping source, not as a system of record.

sota_claims.claim: NautilusTrader's ParquetDataCatalog is the most complete open-source point-in-time market-data catalog that is natively integrated with an event-driven trading engine, exposing a Python interface over a Rust catalog and a DataFusion query engine with Arrow schemas defined in its model and persistence crates.

Lean is the only repository on this shortlist that ships the primitives for survivorship-bias-free US equity universes in-tree, carrying factor_files for split and dividend adjustment, map_files for ticker renames and delistings, and a market-hours-database.json for exchange calendars.

DuckDB has the most rigorous verification pipeline of any embedded analytical engine on this shortlist, running continuous fuzzing (CIFuzz), Coverity static analysis, ASan/TSan suppression-backed sanitizer builds, regression, extended and nightly suites across Linux, macOS, Windows and Android in 42 workflows.

OpenBB ships the deepest standardised open-source SEC EDGAR surface among these candidates, with 23 typed provider models under openbb_platform/providers/sec covering filings, the three financial statements and their growth variants, Form 13F-HR, fails-to-deliver, insider trading, CIK/symbol mapping and NPORT disclosures.

QuestDB is the only purpose-built tick-data time-series database here whose vendor documentation commits to Parquet as the on-disk form of historical partitions specifically so that dataframe and ML tooling can read the data directly and bypass the database, making anti-lock-in an architectural property rather than an export feature.

limits: Shortlist coverage for T-data is NOT comprehensive and the ranking should not be read as full SOTA coverage of this sub-layer. Absent from the twelve rows and never evaluated: dedicated exchange-calendar libraries (exchange_calendars, pandas_market_calendars), broker/data SDKs (alpaca-py and the rest of the alpacahq org, ib_async, databento-python, polygon-io client), SEC/fundamentals tooling (edgartools, sec-edgar-downloader, python-edgar), point-in-time dataset frameworks (zipline-reloaded bundles, qlib, arcticdb, lakeapi), and lighter validation alternatives to Great Expectations (pandera, pointblank, soda-core). ArcticDB in particular is a direct competitor to the storage rows here and its omission is material.

No code was built, no test suite was executed, no benchmark was reproduced and no dataset was ingested. Every score is from public GitHub API metadata, primary repo file listings, README/LICENSE/docs text and vendor documentation read on 2026-09-21 - this is documentary evidence, not measured behaviour.

The recent-commit probe used per_page=1 with a since=2026-08-21 filter on the default branch, so its result distinguishes only 'at least one' from 'none' and is not a volume measure. OpenBB's zero is a real signal worth chasing; the other repos' ones carry no cadence information. OpenBB also shows pushed_at 2026-09-19 against that zero, and the contradiction was left unresolved.

The input shortlist's has_tests field is unreliable and was corrected here from directory listings: polars (py-polars/tests), questdb (core/src/test) and Lean (Tests/) all have substantial test trees despite being marked 'no'. Any downstream use of that field should be re-derived.

Licence findings for timescaledb (Apache-2.0 core plus Timescale License for the tsl/ tree) and OpenBB (AGPL-3.0) were taken from the shortlist's stated LICENSE inspection plus the visible LICENSE/LICENSE-APACHE/NOTICE layout, not from a fresh per-file header audit. The specific question of which tick-data-relevant Timescale features fall under TSL rather than Apache-2.0 remains open and is load-bearing for that row's score.

capability_fit was scored against this sub-layer's stated scope, which includes columnar storage and validation as well as market data - so general-purpose engines (DuckDB, Arrow, Polars, ClickHouse) score highly on fit without providing any US-equities domain knowledge. A reader wanting equities-specific capability should read the notes field, not the number alone.

Scores across repositories are not comparable as a total and were deliberately not averaged or aggregated. The six criteria are independent ordinal judgments; summing them would equate an AGPL network-copyleft constraint with a missing test directory.

Ranking positions 4 and 5 are the least stable. Polars sits above Lean on engineering health but is mid-major-version (py-2.0.0-rc.2), and Lean's unique in-tree corporate-action and delisting data would move it above Polars under a capability-weighted rather than engineering-quality-weighted lens. QuestDB and ClickHouse sit immediately below and would displace entries here if the deployment target were a server rather than a local-first workstation.

The blindness rule was honoured: no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> was opened and no project-selected tool was privileged or excluded. NautilusTrader and Alpaca appear in the injected project instructions; Nautilus was scored from public evidence on its merits and no Alpaca repository was in the shortlist to evaluate.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for US-equities market data: does the tool actually deliver point-in-time correctness (as-of-date timestamps, filing/effective dates), lookahead and survivorship safeguards (ticker mapping, delistings, historical universes), corporate-action handling (splits/dividends/mergers), exchange calendars, cost/licensing realism, paper-live parity and reproducible storage/validation — judged only from public primary sources (repo contents, official docs, release/issue records) dated up to 2026-09-21, with no reference to any local catalog or prior project selection.

unknowns: Whether the repo's bundled Data/equity/usa sample contains complete factor_files/map_files/universes for a full US universe, or only demonstration slices (not verified by download)
Measured accuracy of the generated factor/map files against an independent corporate-actions reference
Cost and licensing terms of the QuantConnect-hosted US equity datasets needed to populate the format at full universe scale
scores.notes: Only shortlisted project with a first-class, file-level point-in-time US equity data model: Data/equity/usa contains factor_files (split/dividend adjustment), map_files (ticker changes/delistings), universes (historical constituents), fundamental, plus Data/market-hours/market-hours-database.json (exchange calendar) and Data/symbol-properties. Code search confirms the engine-side machinery (MapFileResolver 19 hits, CorporateFactorRow 11 hits) and ToolBox/FactorFileGenerator.cs. `lean data generate` documents that for Equity it 'will automatically generate map files, factor files, and coarse universe data'. Lookahead safeguard is architectural: QC 'Understanding Time' docs describe a streaming Time Frontier so an algorithm cannot see data beyond current time, and the same streaming path is used for backtest and live ('no code changes'). Contribution rules require datasets to have 'realistic timestamps for when the data was available (point in time)'. Shortlist metadata said has_tests=no; that is a false negative — a large Tests/ tree exists (Tests/Algorithm, Tests/Engine, Tests/Brokerages, ...). The stale v2.4.0.1 (2017) GitHub tag is also misleading: pushes are daily. Weaknesses for this lens: LeanData is a bespoke on-disk format (portability cost), .NET-centric, and the genuinely survivorship-free data is a paid QuantConnect product, not in-repo.

unknowns: Whether the catalog or adapters apply US equity corporate-action adjustment (splits/dividends) to historical bars — no such component found in docs/concepts/data or crates/persistence
Whether any survivorship-bias-free historical universe/constituent facility exists (code search for 'survivorship' returns 0 hits)
Databento (the only stable US-equities data adapter listed) subscription cost and history depth for the intended universe
scores.notes: Strongest portable storage/lifecycle story of the shortlist: docs/concepts/data/catalog.md documents ParquetDataCatalog as a Python interface over a Rust catalog and DataFusion query engine, with Arrow schemas defined in the model/persistence crates, instants as Timestamp(Nanosecond, 'UTC'), and local/S3/GCS/Azure/HTTP backends — plus an explicit warning that SQL readers mapping to microsecond TIMESTAMPTZ truncate sub-microsecond values (a real reproducibility hazard, documented rather than hidden). Paper/live parity is an explicit design claim: README states 'The same strategy and execution-algorithm code can run across backtest and live systems' and 'Identical strategy implementations between research and live deployment', with a dedicated docs/concepts/live.md 'Backtest and live differences' section rather than an unqualified claim. US-equities-relevant ingest exists via the Databento adapter (marked stable) and Interactive Brokers; there is no Alpaca adapter in docs/integrations. Migration and streaming helpers exist (how_to/migrate_parquet_catalog.md, stream_parquet_catalog.md, data_catalog_databento.py). Gap for this lens: it is a trading-engine data layer, not a point-in-time equity reference-data system — no factor/map-file equivalent, no universe history. LGPL-3.0 is workable but is the most restrictive license among the engine-side candidates here.

unknowns: Independent (non-vendor) benchmark results for ASOF JOIN at the data volumes a US equity tick/quote study implies
Whether all 2026 ASOF correctness fixes are in the pinned v1.5.5 release or only on the development branch
scores.notes: Best cost/effort fit for point-in-time research joins: ASOF JOIN is documented as a first-class SQL feature for aligning imperfectly timed series ('at most one match from the right hand side', left side cannot grow), which is exactly the trade-to-prevailing-quote and fundamentals-as-of-date pattern. Evidence quality for correctness is unusually good but two-sided: the repo carries a very broad test tree (test/sql, test/sqlite, test/parquet, test/arrow, test/fuzzer, test/ossfuzz, test/memoryleak, test/db-benchmark), and at the same time the 2026 issue record shows real ASOF semantic bugs found and closed — #25536 'ASOF JOIN returns a different payload row for the same query on static tables' (2026-09-09), #23933 'ASOF JOIN ignores a valid NULL-safe equality match', #21514 'ASOF LEFT join with empty right table returns empty result'. That is a maintained-and-audited signal, but it also means asof results should be regression-tested against fixtures rather than trusted blindly. No financial-domain semantics at all: no corporate actions, calendars or universe history — it is the compute/storage substrate, MIT-licensed and embeddable with zero service cost.

unknowns: Whether any provider exposes as-reported/unrestated point-in-time fundamentals rather than current-vintage statements
Exchange-calendar support: GitHub code search across the repo returns 0 hits for pandas_market_calendars and only 3 incidental hits for 'holidays', none in a calendar module
Whether recorded-cassette provider tests are re-recorded often enough to detect live upstream schema drift
Cadence of the openbb Python package releases after the April 2026 ODP Desktop pivot (last tagged platform release v4.7.0, 2026-03-09)
scores.notes: Widest legitimate provider surface of the shortlist: openbb_platform/providers holds ~30 providers including sec (SEC/EDGAR), federal_reserve, fred, finra, cftc, bls, nasdaq, cboe, intrinio, fmp, tiingo, tradier, yfinance. The sec provider is genuinely substantive for US equities fundamentals — models for balance_sheet/income_statement/cash_flow, company_filings, compare_company_facts, latest_financial_reports, form_13FHR, insider_trading, equity_ftd, cik_map/symbol_map — and it has its own tests (test_sec_fetchers.py, test_company_facts.py, test_xbrl_taxonomy.py) with recorded HTTP cassettes. 'filing_date' appears in 27 files, so filing-date metadata exists and a point-in-time discipline is constructible, but the platform publishes no point-in-time or restatement guarantee, and I found no exchange-calendar or corporate-action-adjustment layer. Main deployment risk for this lens is licensing: GitHub reports NOASSERTION and the project is AGPL-3.0, which is the strongest copyleft in this shortlist and materially constrains embedding in a closed research/execution service. Provider churn is a documented failure mode (17 'breaking/deprecated' issues; e.g. #7266 IMF API changes breaking). The 2026 releases are 'ODP Desktop' products, so the open-source library's own release rhythm has become harder to read from the release feed.

unknowns: Third-party (non-vendor) verification of the 19M rows/sec ingestion and the August 2026 competitor benchmarks — all published benchmarks found are QuestDB's own
Exact feature split between the Apache-2.0 core in this repo and QuestDB Enterprise (replication/HA/security), which determines what a self-hosted deployment actually gets
Whether the exchange-calendar TICK operator's calendar data (XNYS/XLON/XHKG) is maintained with holiday accuracy sufficient for US equity session logic
scores.notes: The most capital-markets-specific SQL surface among the pure databases: documented ASOF JOIN ('most recent row at or before the left timestamp'), ASOF JOIN TOLERANCE to prevent silently joining stale quotes, plus WINDOW JOIN, HORIZON JOIN, LT/SPLICE JOIN, LATEST ON, SAMPLE BY, designated timestamps with physical time ordering, out-of-order ingest merge, and materialized views. Notably for US equities, the SQL-extensions deep dive documents a TICK operator with exchange calendars (XLON, XHKG and others) — calendar awareness inside the query engine rather than in application code. The TOLERANCE feature is directly a lookahead/stale-data safeguard and is argued as such in the vendor's own writeup. Evidence is capped at 2 because the performance and comparison claims in the README are all self-published (QWP vs ILP ingestion, QuestDB vs InfluxDB 3, 'competitors benchmarked August 2026'), with the README itself saying 'we encourage you to run your own benchmarks'. License is Apache-2.0 for this repo but the product is open-core, so HA/replication is a commercial path; storage is engine-specific (Postgres wire protocol and Parquet interop mitigate but do not remove lock-in). No equities corporate-action or universe semantics.

unknowns: How often the silent-wrong-result path (set_sorted asserted on unsorted data) occurs in practice, and whether the streaming engine's partial sortedness check is sufficient for grouped asof joins
Correctness parity between the in-memory and streaming engines for join_asof with 'by' groups at the pinned py-1.44.2 release
scores.notes: join_asof/join_asof_by is documented with strategy (backward/forward/nearest), 'by' group keys and tolerance — the right primitive for trade-to-quote and signal-to-price alignment, and it is Arrow-native so it composes with Parquet catalogs at no service cost. The lens-relevant hazard is explicit in the vendor's own documentation and should be treated as a first-class failure mode: check_sortedness 'cannot check the sortedness if by groups are provided' in the in-memory engine and the streaming engine checks only rows it processes; and the Polars blog states plainly that set_sorted 'is not a sort. It is a trust-me declaration to the optimizer... Polars will not sort it for you or raise an error', i.e. an unsorted asof key can silently produce wrong (potentially lookahead-contaminated) joins. 101 issues mention join_asof, with open API/behaviour items (#18496 inconsistent API, #22684 relative tolerance, #27638 memory bloat after join_asof). Shortlist has_tests=no is a metadata artifact — tests live under crates/*/tests and py-polars. No financial-domain semantics.

unknowns: Nothing material for this lens beyond the obvious: it defines no market-data semantics, so no point-in-time, corporate-action or survivorship property can be attributed to it
scores.notes: Infrastructure rather than a data solution, scored accordingly: capability_fit is capped because it solves interchange and in-memory layout, not any US-equities requirement. Its value under this lens is reproducibility and lifecycle safety — a versioned, formally specified columnar format (format/Schema.fbs, Message.fbs, File.fbs) plus Flight/FlightSQL wire protocols, under Apache Software Foundation governance with multi-language implementations (cpp, python, r, ruby, c_glib, matlab) and an archive-grade release process. It is the substrate the stronger candidates already stand on: Nautilus defines Arrow schemas for its Parquet catalog and Polars is Arrow-native, so choosing Arrow/Parquet as the interchange boundary is what keeps a dataset portable if any engine above is later replaced. Zero cost, permissive license, no vendor.

unknowns: Behaviour of ASOF JOIN when the right-hand quote table exceeds max_bytes_in_join for a full US equities NBBO history — documented as accumulated in memory, but no measured limit found
Whether ASOF JOIN semantics are covered by the sqllogic/integration suites specifically, versus general join coverage
scores.notes: Strongest general engineering-evidence profile of any candidate here: tests/ contains integration, sqllogic, performance, fuzz, stress and jepsen.clickhouse (distributed-consistency testing) — a class of evidence none of the domain-specific repos offers — with same-day stable and LTS releases (v26.9.1, v26.8.10-lts, v26.7.14 all published 2026-09-21). ASOF JOIN exists and is usable for trade/quote alignment, but the documented constraints matter for research validity: exactly one inequality condition on a well-ordered column plus at least one equality key, join key columns cannot be Nullable, and the right-hand side is loaded into memory sorted by the inequality column, bounded by max_rows_in_join/max_bytes_in_join with an overflow action — so a naive large-scale point-in-time join can silently truncate or fail rather than degrade gracefully. Operationally heavier than DuckDB for single-node research; no financial-domain semantics (no corporate actions, no calendars, no universes). Apache-2.0, self-hostable.

unknowns: Post-transfer release cadence and roadmap commitment under Fivetran stewardship (announced 2026-05-13); no public multi-year maintenance commitment found
Whether any maintained expectation library covers market-data-specific checks (split-adjustment continuity, session completeness against a calendar, NBBO crossing) — none found in the repo
Migration cost from the 0.x API to GX Core 1.x for existing suites, and 1.x API stability going forward
scores.notes: The only shortlisted tool aimed squarely at the sub-layer's 'validation' requirement: declarative Expectations as data unit tests with generated documentation and validation results, a substantial tests/ tree, contrib/ expectation packages, a Zenodo DOI for citation, and active pushes (1.23.1 released 2026-09-18). For US equities it is generic: every domain check (no negative volume, no zero-price bars, dividend-adjusted continuity across split dates, session coverage versus an exchange calendar, no future-dated filings) must be authored by the user — GX contributes the harness and the audit trail, not the semantics. Provenance is the item to watch and is the reason maintenance is scored 2 rather than 3: the canonical great-expectations/great_expectations path now resolves to fivetran/great_expectations, and Fivetran announced on 2026-05-13 it would 'become steward of the Great Expectations open source community and GX Core project'. README badges still point at the old org and CI at the old Azure DevOps project, i.e. the transition is recent and incomplete. A third-party comparison page additionally claims GX Cloud shut down 2026-06-01 with assets acquired by FICO; that is a vendor-competitor source and is reported here as unverified.

unknowns: Whether release 2.30.1 provides a native ASOF JOIN keyword; the only public material found is a vendor blog on 'Implementing ASOF Joins in PostgreSQL and Timescale' (i.e. a recipe/LATERAL-join pattern), not a documented first-class operator
Which of the features relevant here (compression, continuous aggregates, hyperfunctions) fall under the /tsl directory and therefore under the Timescale License rather than Apache-2.0
scores.notes: Postgres-extension approach is the most operationally familiar and the best integrated with an existing relational reference-data schema (instruments, corporate actions, universes can live in the same database as the bars, with real constraints and transactions — a genuine research-validity advantage no columnar engine here offers). Time-series features are mature: hypertables, continuous aggregates, time_bucket/time_bucket_gapfill, locf/interpolate, first()/last(). The weakness under this lens is the point-in-time join: unlike QuestDB, DuckDB, ClickHouse and Polars, no native ASOF JOIN operator is documented in the core product — the public material is an implementation blog, so as-of alignment is a user-authored LATERAL pattern with the correctness burden on the user. Licensing needs care: the repository LICENSE states source is 'variously licensed under the Apache License Version 2.0, an Apache compatible license, or the Timescale License', with the /tsl directory under TSL, and the vendor's licensing page confirms Community features are TSL-restricted chiefly against offering a hosted DBaaS. That is compatible with internal research use but is not a plain Apache-2.0 story, hence 2.

unknowns: Quantified accuracy of yfinance adjusted prices, dividends and splits versus a reference vendor for a US equity universe — no public audit found
Whether delisted US tickers are retrievable at all for a historical window, which determines if any survivorship-free study is even possible
Actual Yahoo rate limits (undocumented; inferred only from recurring 429 reports)
scores.notes: Highest convenience, lowest research validity of the shortlist, and the license/terms issue is decisive rather than cosmetic: the README states yfinance is 'not affiliated, endorsed, or vetted by Yahoo', points to Yahoo's terms, and states in bold 'the Yahoo! finance API is intended for personal use only'. The Apache-2.0 code license therefore does not confer a right to the data for a production or commercial research pipeline — score 1 on license_deployment_fit is about the data terms, not the code. Data-correctness failure modes are documented in the project's own issue tracker: #2070 'Adjusted Close from yfinance is not the same as total return from Yahoo Finance' (open since 2024-10-03), #2666 'Dividends data is really sum of dividends and Capital gain (incorrectly)', #2660 'Price repair split false-positive', plus six rate-limit issues including #2125 with 41 comments. Credit where due on evidence: maintainers ship an explicit data-repair subsystem with its own test file (tests/test_price_repair.py) alongside ~20 other test modules, and 2026 work (#2944) removed misleading 'possibly delisted' speculation from errors — the project is honest about its own defects. Structurally it offers no point-in-time vintages, no historical constituent universes, and a single undocumented upstream that can change without notice.

unknowns: Whether delisted or historically-listed-only US symbols are present at all, and with what listing/delisting dates — no point-in-time listing history is described
Provenance of the symbol records and any validation against exchange or SEC listing files; the contribution model is manual CSV edits by the community
Freshness/error rate of the 112,707 equity records; no published audit or data-quality CI found
scores.notes: Useful as a free symbol taxonomy (112,707 equities across 84 exchanges, plus ETFs/funds/indices, with sector/industry/country fields) and cheap to consume — plain CSVs, MIT licensed, so lifecycle portability and license fit are genuinely strong. But it does not meet the sub-layer's core requirement and says so itself: the README states 'The aim of this database is explicitly not to provide up-to-date fundamentals or stock data'. It is a current-snapshot taxonomy maintained by community CSV edits ('relies on community involvement to add, edit, and remove tickers over time'), which is structurally the opposite of a survivorship-bias-free point-in-time universe — symbols removed over time make the snapshot progressively less representative of any historical date. Evidence is scored 1 because the only support for the data is the README's own counts; no tests of data content, no external validation, no versioned historical vintages were found. Reasonable as a discovery/enrichment side-table, not as a universe source for backtests.

sota_claims.claim: Lean carries the most complete open-source point-in-time data model for US equities, shipping ticker map files, split/dividend factor files and coarse universe files as a generated, versionable on-disk format rather than leaving corporate actions and survivorship to the user.

Lean is the only shortlisted engine whose lookahead safeguard is architectural rather than conventional: a streaming Time Frontier makes future data unreachable in backtests and runs the identical path in live trading with no code changes.

NautilusTrader's ParquetDataCatalog is the most portable open-source market-data catalog for backtest/live parity, defining Arrow schemas with nanosecond UTC instants over a Rust/DataFusion query layer and local, S3, GCS, Azure and HTTP backends, while explicitly documenting the sub-microsecond truncation risk of microsecond-precision SQL readers.

QuestDB offers the most capital-markets-specific SQL surface of any open-source time-series database here — ASOF, WINDOW and HORIZON joins, an ASOF TOLERANCE clause that prevents silently joining stale quotes, and exchange-calendar-aware TICK semantics — though all of its published performance comparisons are vendor-run and unverified.

yfinance is the most widely used free US equity data client but is the weakest research-validity option in this set: its own README states the Yahoo API is intended for personal use only, and adjusted-close, dividend and split-repair defects remain open in its tracker.

limits: Shortlist coverage gap — the candidate set contains no dedicated tool for several named sub-layer requirements, so those requirements are unrepresented rather than poorly served: exchange calendars (e.g. exchange_calendars, pandas-market-calendars), SEC EDGAR clients (e.g. edgartools, sec-edgar-downloader), broker/data SDKs for US equities (e.g. alpaca-py, databento-python, ib_insync/ib_async), point-in-time fundamentals or survivorship-bias-free universe datasets, and time-series stores or table formats built for this shape (e.g. ArcticDB, Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake). Ranking positions should be read as 'best of this list', not 'best available'.

No code was executed, installed, downloaded or benchmarked; every score derives from repository contents, official documentation, release feeds and issue records read through gh api and web search. No claim here is a measured result.

Point-in-time and survivorship properties were assessed from documented mechanisms and directory structure (e.g. Lean's factor_files/map_files/universes, OpenBB's filing_date fields), not from inspecting actual data files; whether the shipped or purchasable data is genuinely complete and correct at universe scale is untested.

Performance and scale claims for QuestDB, ClickHouse, DuckDB, Polars and TimescaleDB are vendor-published or third-party blog material; no independent benchmark under a US equities workload was found or run, so quality_cost and evidence scores deliberately avoid crediting them.

GitHub code search was used for several negative findings (no 'survivorship' in nautilus_trader, no calendar module in OpenBB). Code search indexes are incomplete and case/path sensitive, so these are weak absence evidence and are recorded as unknowns rather than as established absences.

Two shortlist metadata fields were wrong and were corrected from primary listings — QuantConnect/Lean and pola-rs/polars both have extensive tests (Tests/ and crates/*/tests + py-polars respectively) despite has_tests='no', and Lean's 2017 release tag does not reflect its actual daily release activity. Other mechanical fields in the shortlist were not re-verified.

The claim that GX Cloud shut down on 2026-06-01 with assets going to FICO comes from a competing vendor's comparison page and is reported as unverified; only the Fivetran stewardship announcement (2026-05-13) is treated as primary.

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader's ParquetDataCatalog is the most complete open-source point-in-time market-data catalog natively integrated with an event-driven trading engine (Python over Rust catalog + DataFusion, Arrow schemas).
verdicts.reason: The mechanism (Python->Rust->DataFusion, Arrow schemas) is real, but 'point-in-time' is not. docs/concepts/data/catalog.md describes an event-timestamped Parquet store keyed on nanosecond UTC instants with object-store backends. There is no as-of/version/snapshot read, no bitemporal correction or restatement handling, and no corporate-action or security-master model anywhere under docs/concepts/data/ (bar.md, catalog.md, quote_tick.md, trade_tick.md, order_book_*.md - nothing on splits, dividends, ticker changes or delistings), and a GitHub code search for 'corporate action' across the repo returns nothing. That is a time-series archive, not a point-in-time catalog: it cannot answer 'what did the data look like as of date X' after a vendor restatement. ArcticDB does exactly that ('Bitemporal versioning: ArcticDB versions data automatically on every write, enabling point-in-time queries, reproducible research, efficient daily appends, and historical corrections'), and Lean's map_files/factor_files encode point-in-time corporate actions. The defensible superlative is 'most portable backtest/live catalog' (claim 8), not 'most complete point-in-time'.

verdicts.claim: Lean is the only repository on this shortlist that ships survivorship-bias-free US equity universe primitives in-tree: factor_files, map_files and market-hours-database.json.
verdicts.reason: Verified literally via the GitHub contents API. Data/equity/usa/ contains factor_files, map_files, universes, fundamental, shortable plus the resolution directories; Data/market-hours/market-hours-database.json exists. No other shortlist repo (nautilus_trader, duckdb, arrow, polars, OpenBB, questdb) ships an equivalent. CAVEAT the claim's wording avoids but a reader should not: what is in-tree is the format plus a demo sample, not a universe. map_files holds 26 files (aaa, aapl, aig, bac, bno, eem, fb, gdvd, gooav, goog, googl, ibm, iwm, qqq, spwr, spy, tap.a, tfcfa, twx, uso, vxx, wm and .1 variants) and factor_files holds 22. The real survivorship-bias-free master covers ~27,500 securities and is the paid US Equity Security Master ($600 initial + $600/yr, 'designed to be used in the LEAN Engine and cannot be consumed another way'). Survives as worded ('primitives'), fails if read as 'ships the universe'.

verdicts.claim: DuckDB has the most rigorous verification pipeline of any embedded analytical engine on this shortlist, RUNNING continuous fuzzing (CIFuzz), Coverity static analysis, ASan/TSan sanitizer builds, regression/extended/nightly suites across 4 OSes in 42 workflows.
verdicts.reason: The judge counted configuration files and inferred execution. The count checks out (actions/workflows total_count = 42; cifuzz.yml, coverity.yml, Regression.yml, ExtendedTests.yml, NightlyTests.yml, OSX.yml, Windows.yml, Android.yml present; .sanitizer-leak-suppressions.txt and .sanitizer-thread-suppressions.txt present at repo root). The execution does not. Queried via the Actions API: coverity.yml has total_count = 0 runs - the workflow was created 2024-02-02 and last touched 2025-02-11 and has never produced a run visible through the API, so 'Coverity static analysis' is not running. cifuzz.yml has 9 runs in its entire lifetime, and the three most recent are failure (2026-07-30), failure (2026-04-13) and cancelled (2026-04-03); the last success was 2025-12-11. Nine lifetime runs in a currently failing state is not 'continuous fuzzing'. Separately, the 42-workflow figure is not a distinguishing superlative: apache/arrow reports 43 workflows on the same API.

verdicts.claim: OpenBB ships the deepest standardised open-source SEC EDGAR surface among these candidates, with 23 typed provider models under openbb_platform/providers/sec covering filings, the three statements and growth variants, 13F-HR, fails-to-deliver, insider trading, CIK/symbol mapping and NPORT.
verdicts.reason: Count and coverage verified exactly. openbb_sec/models contains precisely 23 model modules once __init__.py and py.typed are excluded: balance_sheet, balance_sheet_growth, cash_flow, cash_flow_growth, cik_map, company_filings, compare_company_facts, equity_ftd, equity_search, form_13FHR, htm_file, income_statement, income_statement_growth, insider_trading, institutions_search, latest_financial_reports, management_discussion_analysis, nport_disclosure, rss_litigation, schema_files, sec_filing, sic_search, symbol_map. Every named capability maps to a file. 'Among these candidates' is the load-bearing qualifier and holds - no other shortlist repo has an EDGAR surface at all. Two things the claim omits: the licence is AGPL-3.0 (LICENSE: 'All files in this repository are licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0'), a real constraint for embedding, and outside the shortlist dgunning/edgartools (MIT, 2,734 stars, pushed 2026-09-21) is a deeper EDGAR surface.

verdicts.claim: QuestDB is the only purpose-built tick-data TSDB here whose vendor documentation commits to Parquet as the on-disk form of historical partitions specifically so tooling can bypass the database, making anti-lock-in an ARCHITECTURAL PROPERTY rather than an export feature.
verdicts.reason: Three problems. (1) The cited source is questdb/questdb-trading-data-demo - a vendor demo repo's marketing doc, not product documentation; marketing was treated as a primary architectural commitment. (2) QuestDB's own product docs contradict 'architectural property': the storage-engine page states 'QuestDB native binary format (the default): the append-friendly columnar format used for all partitions unless configured otherwise', i.e. Parquet is opt-in and NATIVE is the default, and the Parquet docs confine FORMAT PARQUET to 'partitions written after' the setting. (3) QuestDB's own Parquet blog carries an explicit warning: 'Converting partitions in-place is experimental right now. Please read more about the limitations and risks at the Parquet Export and Conversion Guide.' An experimental, non-default, forward-only conversion path is an export feature, which is exactly what the claim denies. The 'only ... here' framing is also vacuous - QuestDB is the sole time-series database on the shortlist, so the superlative is a set of one.

verdicts.claim: Lean carries the most complete open-source point-in-time data model for US equities, shipping map files, split/dividend factor files and coarse universe files as a generated, versionable on-disk format rather than leaving corporate actions and survivorship to the user.
verdicts.reason: The cited source does not say what the claim says it says. The QuantConnect docs for `lean data generate` open with 'Generate random market data' and 'Runs the random data generator in the LEAN ToolBox to generate realistic market data using a Brownian motion model.' It is true that 'If the security type is set to Equity, this command will automatically generate map files, factor files, and coarse universe data' - but those are synthetic artefacts of a Brownian-motion simulator, carrying no real split, dividend, merger or delisting. Citing a random-data generator as evidence of a point-in-time corporate-actions model is the core error. The real data is not open source: the US Equity Security Master 'tracks US Equity corporate actions, including splits, dividends, delistings, mergers, and ticker changes through history ... approximately 27,500 US Equities', is priced at $600 initial + $600 USD/year for on-premise download, and is 'designed to be used in the LEAN Engine and cannot be consumed another way'. Lean ships only 26 sample map files and 22 sample factor files in-tree. So corporate actions and survivorship ARE left to the user unless the user buys a proprietary, LEAN-locked subscription - the opposite of the claim's final clause, and against the lens's own 'cost/licensing realism' criterion.
verdicts.source: https://www.quantconnect.com/docs/v2/lean-cli/datasets/generating-data ('Generate random market data ... Brownian motion model') and https://www.quantconnect.com/data/quantconnect-us-equity-security-master

verdicts.claim: Lean is the ONLY shortlisted engine whose lookahead safeguard is architectural rather than conventional: a streaming Time Frontier makes future data unreachable in backtests and runs the identical path in live trading with no code changes.
verdicts.reason: The Time Frontier itself is real; 'only' is false, and NautilusTrader refutes it in almost the claim's own vocabulary. NautilusTrader's own writing: 'In NautilusTrader, research-to-live parity means the engine kernel, event ordering, time handling, and execution flow are all shared across both environments. Parity is built into the architecture rather than relying on convention.' The README states 'The same strategy and execution-algorithm code can run across backtest and live systems' and 'Live: Identical strategy implementations between research and live deployment', with backtests replaying quote/trade/bar/order-book data 'with nanosecond resolution' through the same event loop. A shared NautilusKernel with a simulated clock and time-ordered event delivery makes future data equally unreachable by construction. Secondary problem: the claim's source is the deprecated /docs/v1/ documentation tree, not current v2 docs.
verdicts.source: https://nautilustrader.io/blog/why-nautilustrader-exists ('Parity is built into the architecture rather than relying on convention') and https://github.com/nautechsystems/nautilus_trader#readme

verdicts.claim: NautilusTrader's ParquetDataCatalog is the most portable open-source market-data catalog for backtest/live parity: Arrow schemas with nanosecond UTC instants over a Rust/DataFusion query layer, local/S3/GCS/Azure/HTTP backends, and it explicitly documents the sub-microsecond truncation risk of microsecond-precision SQL readers.
verdicts.reason: Every falsifiable component verified against the primary file. catalog.md states: 'ParquetDataCatalog is the Python interface to the Rust catalog and DataFusion query engine. The Rust model and persistence crates define the Arrow schemas'; 'Instant timestamps use Timestamp(Nanosecond, Some("UTC"))'; and verbatim 'SQL readers that map these columns to microsecond-precision TIMESTAMPTZ can truncate sub-microsecond values.' The backend table lists Amazon S3 (s3), Google Cloud Storage (gs/gcs), Azure Blob Storage (az/abfs) and HTTP/WebDAV (http/https) alongside local paths, with 'The catalog stores these files under one root without requiring a separate database service.' Notably this judge scoped the superlative to PORTABILITY, which the evidence supports, rather than to point-in-time correctness, which it does not. One caveat the claim does not raise: the project is LGPL-3.0, not permissive.

verdicts.claim: QuestDB offers the most capital-markets-specific SQL surface of any open-source time-series database here: ASOF, WINDOW and HORIZON joins, an ASOF TOLERANCE clause, and exchange-calendar-aware TICK semantics (vendor-run benchmarks noted as unverified).
verdicts.reason: Refuted on the exchange-calendar component, the claim's most load-bearing US-equities feature. The SQL-extensions page confirms ASOF JOIN, LT JOIN, SPLICE JOIN, WINDOW JOIN, HORIZON JOIN ('evaluates the right table at a list or range of time offsets from each left row ... post-trade markout, implementation-shortfall'), LATEST ON, SAMPLE BY, the TICK interval syntax and 'A TOLERANCE clause caps how far back the join will look.' But the same page says verbatim: 'On QuestDB Enterprise, exchange calendars let TICK address venue schedules directly. XNYS is the ISO 10383 MIC code for the New York Stock Exchange; QuestDB knows the exchange's actual schedule, so holidays and early closes are excluded automatically.' Exchange-calendar-aware TICK is a closed, paid Enterprise feature, so it is not part of the 'open-source time-series database' surface the claim asserts - the claim's own qualifier excludes the feature it cites. The self-awareness about vendor-run benchmarks is correct and to the judge's credit, but does not rescue the calendar assertion. Open-source, Apache-2.0 exchange calendars for 50+ venues exist separately in gerrymanoim/exchange_calendars.
verdicts.source: https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/deep-dive/sql-extensions ('On QuestDB Enterprise, exchange calendars let TICK address venue schedules directly') -> https://questdb.com/docs/query/operators/exchange-calendars/

verdicts.claim: yfinance is the most widely used free US equity data client but the weakest research-validity option in this set: its README states the Yahoo API is intended for personal use only, and adjusted-close, dividend and split-repair defects remain open in its tracker.
verdicts.reason: Both falsifiable parts verified. The README carries verbatim 'Remember - the Yahoo! finance API is intended for personal use only.' (line 26) and 'yfinance is not affiliated, endorsed, or vetted by Yahoo, Inc. ... intended for research and educational purposes' (line 22), plus a pointer to Yahoo's terms of use. Issue #2070, 'Adjusted Close from yfinance is not the same as total return from Yahoo Finance', was opened 2024-10-03 and remains state=open with no closed_at as of 2026-09-21 - roughly two years unresolved, which is stronger evidence for the claim than the judge asserted. Popularity is consistent with 25,309 stars, above every other data client checked (alpaca-py 1,526; polygon client-python 1,512; databento-python 302). This is the one claim in the set that is appropriately calibrated and appropriately negative about its own subject.

survivors: Lean ships factor_files, map_files and market-hours-database.json in-tree and is the only shortlist repo that does (https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean) - survives as worded, but what is in-tree is the format plus a 26-file/22-file demo sample, not a universe.

OpenBB ships exactly 23 typed SEC provider models under openbb_platform/providers/sec and has the deepest EDGAR surface AMONG THE SHORTLIST (https://github.com/OpenBB-finance/OpenBB) - verified count; AGPL-3.0, and edgartools is deeper outside the shortlist.

NautilusTrader's ParquetDataCatalog is the most portable catalog for backtest/live parity: nanosecond UTC Arrow schemas, Rust/DataFusion, local/S3/GCS/Azure/HTTP backends, documented sub-microsecond truncation risk (https://github.com/nautechsystems/nautilus_trader) - all specifics verified in catalog.md.
yfinance is the most widely used free US equity client and the weakest on research validity: README 'personal use only', issue #2070 open since 2024-10-03 (https://github.com/ranaroussi/yfinance).

better_alternatives_found.name: ArcticDB
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The strongest counter to the shortlist's point-in-time story, and absent from both rankings. It is the only candidate that implements point-in-time as a storage property rather than as timestamped rows: 'Bitemporal versioning: ArcticDB versions data automatically on every write, enabling point-in-time queries, reproducible research, efficient daily appends, and historical corrections.' Reads take an as_of= argument to rewind to any prior version, which is what survives a vendor restatement and what NautilusTrader's ParquetDataCatalog cannot do. Built by Man Group for exactly this workload, 2,518 stars, pushed 2026-09-21, local-first (LMDB backend, no server required) so it fits Linux/WSL2 + Python 3.12 without infrastructure. MATERIAL CAVEAT: Business Source License 1.1, not open source under the OSI definition - the Additional Use Grant forbids offering it as a 'Database Service'. That constrains redistribution, not local research use.

better_alternatives_found.name: edgartools
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Directly beats OpenBB on the SEC EDGAR axis the T-data lens cares about, and was not ranked. Self-described as 'Read and analyze SEC EDGAR filings in Python. 10-K, 8-K, XBRL financials, Form 3/4/5, 13F, ADV - clean API, well-typed, MIT-licensed', i.e. filing-level XBRL and the full Form 3/4/5 insider set rather than 23 REST-shaped models. MIT beats OpenBB's AGPL-3.0 for embedding, it is single-purpose rather than a 73k-star platform you inherit wholesale, and it is actively maintained (2,734 stars, pushed 2026-09-21, the same day as the evaluation). For filing-date/as-of-date point-in-time fundamentals, a dedicated EDGAR library is the right layer.

better_alternatives_found.name: exchange_calendars
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The exchange-calendar gap both judges papered over. Lean's answer is one market-hours-database.json locked to the LEAN engine; QuestDB's answer is an Enterprise-only closed feature. This is 'A Python library for defining and querying calendars for security exchanges. Calendars for more than 50 exchanges available out-the-box!' - Apache-2.0, 667 stars, pushed 2026-09-15, the maintained successor to the abandoned quantopian/trading_calendars (last push 2023-07-17). It composes with any storage or engine choice instead of being captive to one. rsheftel/pandas_market_calendars (MIT, 998 stars, pushed 2026-07-12) is a viable second source for the same layer.

better_alternatives_found.name: Qlib (Point-In-Time database)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Ships an explicitly named Point-In-Time database for fundamentals with documented filing-date semantics - the capability the judges attributed to Lean and NautilusTrader without primary support. Microsoft-maintained, MIT, 48,738 stars, pushed 2026-09-22, with qlib/data/pit.py in-tree. Its docs state their own limitation up front ('Currently, the PIT database is designed for quarterly or annually factors, which can handle fundamental data of financial reports in most markets'), a better evidentiary posture than either judge's superlatives. Worth a head-to-head against the assumption that a trading engine's data catalog covers point-in-time fundamentals; it does not, and this does.

better_alternatives_found.name: databento-python
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The shortlist has no credible answer for licensed, survivorship-complete US equity market data: yfinance is personal-use-only by its own README, and Lean's security master is $600/yr and LEAN-locked. Databento's official client (Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-09-17) provides normalised US equities down to MBO with instrument-definition and symbology history, the mechanism that makes ticker changes and delistings resolvable rather than a user problem. The small star count (302) reflects a thin vendor SDK, not weak maintenance - judge it on the data contract, not repo metrics. Include it as the paid-data comparison point against the QuantConnect security master rather than as a free substitute.

limits: Search rate cap: Tavily CLI/tvly was available and authenticated (no keyless-limit error hit); not invoked because all 40 candidates were already GitHub URLs from the computed-task candidate list and gh api sufficed for the required mechanical fields (stars/forks/pushed_at/created_at/archived/license/open_issues/release/tests/CI). gh core rate limit was 5000/h (0 used at start) and search 30/min (0 used); no rate limits were hit.

Shared scratchpad collision: this session's scratchpad directory (…/scratchpad/repos.txt) was concurrently overwritten by another parallel sub-layer worker writing the same filename mid-run (its content became an unrelated alpacahq/trading-engine repo list). Detected via a sudden content mismatch after the first CI-check loop; recovered by re-running the untouched results.tsv (confirmed intact, all 40 target repos still present) and redoing only the corrupted CI-workflow-count step under a private path (scratchpad/portfolio_risk/). No candidate data was lost, but this indicates the shared scratchpad needs per-worker-unique filenames/subdirectories when multiple sub-layer workers run in the same session scratchpad concurrently.

GitHub's repo license-detection API reports spdx_id=NOASSERTION/name=Other for 5 shortlisted repos (OpenBB, vectorbt, arch, QuantLib, mlfinlab) because their LICENSE file text doesn't exactly match a GitHub-recognized template; raw LICENSE file content was fetched and read directly for these 5 to determine actual terms (AGPL-3.0, Commons-Clause-modified source-available, custom MIT-style text, and a permissive BSD-style 'QuantLib License', and a restrictive proprietary EULA respectively) rather than relying on the parsed spdx_id alone.

The computed task caps the shortlist at 'at most 12' but gives no tie-break rule for the 31 candidates that passed all four mechanical filters (not archived / pushed within 12mo or release within 18mo / recognised-OSI-or-noted-source-available license / clear sub-layer relevance). Stars (an already-collected mechanical/objective field, not a subjective quality judgment) was used as the sole tie-break, ranked descending, to select the final 12. This is a methodological choice made in the absence of an explicit rule and should be treated as such, not as an additional hidden mechanical filter.

has_tests/has_ci were detected cheaply from a single root-level `contents` listing plus one `.github/workflows` listing per repo (not a recursive scan), per the task's 'cheap' instruction; a repo with tests nested under a differently-named top-level folder (e.g. inside the package directory rather than a top-level tests/ folder) could be mechanically under-recorded as has_tests=no. This is noted as a known false-negative risk, not corrected further, to keep the check cheap as instructed.

judges.lens: Engineering quality for the T-portfolio-risk sub-layer (portfolio construction, risk models, position sizing, performance/tearsheet evaluation, transaction-cost modelling). Judged on: does CI actually execute the test suite and is it green; release discipline and API/versioning signals; documentation depth and currency; dependency/platform hygiene for Linux/WSL2 + Python 3.12+ local-first use; security and provenance artefacts (CodeQL, SBOM, dependency review, DOI/peer review); maintainer organisation and bus factor; and the integration cost of adopting the repo only for this sub-layer. All evidence is public GitHub API / repository file / PyPI / arXiv data collected 2026-09-21..22; no local project files were read, and the shortlist's own "chosen tool" context was ignored. Capability fit is scored against the sub-layer's five functions, so general-purpose data platforms and derivatives-pricing libraries score low there even when their engineering is excellent.

scores.notes: Only shortlisted repo that covers the whole sub-layer in one API: optimization/ (MeanRisk, RiskBudgeting, HierarchicalRiskParity, NestedClustersOptimization), moments/ + prior/ (shrinkage, denoising, Gerber, Black-Litterman, EntropyPooling, OpinionPooling, factor models), uncertainty_set/ (distributionally robust), measures/ + metrics/ (risk & performance measures), model_selection/ (WalkForward, CombinatorialPurgedCV), and explicit transaction-cost support (38 code hits for transaction_costs). CI is the strongest evidence in the set: ci.yml runs the suite on Python 3.10/3.11/3.12/3.13/3.14 with a `--resolution lowest-direct` minimum-dependency job plus cross-OS and docs jobs, and the last five runs on main and on feature branches were all success (2026-09-21). 162 test files under tests/. Security/provenance hygiene is unusually complete for this domain: CodeQL, dependency-review, export-sbom and Dependabot workflows all active. Release discipline is automated (Semantic Release workflow; v1.2.6 -> v1.3.0 between 2026-09-15 and 2026-09-20, PyPI 1.3.0 on 2026-09-20). Provenance: arXiv preprint 2507.04176 and Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.16148630. Maintenance is live: 86 commits in the last 90 days, 21 issues closed in 90 days, 17 open PRs. quality_cost is held at 2, not 3: HugoDelatte holds 251 of the top contributions (real bus factor despite the org account), the 5-releases-in-6-days cadence implies API churn that a downstream pin has to absorb, and enterprise support sits behind Skfolio Labs.

Maintainer organisation is the best in the shortlist after skfolio and arguably better distributed: robcarver17 (1415), bug-or-feature (714), tgibson11 (236), james-ward (77) — a genuine multi-maintainer project now under the pst-group org. CI is broad and green: Quick test, Slow test, OS test, Lint and Format workflows, with Quick/OS/Lint all success on 2026-09-21; 27 commits in 90 days. Documentation is deep prose (docs/backtesting.md, production.md, data.md, instruments.md, IB.md). Costs against the lens: GPL-3.0 is strong copyleft and constrains any proprietary or redistributed deployment (license_deployment_fit 2); the last tagged release is 1.8.2 from 2024-11-06, so release discipline lags the commit stream; and the codebase is a full futures trading stack tightly coupled to MongoDB, IB and futures instrument handling, so extracting only the portfolio-risk layer carries real integration cost.

But under an engineering-quality lens the evidence is the weakest of the credible candidates: tests/ contains exactly one test module (test_portfolio.py) plus CSV fixtures, and in .github/workflows/build.yml the Test step is commented out (lines 63-65: '#      - name: Test' / '#          source continuous_integration/test_script.sh'), so the green 'build' runs are wheel builds, not test runs. build.yml does exercise a genuine wheel matrix (ubuntu-22.04/macos-15/windows-2022 x Python 3.10-3.14), which is why lifecycle_portability is 2 rather than 1 despite the C++ extension in lib/. Release discipline is off-GitHub: zero GitHub releases/tags, PyPI 7.3.0 on 2026-05-31 with only CHANGELOG.rst to track. Activity is thin: 2 commits and 2 closed issues in 90 days, 7 open PRs. Single-author project (dcajasn 397 of ~410 top contributions) monetised through affiliate book links and GitHub Sponsors — capability is real, sustained engineering assurance is not established.

scores.notes: The de facto open-source tearsheet layer — stats.py, plots.py, reports.py, _montecarlo.py — covering performance and risk evaluation only; no portfolio construction, no risk-model estimation, no transaction-cost modelling, hence capability_fit 2. It does ship a real test suite (tests/: test_stats.py, test_plots.py, test_reports.py, test_montecarlo.py, test_compat.py, test_extend_pandas.py, test_utils.py), which is why evidence is 2 and not 1, but nothing runs it: the repository's only workflows are python-publish.yml (no pytest step), Dependabot Updates, and test-compatibility.yml whose state is 'disabled_manually'. The consequence lands exactly where this library is historically fragile — the presence of _compat.py and _numpy_compat.py shows pandas/numpy major-version breakage is a recurring problem, and the compatibility check for it is switched off. limits: No code was executed and no package was installed: every score rests on public GitHub API metadata, repository file contents, workflow run conclusions, PyPI metadata and project documentation read on 2026-09-21..22. Numerical correctness was not assessed for any repository. Nothing here compares optimizer results, covariance estimators, risk-measure definitions or tearsheet statistics against a reference, so 'evidence' scores measure the presence and execution of tests and CI, not the accuracy of the maths.

License judgements are readings of LICENSE text, not legal advice. In particular, whether vectorbt's Commons Clause or OpenBB's AGPL-3.0 network clause constrain a specific deployment is a question for counsel, not for this review.

Coverage percentages are unknown for every repository. Codecov and coverage workflows were observed for skfolio, PyPortfolioOpt, zipline-reloaded and QuantLib, but no badge value or report was read, so test-suite thoroughness is only proxied by file counts and CI matrix breadth.

Candidates that the upstream mechanical screen dropped were not re-examined, so this is not evidence of comprehensive coverage of the sub-layer; notably the tearsheet slice was judged only through quantstats, and its companion pyfolio-reloaded was never in scope.

Per the blindness rule, no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> was opened and no prior project selection influenced these scores. The consequence is that fit to any already-chosen execution engine, adapter or data layer is not assessed here — capability_fit measures only coverage of the five stated sub-layer functions.

Activity counters (commits, closed issues, open PRs) are 90-day snapshots taken on one day and can misread a project that batches work or that develops on non-default branches; skfolio, vectorbt and PyPortfolioOpt all showed meaningful feature-branch traffic that a default-branch-only count would miss.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for T-portfolio-risk (portfolio construction, risk models, position sizing, performance/tearsheet evaluation, transaction-cost modelling) on US equities: does the tool actually solve the sub-layer correctly (point-in-time correctness, lookahead/survivorship safeguards, corporate actions, cost modelling, paper/live parity, reproducibility), what published evidence/benchmarks/papers/upstream tests support it, and what failure modes are documented. All findings derived from public GitHub API reads of primary sources (READMEs, source files, test trees, release lists, open issues) and public web pages; no project-local files were opened.

unknowns: No in-repo handling of corporate actions, survivorship or point-in-time universe construction — it consumes a price/return matrix the caller must make point-in-time correct.
No published head-to-head benchmark against Riskfolio-Lib or PyPortfolioOpt on identical US-equity data that I could locate.
Mixed-integer features (cardinality, threshold constraints) need MIP solvers whose commercial licensing cost was not established.
scores.notes: Best direct fit for the sub-layer as a whole. Transaction costs and management fees are first-class terms inside the optimization objective, not a post-hoc adjustment: src/skfolio/optimization/convex/_mean_risk.py exposes transaction_costs, management_fees and previous_weights, with an explicit docstring warning that costs must be expressed on the same frequency as X (daily returns -> daily costs), which is the turnover-aware formulation the sub-layer requires. Lookahead safeguards are explicit and cited: src/skfolio/model_selection/_combinatorial.py implements CombinatorialPurgedCV with purged_size and embargo_size, referencing Marcos Lopez de Prado (2018); the module also ships WalkForward, MultipleRandomizedCV and covariance-forecast evaluation. Risk modelling breadth covers empirical/Black-Litterman/factor/entropy-pooling/opinion-pooling priors, uncertainty sets (distributionally robust), HRP/HERC/NCO/Schur clustering, risk budgeting and a benchmark tracker. Evidence is strong: 216 Python test files under tests/, codecov, a Zenodo concept DOI (10.5281/zenodo.16148630) and an arXiv paper (2507.04176, Nicolini/Manzi/Delatte). Maintenance is the strongest in the shortlist: v1.3.0 released 2026-09-20 with v1.2.6-v1.2.9 all inside the preceding week, org-owned with a commercial backer (Skfolio Labs) providing continuity. BSD-3-Clause imposes no deployment constraint. Lifecycle scores 2 rather than 3 because it is a library, not an engine: there is no execution, no broker adapter and therefore no paper/live parity of its own; it must be paired with an engine that supplies point-in-time data and fills. Quality/cost 2: cvxpy plus solver stack is a real dependency weight, and the fastest paths for large universes lean on commercial solvers.

unknowns: Upstream test coverage of the 26 risk measures: tests/test_portfolio.py is a single ~9.3 KB file with 7 test functions plus CSV golden files, so most risk measures have no visible regression test.
No tagged GitHub release exists (latest_release: none) even though the docs site advertises version 7.3, so the mapping from a docs version to a repo commit is unverified.
Bus factor: activity is concentrated in one maintainer (dcajasn); no organisational succession mechanism was found.
scores.notes: Widest published risk-measure catalogue in the shortlist, and the one whose risk measures are themselves the subject of peer-reviewable research rather than only implementations of others' work: EVaR (Cajas 2021, SSRN 3792520, cited 30+), RLVaR (Cajas 2023, SSRN 4378498), EDaR, Tail Gini, Brownian distance variance, plus the Springer monograph 'Advanced Portfolio Optimization' (9783031843037) that documents the models the library implements. Covers mean-risk and logarithmic mean-risk (Kelly) objectives across 26 convex risk measures, risk parity across 22, HRP/HERC/NCO, and worst-case (box/elliptical uncertainty set) optimization — directly the position-sizing and risk-model half of the sub-layer. Evidence is scored 2, not 3, because theoretical grounding and code verification are different classes: the SSRN/Springer work establishes the mathematics, but the repository's own regression evidence is one test module with 7 tests and CSV fixtures, and CI is only build.yml/docs.yml. Maintenance 2: pushed 2026-09-21, actively developed, but single-maintainer with no GitHub releases to pin against. Lifecycle 1: pure allocator — no backtest engine, no execution, no point-in-time or corporate-action machinery, so paper/live parity is entirely the integrator's problem. BSD-3-Clause. Quality/cost 2: CVXPY-based, and the maintainer's own demonstrations of large problems (612 assets x 4943 observations) use MOSEK, a commercial solver.

Whether the project is still accepting substantive changes: I could not find a maintainer statement on future direction.
Corporate-action completeness for US equities beyond splits/dividends/mergers (e.g. spin-offs, symbol changes) was not established from the sources read.
