sota_claims.claim: Codex is the only shortlisted coding client that ships OS-level sandboxing on all three desktop platforms (macOS seatbelt, a bundled sigstore-signed bwrap for Linux, and a Windows sandbox config path) together with first-party git-worktree isolation that has its own integration test suite and both Python and TypeScript SDKs, making it the most complete single-repo answer to the isolation-plus-SDK requirement of this sub-layer.

On Terminal-Bench 2 — the benchmark that scores the agent, harness and shell as one system rather than the model alone — the verified top entry is Codex on GPT-5.5 at 82.0% while OpenHands holds the open-harness record at 51.9%, so OpenHands is the strongest publicly benchmarked open coding harness and the open/closed gap is roughly 30 points.

DeepSeek Harness is the most completely plugin-decomposed agent runtime available in the open — sandbox, subagent, skill, workflow, schedule, jobs, guard, ACP, MCP and LSP are each a separate package with a Python SDK alongside — but it is a self-declared developer preview shipping only alpha/rc tags and running with its GitHub issue tracker disabled, so its architecture is state of the art while its lifecycle guarantees are not.

goose has the strongest supply-chain and release discipline of the twelve: it is the only one running an OpenSSF Scorecard workflow, it publishes true semver 1.x releases weekly, and it ships the broadest Linux artifact matrix in the shortlist (aarch64/x86_64 in both gnu and musl, plus rpm and a source tarball).

Two shortlisted entries are no longer live options and should not anchor any future selection: AutoGen carries an explicit maintainer 'Maintenance Mode' notice redirecting to microsoft/agent-framework with 11 commits in 52 weeks, and Aider has had zero commits in eight weeks and no release since 2025-08-09 despite 1,882 open issues.

limits: Shortlist bias, not corrected by me: the twelve rows were selected by star count among repos passing mechanical filters, which systematically favours marketing reach over engineering quality. Named absences that plainly belong in an F-agents sub-layer and that I could not score because they were not shortlisted include Anthropic's Claude Code and its agent SDK, SWE-agent/mini-SWE-agent (the reference research harness), Roo Code, Kilo Code, Continue, Zed's ACP agent work, dedicated sandbox/isolation projects (E2B, microsandbox, container-use) and dedicated agent task-queue projects. Treat this as a ranking within a star-ranked sample, not as full SOTA coverage of the sub-layer.

Star counts survive organisation renames, so they measure the lineage rather than the current maintainer. I verified four redirects in this pass: sst/opencode -> anomalyco/opencode, block/goose -> aaif-goose/goose, All-Hands-AI/OpenHands -> OpenHands/OpenHands, paul-gauthier/aider -> Aider-AI/aider. In the OpenHands case the repository's scope also changed (the agent and SDK moved to sibling repos and the main repo is now the 'Agent Canvas' control center), so its 88k stars were substantially earned by different software than the one I scored.

Nothing here was executed. No repository was cloned, installed, built or run, and no acceptance command was reproduced. Every score is documentary — GitHub API metadata, git-tree path inventories, primary README/docs files and release asset listings — so capability_fit in particular reflects claimed and code-present capability, not demonstrated behaviour on this PC or any other.

Benchmark figures are secondary sources, not independently reproduced. The Terminal-Bench 2 numbers (82.0% closed-track, 51.9% open-track) come from an aggregator page; the official tbench.ai leaderboard table is JavaScript-rendered and returned an empty table body to extraction, so I could not confirm the figures against the primary leaderboard in this pass.

Two mechanical-metadata errors in the supplied shortlist were found and corrected by direct inspection, which means other rows may carry errors I did not check: langchain-ai/langgraph is recorded as has_tests='no' but its main-branch tree contains 248 test-matching paths and it runs a CI workflow; deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness's flagged open_issues=0 anomaly is simply has_issues=false (tracker disabled, Discussions only), not suppressed activity.

CI pass rates are only partially computable. Many recent completed runs on default branches return a null conclusion (skipped/cancelled/stale), and for several repos the visible completed runs on the default branch are dominated by bot workflows (issue triage, labelling, deduplication, CLA) rather than the test gate, so 'CI is green' could be confirmed for herdr and crewAI but not for codex, opencode, OpenHands or goose.

Derived counts are approximations. Test and docs figures are path-pattern matches over the recursive git tree, not executed test counts, and they are distorted by repo layout — crewAI's 33,153 docs paths and cline's protobuf-generated SDK paths both inflate raw counts. GitHub's contributor API also caps enumeration at 500, so the 443-474 figures for codex, gemini-cli, autogen and OpenHands are floors, not true counts. GitHub code search returned 0 for most queries (index coverage limits) and was discarded in favour of tree inspection.

Security and provenance were assessed from repository surface only: presence of SECURITY.md, dependabot.yml, CodeQL/Scorecard workflows, and signed release assets. No dependency audit, no SBOM review, no CVE history check and no review of the actual code-review/merge process was performed, and for DeepSeek Harness the merge process is not publicly auditable at all because the issue tracker is disabled.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for US equities. For this sub-layer (agentic coding foundation) I scored the enabling properties that a quant research/backtest/paper-trading program actually depends on — reproducibility of agent runs, execution isolation (sandbox + worktree), deterministic replay/checkpointing, headless/scriptable operation, supply-chain and documentation provenance, and documented failure modes — because no tool in this layer supplies equities-specific safeguards itself. Evidence was taken only from public artifacts dated to 2026-09-21: GitHub API metadata, repository trees, in-repo docs/CI configs, published GitHub security advisories, vendor docs and third-party papers. I did not execute any tool, so no latency or cost figure here is measured.

unknowns: Per-task token and compute cost of the containerized runtime (no published figures)
Whether the container runtime enforces network egress restrictions by default
Applicability to point-in-time equities data handling (not addressed by the project)
scores.notes: Strongest evidence posture of the shortlist on two independent axes. (1) Reproducible self-testing: the repo ships deterministic mock-LLM end-to-end harnesses (playwright.mock-llm.config.ts, playwright.mock-llm-docker.config.ts, driven by mock-llm-e2e.yml and mock-llm-docker-e2e.yml) plus stryker.config.mjs mutation testing — this is the only candidate that tests agent behaviour without a live model in the loop, which is exactly the determinism property a research pipeline needs. (2) Published external evidence: CodeAct 2.1 published a reproducible 53% SWE-bench Verified / 41.7% SWE-bench Lite result, and the project is subject to independent academic scrutiny — arXiv 2510.08996 measures a 20-40% relative degradation of the OpenHands agent when SWE-bench Verified issues are mutated into realistic user queries. I count that third-party negative result as high-grade evidence, not a demerit: it is the only candidate whose validity limits are quantified by outsiders. Lifecycle is the best of the set: stable v1.x major (v1.21.0 released 2026-09-22), release-please manifest, CHANGELOG.md, sdk-version-sync.yml, helm/ and docker/ for self-hosting, MIT. 460 contributors. Documented failure mode: GHSA-7h8w-hj9j-8rjw, high-severity command injection in the git diff handler (2026-03-23) — patched, and disclosed through a proper advisory channel. Marked down only on quality_cost: container-per-session isolation is resource-heavy and no public cost data exists.

unknowns: Token/cost efficiency versus alternatives (no published comparison)
Stability of the git-worktree feature, which docs label experimental
Whether behavioural eval results are published, or only the harness
scores.notes: Most complete coverage of the stated sub-layer requirements in one codebase, with docs for every element: docs/cli/sandbox.md (which explicitly names 'Consistency: ensure reproducible environments across different systems' as a design goal), git-worktrees.md, headless.md, checkpointing.md, rewind.md, session-management.md, skills.md, using-agent-skills.md, trusted-folders.md, telemetry.md, enterprise.md, acp-mode.md. Evidence discipline is the strongest in-repo of any candidate: evals/ holds ~40 behavioral eval specs including sandbox_recovery, prompt_injection_mcp, provenance_attribution, concurrency-safety, subagents and subtask_delegation, supported by llm-judge.ts and statistics-helper.ts, formally documented in docs/behavioral-evals.md as an 'Eval Development Kit' with eval:inventory/eval:validate tooling and JSON output for CI. This is backed by eval.yml, eval-pr.yml, evals-nightly.yml and deflake.yml — i.e. it treats model non-determinism as a statistical problem rather than asserting pass/fail, which is the correct methodology. Separate integration-tests/, perf-tests/ and memory-tests/ trees. 443 contributors, Apache-2.0, nightly releases. Zero published security advisories — I read that as unproven rather than clean, and note the project was named in a cross-vendor container-privilege sandbox-escape class reported publicly and since fixed. Held to 2 on lifecycle_portability: still pre-1.0 (v0.60/v0.62 nightlies), worktrees explicitly experimental, and the agent is coupled to Google's models despite ACP interop.

unknowns: No in-repo behavioural eval or agent benchmark suite was found (CI is engineering CI, not agent evaluation)
Whether published agent benchmark numbers are independently reproducible from this repo
Cost per task; not published
scores.notes: Best-documented execution-isolation controls for automated, non-interactive runs, which is the single most load-bearing property for an unattended research pipeline. developers.openai.com/codex/noninteractive documents `codex exec` with explicit three-level sandboxing (`--sandbox read-only` as the default, `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access`), and `--ephemeral` to suppress persistence of session rollout files to disk — a genuine reproducibility and data-hygiene control I did not find an equivalent of elsewhere. Also ships docs/execpolicy.md, docs/skills.md, a `.worktreeinclude` for worktree scoping, and first-party SDKs in sdk/typescript, sdk/python and sdk/python-runtime. Engineering rigor is high: Bazel build, rust-ci-full with nextest, cargo-deny, codespell, blob-size policy; 474 contributors; multiple alpha releases per day (rust-v0.157.0-alpha.3 on 2026-09-22). Two real deductions. First, evidence: the in-repo docs/sandbox.md, docs/exec.md and docs/execpolicy.md are two-line stubs that redirect to developers.openai.com — the authoritative documentation is not versioned with the source revision, which weakens source-pinning and auditability, and I found no agent-behaviour eval suite in-repo. Second, documented failure mode: GHSA-w5fx-fh39-j5rw, a high-severity sandbox bypass caused by path-configuration logic — i.e. the very isolation boundary this tool is selected for has failed once in the public record. 18,188 open issues indicates heavy triage debt.

unknowns: No published headline benchmark results found in-repo (harness present, results absent)
Effectiveness and model coverage of the goose-local-inference crate
Measured cost/latency
scores.notes: The most governance-mature candidate, which matters for a multi-year R&D dependency. It is the only shortlisted repo publishing both GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md alongside SECURITY.md, and it runs OpenSSF scorecard.yml, cargo-deny, cargo-machete and dependabot auto-merge in CI. Conformance testing is unusually rigorous and directly relevant to reproducibility across model swaps: mcp-conformance.yml and model-toolcall-conformance.yml assert protocol and tool-call behaviour independent of any one provider, plus goose-self-test.yaml and update-health-dashboard.yml. evals/harbor is a real harness (runner.py, reporter.py, reporter recipes, config_template.yaml), and workflow_recipes/ plus recipes give parameterized, re-runnable agent invocations — the closest thing in the set to a reproducible experiment definition. Crate layout is clean for embedding (goose-agent, goose-sdk, goose-context-management, goose-test-support), and goose-local-inference is the only first-class local/offline inference path among the twelve, which is materially relevant where market data or positions cannot leave the premises. Stable lifecycle: v1.51.0, RELEASE.md + RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md, release-plz, canary and separate patch/minor release workflows, Apache-2.0, 452 contributors. Evidence held at 2 because the harness exists but I found no published result set. Documented failure mode: GHSA-r5pp-p5r8-466r, high-severity arbitrary command execution in `goose review` via git core.fsmonitor — a repo-content-triggered execution path, which is a relevant threat when agents check out third-party data or strategy repos.

unknowns: No agent-capability benchmark published for the framework itself
Division of function between OSS core and the commercial LangGraph Platform for production deployment
Overhead of checkpoint persistence at research-sweep scale
scores.notes: Not a coding client and it supplies no sandbox, worktree isolation or skills framework, so it only partially answers this sub-layer — hence capability_fit 2. But it is the one candidate that provides the durable-execution and replay primitive a reproducible research pipeline needs as a first-class, separately-tested concern: libs/checkpoint, libs/checkpoint-postgres, libs/checkpoint-sqlite and, notably, libs/checkpoint-conformance, with libs/checkpoint/tests containing test_conformance_delta.py, test_encrypted.py, test_jsonplus.py and test_store.py. Checkpointed, resumable, inspectable state is what makes an agent-driven backtest sweep auditable after the fact. This also corrects the shortlist: its has_tests="no" flag is wrong — the tests live under libs/, not repo root. Maintenance and disclosure are mature: 1.2.12 released 2026-09-21, stable 1.x, SDKs for Python and JS, and nine published security advisories, which I read as a sign of a functioning disclosure process rather than of poor quality. One caveat bears directly on the lens: GHSA-fjqc-hq36-qh5p is unsafe JSON deserialization in checkpoint loading — a vulnerability in the exact replay primitive the tool would be chosen for, so restored checkpoints must be treated as untrusted input. GHSA-fvww-7h3r-vfhp (SDK custom auth silently ignoring `actions=` on resource decorators) is a silent-failure class worth noting for anything permissioned. MIT for the OSS core; the managed Platform is a separate commercial product.

unknowns: Current operational status of the eval framework (self-documented as partially disabled)
Whether npm supply-chain controls were hardened after the 2026-02 incident
Cost per task
scores.notes: Methodologically the most statistically literate eval design of the twelve, and I want to credit that explicitly: evals/analysis/src/metrics.ts computes pass@k AND pass^k, with classifier.ts doing failure-pattern matching against patterns/cline-failures.yaml, plus baselines/ for regression detection and a layered structure (contract/unit tests without LLM calls, smoke tests, then full cline-bench e2e over 12 production bug fixes). pass^k is the right reliability metric for a non-deterministic agent and nobody else in this set computes it. However, evals/README.md openly states that Layer 2 smoke tests are 'partially disabled while the eval framework is repointed at the new SDK CLI' and that the auto-running cline-evals-regression.yml workflow is 'off until someone wires the build step' — a self-disclosed, currently-unenforced evidence gap, so evidence stays at 2 despite good design. Capability coverage is broad (sdk/, CLI, `.worktreeinclude`, hooks, kanban). The serious concerns are provenance and attack surface: three published advisories, including GHSA-9ppg-jx86-fqw7, an unauthorized npm publish of cline@2.3.0 with a modified postinstall script — an actual supply-chain compromise, which is the failure mode that most directly threatens a trading research environment — plus GHSA-5c57-rqjx-35g2 (critical) and GHSA-3cj3-hqcr-g934 (high), both cross-origin WebSocket hijacks in locally-bound server components. Maintaining VS Code, JetBrains, desktop and CLI surfaces simultaneously adds version-matrix risk.

unknowns: No evals/ or benchmark directory found; no published agent evaluation
Whether sandboxing exists beyond container packaging (containers.yml)
Real open-issue backlog, given aggressive auto-close automation
Cost per task
scores.notes: Provenance note first, since the shortlist flagged it as open: the historical sst/opencode path resolves to anomalyco/opencode with an identical repository id and created_at of 2025-04-30, so this is a confirmed org rename (Anomaly, anoma.ly), not a fork or a namespace hijack. GitHub redirects handle the old path. Capability is a capable, model-agnostic, plugin-extensible coding agent with a server/SDK and nix packaging, but I found no dedicated sandbox or worktree-isolation documentation and no eval or benchmark tree at all — hence evidence 1, the weakest evidence posture of any actively-maintained candidate here. Maintenance is genuinely high-velocity but the governance signals give me pause under a research-validity lens: .github/workflows contains close-issues.yml, close-prs.yml, duplicate-issues.yml and compliance-close.yml running against a 6,016-issue open backlog, which makes the public issue record an unreliable source for discovering failure modes — an important limitation when the issue tracker is the main way outsiders learn what breaks. Two serious documented failure modes, both disclosed 2026-01-12: GHSA-c83v-7274-4vgp (critical — a malicious website can execute commands on the local system via XSS) and GHSA-vxw4-wv6m-9hhh (high — unauthenticated HTTP server allowing arbitrary command execution). Both are drive-by local-code-execution classes, which is disqualifying for an unattended runtime unless the version is pinned well past the fix. MIT, self-hostable, 209k stars.

unknowns: No benchmark results published — BENCHMARK.md is a pointer, not a result set
No releases at all; no versioning or stability contract
Cost, latency and quality entirely unmeasured publicly
Issues are disabled, so no public user-reported failure-mode record exists
The 232k-star / 27.9k-fork figure at ~5.5 weeks of age is not corroborated by 36 contributors and 994 watchers
scores.notes: On paper this is the most complete architectural match to the sub-layer definition of any candidate: packages/ contains sandbox (with sandbox-local, sandbox-policy and sandbox-windows-acl), guard (timeout-policy, repeat-tool-reminder), jobs and schedule (task queues), credentials, identity, hooks, compaction, context, plan, goal, preset, skills-adjacent tooling, plus acp, mcp, lsp, sdk and host. CI is correspondingly broad, including e2e.yml, sandbox.yml and a weighted-approval review process. MIT with THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and SAFETY.md. But I scored capability on structure and everything else on demonstrated evidence, and the evidence is close to absent. BENCHMARK.md is a single paragraph telling you to install the SDK and run a minimal variant — there are no published numbers; benchmarks/ holds scenario scaffolding (session-open, terminal-io, conversation-fold, agent-continuation) with no results. The README states it is in developer preview and, in capitals, that there WILL BE compatibility-breaking changes; there are zero releases, so lifecycle_portability is 0, not low. Issues are disabled in favour of Discussions, which explains the open_issues=0 in the shortlist metadata (it is not a clean backlog) and also means there is no public record of user-observed failures. Velocity is extreme — roughly 4,600 commits in 30 days — but from only 36 contributors. I deliberately did not let the star count influence any score.

unknowns: No published evaluation, benchmark or third-party assessment found
Durability semantics beyond the documented process-loss-on-restart behaviour
Security posture: zero advisories at 6 months of age is unproven, not clean
scores.notes: Narrow but genuinely well-matched to two of the sub-layer's requirements — worker/subagent orchestration and worktree isolation. The source tree is explicit about it: worktree.rs, session.rs, persist.rs, agent_resume.rs, handoff_runtime.rs, remote.rs, plus a documented socket API and an agent skill so agents can spawn panes, prompt each other and block until another agent is genuinely blocked. Crucially it is agent-agnostic — it owns the terminals of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode and others rather than replacing them — which makes it a low-lock-in coordination layer rather than a competing client. quality_cost is the one 3 I awarded in this column and it is design-evidenced rather than merely asserted: a single Rust binary with no Electron, and as a multiplexer it adds no model cost of its own. Two honest limits. It provides session and worktree isolation but not sandboxing — it does not confine the processes it hosts, so it is not a security boundary. And the README itself documents a durability limit: after a server or machine restart it restores the saved layout and can resume supported agent sessions, but 'the original processes do not survive'. Evidence is thin — tests/, ci.yml, pr-gate.yml and agent_view_eval.rs exist, but there is no published evaluation. At v0.9.1 with rolling preview builds, 87 contributors and six months of history, it is pre-1.0 and should be treated as keep-but-compare rather than a foundation commitment.

unknowns: No eval or benchmark directory found in the repository
No published agent-capability evaluation located
Token/cost profile of role-playing multi-agent patterns — not measured, no public data found
scores.notes: Weakest fit to this sub-layer's stated requirements. CrewAI is a role-playing multi-agent orchestration framework, not a coding foundation: I found no sandbox, no worktree or process isolation, no task-queue durability primitive, no skills/instructions framework and no coding client. It would sit above this layer, not in it. Evidence is the thinner half of the problem — the repo has conftest.py and a lib/ monorepo (crewai-core, crewai-tools, crewai-files, cli, devtools) but no evals/ or benchmarks/ tree and no published capability evaluation I could locate, and the README is largely promotional. Maintenance is unambiguously strong: 1.15.22 released 2026-09-16, pushed 2026-09-21, uv.lock and pre-commit config, MIT, zero published security advisories. Lifecycle held at 2 because the recent restructure into lib/ is a non-trivial layout migration for downstream users. quality_cost is 0 rather than low: I found no public cost or efficiency data for this project and I am not willing to infer a number from reputation, so it stays unknown.

unknowns: Whether any maintainer intends to resume development
Whether the benchmark harness still runs against current model APIs
Security posture: no advisories published, but also no active maintainer to receive a report
scores.notes: An unusual profile: excellent evidence, no maintenance. Evidence earns a 3 on its own merits — benchmark/ is a fully reproducible, containerized evaluation harness (Dockerfile, docker_build.sh, benchmark.py, swe_bench.py with swe-bench.txt and swe-bench-lite.txt instance lists, clone-exercism.sh for the polyglot exercises, rungrid.py for sweeps, and problem_stats.py / over_time.py / plots.py for analysis and longitudinal reporting). Publishing the harness, the instance lists and the plotting code together is better research practice than most vendor benchmark claims in this set. Capability is limited for this sub-layer: strong git-native editing and repo-map context plus headless `--message`/`--yes` operation, but no sandbox, no worktree orchestration, no subagents and no skills framework. Maintenance is the decisive problem and is 0 on the evidence: exactly one commit in the 120 days to 2026-09-21 (latest commit 2026-05-22), the last release was v0.86.0 on 2025-08-09 — over thirteen months ago — against 1,882 open issues and 503 open pull requests. A dependency with 503 unreviewed PRs and no releasing maintainer is an unpatched-vulnerability vector regardless of code quality. Apache-2.0 and self-hostable, so the harness remains usable as a frozen, forkable reference even though the agent should not be a foundation choice.

unknowns: Whether Microsoft will apply security patches during maintenance mode
Whether the CC-BY-4.0 designation is intentional or an unremediated licensing error
Cost profile — not measured
scores.notes: Should be excluded from consideration for this sub-layer on two independent grounds, each sufficient. First, end of life: the README carries a maintenance-mode badge and a CAUTION block stating AutoGen 'will not receive new features or enhancements and is community managed going forward', directing new users to microsoft/agent-framework, and the commit record confirms it — zero commits in the 90 days to 2026-09-21, last release python-v0.7.5 on 2025-09-30. Second, licensing: GitHub reports the license as CC-BY-4.0 and the LICENSE file opens with 'Attribution 4.0 International'. Creative Commons explicitly does not recommend CC licenses for software; CC-BY-4.0 grants no patent license and its warranty and attribution terms are drafted for creative works, so redistribution or production deployment carries real legal ambiguity. That is a deployment-fit problem independent of code quality, and it scores 1 rather than 0 only because the intent is evidently permissive. Capability fit was weak for this sub-layer anyway — a multi-agent conversation framework with no sandbox, isolation or coding-foundation primitives. Evidence gets a 2 for the genuine published research lineage behind AutoGen. One credit worth recording: a documented migration guide to Microsoft Agent Framework exists, so existing users have a defined exit path. The successor, microsoft/agent-framework, is MIT-licensed and actively developed but was absent from the shortlist.

sota_claims.claim: Gemini CLI ships the most extensive in-repository behavioral-evaluation apparatus of any open-source coding agent in this shortlist — roughly 40 executable eval specifications governed by a documented Eval Development Kit with an LLM judge, a statistics helper and dedicated de-flaking CI — making it the only candidate that treats model non-determinism as a statistical measurement problem rather than a pass/fail assertion.

OpenHands is the only shortlisted agent whose capability claims have been both published as reproducible results by its authors (53% on SWE-bench Verified with CodeAct 2.1) and independently stress-tested by third-party researchers, who measured a 20-40% relative degradation when benchmark issues are mutated into realistic user queries — giving it the only quantified external estimate of benchmark-to-reality validity gap in this set.

OpenAI Codex provides the most explicitly documented execution-isolation controls for unattended agent runs among these candidates, defaulting `codex exec` to a read-only sandbox with named escalation tiers (workspace-write, danger-full-access) plus an `--ephemeral` flag that suppresses on-disk session persistence — though its own advisory record contains a high-severity sandbox bypass, so the boundary is documented rather than proven.

Goose is the most governance- and supply-chain-mature candidate in the shortlist — the only one publishing both GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md while running OpenSSF Scorecard, cargo-deny, and dedicated MCP and model-tool-call conformance suites in CI — and the only one shipping a first-class local-inference crate for environments where data cannot leave the premises.

Cline's evaluation framework is the only one in this shortlist that computes pass^k alongside pass@k with an automated failure classifier and stored regression baselines — the methodologically correct reliability metric for non-deterministic agents — but the framework's own README documents that its smoke-test layer and regression workflow are currently disabled, so the design is ahead of the enforcement.

limits: Selection bias in the supplied shortlist: it was built as the top 12 by star count among mechanically-passing candidates, and star count is a popularity proxy, not a merit proxy for this sub-layer. That filter excluded the tools most directly matching the stated requirements of worktree/sandbox isolation — e2b-dev/E2B (13,906 stars, Apache-2.0, active), dagger/container-use (4,046 stars, 'enable multiple agents to work safely and independently', active), daytonaio/daytona (71,740 stars) — and SWE-agent/SWE-agent (20,384 stars, MIT, NeurIPS 2024, actively pushed 2026-09-21), which is the canonical published agent-computer-interface reference. It also omitted microsoft/agent-framework (MIT, active), the official successor to the shortlisted-but-EOL AutoGen, and anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python. Coverage of this sub-layer is therefore not comprehensive, and the gap is systematically biased against smaller, more specialized, more task-appropriate infrastructure.

Lens-to-layer mismatch that must not be papered over: none of the twelve repositories addresses any US-equities research-validity requirement — point-in-time correctness, lookahead or survivorship safeguards, corporate-action handling, cost modelling, or paper/live parity. I scored capability_fit strictly on the enabling properties a coding foundation can supply (execution isolation, deterministic replay, checkpointing, headless automation, provenance and auditability). A high score here is evidence about engineering hygiene only and confers no assurance whatsoever about backtest validity; those safeguards must be established at the data and execution-engine layers and cannot be inherited from this one.

Two errors in the supplied mechanical metadata that would have distorted scoring if taken at face value. LangGraph is recorded as has_tests="no", which is incorrect — it has libs/checkpoint/tests plus an entire libs/checkpoint-conformance package; the probe evidently only looked for a root-level tests/ directory. DeepSeek Harness is recorded with open_issues=0, which reflects that GitHub Issues are disabled in favour of Discussions, not a cleared backlog; read naively that field inverts its meaning, since it also means no public user-reported failure record exists for that project.

Unverifiable popularity signal on the newest entry: deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness shows 232,449 stars and 27,899 forks at roughly 5.5 weeks of age, against 36 contributors and 994 watchers. I could not corroborate that ratio from any independent source and I make no claim about its cause. I scored the project only on inspectable artifacts — repository tree, CI configuration, README, license — and excluded stars and forks from every criterion. The same exclusion was applied to all twelve for consistency.

Evidence class and recency boundaries. I executed none of these tools and ran no benchmark, so every score derives from published artifacts (GitHub API metadata, repository trees, in-repo documentation and CI configuration, published security advisories, vendor documentation and third-party papers) observed on 2026-09-21; nothing here is a measured local result. In particular no latency, token or dollar figure was measured for any candidate, so quality_cost is the weakest-evidenced column throughout and several entries are deliberately left at 0/unknown rather than estimated. Absence of published security advisories was treated as unproven rather than safe, which matters for the newest projects (deepseek-harness, herdr) and for gemini-cli, which was publicly named in a cross-vendor container-privilege sandbox-escape class that was subsequently fixed.

verdicts.claim: Codex is the only shortlisted coding client shipping OS-level sandboxing on all three desktop platforms plus first-party git-worktree isolation with its own integration test suite and both Python and TypeScript SDKs.
verdicts.reason: The component facts check out (codex-rs/cli/tests/worktree.rs is 35,532 bytes; sdk/ contains python, python-runtime and typescript; stable release rust-v0.155.1 ships bwrap-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.sigstore; codex-rs has bwrap, linux-sandbox, windows-sandbox-*, mxc-sandbox and sandboxing crates). The 'only' fails: deepseek-harness packages/sandbox documents per-platform OS backends in sandbox-local ('Linux bwrap then Landlock, macOS Seatbelt, Windows restricted token') plus a separate sandbox-windows-acl backend and the same read-only / workspace-write / danger-full-access mode vocabulary, and ships both a Python SDK (python/sdk with pyproject.toml, src, tests, examples, uv.lock) and a TypeScript SDK (packages/sdk with client/protocol/server), with 82 worktree code hits in-tree. Codex may still be the better-run repo, but it is not uniquely complete on this combination.

verdicts.claim: On Terminal-Bench 2 the verified top entry is Codex on GPT-5.5 at 82.0% while OpenHands holds the open-harness record at 51.9%, making OpenHands the strongest publicly benchmarked open coding harness with a ~30 point open/closed gap.
verdicts.reason: Three separate errors. (1) Stale board: Terminal-Bench 2.0 is archived and superseded by 2.1 (28 of 89 tasks fixed); on 2.1 the top entry is Claude Code / Claude 5 Fable at 83.8% and Codex CLI / GPT-5.5 is second at 83.1% - 82.0% is neither the current top nor a current Codex figure. (2) OpenHands does not appear anywhere on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 leaderboard; the highest-placed open-source harness is mini-SWE-agent (Princeton, MIT) at 76.2% with Muse Spark 1.1, refuting 'strongest publicly benchmarked open coding harness'. (3) The 51.9% / 30.1pp figures come from codesota's open-WEIGHT MODEL track (OpenHands + Claude Opus 4.5, Jan 2026), not an open-vs-closed HARNESS comparison; against the actual top open harness the gap is ~7.6pp, not ~30. 51.9% also appears verbatim in the TB2.0-vs-2.1 table as the Sonnet 4.6 / Claude Code TB2.0 cell, so a cell misread is plausible.

verdicts.claim: DeepSeek Harness is the most completely plugin-decomposed open agent runtime (sandbox, subagent, skill, workflow, schedule, jobs, guard, ACP, MCP, LSP each a separate package, with a Python SDK) but is a developer preview shipping only alpha/rc tags with its issue tracker disabled.
verdicts.reason: Every checkable element verified. packages/ contains acp, guard, jobs, lsp, mcp, sandbox, schedule, sdk, skill, subagent and workflow as separate packages; python/ contains sdk and sdk-runtime. GitHub API reports has_issues=false and open_issues_count=0 (tracker disabled). All 8 most recent releases are prereleases: dsh-v0.1.6-alpha.2, -alpha.1, dsh-v0.1.5-rc.2, -rc.1, -alpha.2, -alpha.1, dsh-v0.1.3-alpha.2, -alpha.1; no stable tag exists. Only the 'most completely' superlative is unfalsifiable, and I found no open runtime with finer decomposition.

verdicts.claim: goose has the strongest supply-chain and release discipline of the twelve: the only one running OpenSSF Scorecard, publishing true semver 1.x releases weekly, and shipping the broadest Linux artifact matrix in the shortlist.
verdicts.reason: Supported, with one overstatement. .github/workflows/scorecard.yml exists and runs on schedule/push/branch_protection_rule; no scorecard workflow or code hit exists in codex, cline, opencode, gemini-cli, OpenHands or deepseek-harness. Releases v1.48.0 (2026-08-27), v1.49.0 (09-03), v1.50.0 (09-08), v1.50.1 (09-14) and v1.51.0 (09-17) are all non-prerelease semver at roughly weekly cadence with 37 assets each. Linux matrix confirmed: aarch64/x86_64 in gnu and musl plus deb, rpm, flatpak and a source tarball - broader than Codex, whose stable rust-v0.155.1 ships only gnu/musl tarballs, zst and manylinux wheels with no distro packages. Overstatement: 'strongest supply chain' is contestable because Codex publishes a cosign/sigstore bundle as a release asset for every Linux binary (including bwrap), whereas goose's v1.51.0 asset list contains no signature or attestation file - its Sigstore OIDC signing and SLSA provenance appear only as release.yml permissions (id-token/attestations: write).

verdicts.claim: AutoGen (Maintenance Mode notice, 11 commits in 52 weeks) and Aider (zero commits in eight weeks, no release since 2025-08-09, 1,882 open issues) are no longer live options.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, and the Aider half understates the problem. AutoGen's README carries a 'Maintenance Mode' badge and a CAUTION block redirecting to microsoft/agent-framework; the commits API returns exactly 11 commits since 2025-09-21 and pushed_at is 2026-04-15. Aider's newest release is v0.86.0 published 2025-08-09 (previous v0.85.0, 2025-06-27) and open_issues_count is 1883. Correction: Aider's last commit is 2026-05-22T14:02:20Z - about 17 weeks of dormancy, not eight, with zero commits since 2026-07-01. The conclusion that neither should anchor a future selection stands.

verdicts.claim: Gemini CLI ships the most extensive in-repository behavioral-evaluation apparatus (roughly 40 eval specs, an Eval Development Kit with LLM judge, statistics helper and de-flaking CI) and is the only candidate treating model non-determinism as a statistical measurement problem rather than pass/fail.
verdicts.reason: Volume is right, the statistical superlative is inverted. evals/ holds exactly 38 *.eval.ts specs plus llm-judge.ts, statistics-helper.ts and test helpers; docs/behavioral-evals.md exists (7,119 bytes); deflake.yml, eval.yml, eval-pr.yml and evals-nightly.yml are present. But statistics-helper.ts in full implements only countMatchingIds, roundStat, average and averageNullable - no variance, confidence interval or reliability estimator. Cline's evals/analysis/src/metrics.ts implements passAtK and passCaretK (documented as 'P(all k trials pass) - reliability measure') plus a variance function, so Cline, not Gemini CLI, is the candidate that models non-determinism statistically. The 'only candidate' clause is false.

verdicts.claim: OpenHands is the only shortlisted agent whose capability claims were both published as reproducible results by its authors (53% SWE-bench Verified with CodeAct 2.1) and independently stress-tested by third parties measuring 20-40% relative degradation on mutated benchmark issues.
verdicts.reason: The third-party half verifies: arXiv 2510.08996 ('Saving SWE-Bench: A Benchmark Mutation Approach for Realistic Agent Evaluation', accepted CAIN 2026) states OpenHands 'suffers a 20-40% drop in relative success rates' on mutated SWE-bench Verified across all agent-model combinations. The claim fails on currency and on 'only'. Currency: the 53% figure comes from the CodeAct 2.1 post whose own text says it is 'powered by the new Claude Sonnet 3.5' - a late-2024 result, while SWE-bench Verified leaders in Sept 2026 sit near 96% and the benchmark is widely described as saturating/contaminated; presenting it as the ranked #1's capability evidence anchors on a two-year-old number. 'Only': Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and Claude Code all carry Terminal-Bench 2.1 scores produced and verified by the Terminal-Bench team rather than by the vendors, which is independent third-party measurement of those harnesses.

verdicts.claim: Codex provides the most explicitly documented execution-isolation controls for unattended runs (codex exec read-only by default, workspace-write / danger-full-access tiers, --ephemeral), though its advisory record contains a high-severity sandbox bypass so the boundary is documented rather than proven.
verdicts.reason: All facts confirmed from primary sources. The cited page states 'By default, codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox', documents --sandbox workspace-write and --sandbox danger-full-access, deprecates --full-auto, and documents --ephemeral for not persisting session rollout files. The repository's own security-advisories endpoint returns GHSA-w5fx-fh39-j5rw, severity high, 'Sandbox bypass due to bug in path configuration logic' (published 2025-09-19), so the hedge is accurate. Caveat on the superlative only: deepseek-harness documents the identical three-mode vocabulary plus per-platform backends, escalation choreography and fail-closed errors in packages/sandbox and docs/subsystems/sandbox.md, so 'most explicitly documented' is arguable rather than established.

verdicts.claim: Goose is the most governance- and supply-chain-mature candidate: the only one publishing both GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md while running OpenSSF Scorecard, cargo-deny and MCP/model-tool-call conformance suites in CI, and the only one shipping a first-class local-inference crate.
verdicts.reason: Verified. goose's root tree contains GOVERNANCE.md, MAINTAINERS.md, SECURITY.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, RELEASE.md, RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md and deny.toml; none of codex, cline, opencode, gemini-cli, OpenHands or deepseek-harness has GOVERNANCE.md or MAINTAINERS.md at root. CI includes scorecard.yml, cargo-deny.yml, cargo-machete.yml, mcp-conformance.yml and model-toolcall-conformance.yml. crates/ contains goose-local-inference alongside goose-providers. Caveat: 'the only one for premises-bound data' overstates the gap - Codex ships dedicated ollama and lmstudio crates in codex-rs covering the same operational need through a local server rather than an in-process crate.

verdicts.claim: Cline's eval framework is the only one in the shortlist computing pass^k alongside pass@k with an automated failure classifier and stored regression baselines, but its own README documents that the smoke-test layer and regression workflow are disabled, so the design is ahead of the enforcement.
verdicts.reason: Mostly verified, one element does not exist. evals/analysis/src/metrics.ts implements passAtK and passCaretK with a documented variance measure; classifier.ts and patterns/cline-failures.yaml are present; the README confirms 'Smoke tests (Layer 2) are partially disabled' and that 'the auto-running cline-evals-regression.yml workflow are off'. Code searches for pass^k in goose, OpenHands and gemini-cli return zero, supporting the 'only' clause. Correction: 'stored regression baselines' is unsupported - evals/ contains .gitignore, ARCHITECTURE.md, README.md, analysis, benchmarks, cline-bench, e2e, smoke-tests and configs, and evals/baselines returns HTTP 404; baselines/ exists only in the README's ASCII diagram. That strengthens rather than weakens the claim's 'design ahead of enforcement' conclusion.

survivors: DeepSeek Harness is the most completely plugin-decomposed open agent runtime (separate sandbox/subagent/skill/workflow/schedule/jobs/guard/ACP/MCP/LSP packages plus a Python SDK) but is a developer preview with alpha/rc-only tags and a disabled issue tracker.

goose is the only shortlisted repo running an OpenSSF Scorecard workflow, publishes non-prerelease semver 1.x roughly weekly, and ships the broadest Linux artifact matrix (gnu+musl on aarch64/x86_64 plus deb, rpm, flatpak and source tarball) - though Codex, not goose, publishes per-artifact sigstore signatures.
AutoGen (Maintenance Mode notice, 11 commits in 52 weeks) and Aider (last release 2025-08-09, last commit 2026-05-22, 1,883 open issues) are not live options and should not anchor a future selection.

Codex documents read-only-by-default codex exec with workspace-write / danger-full-access tiers and an --ephemeral flag, while its own advisory GHSA-w5fx-fh39-j5rw (high, sandbox bypass) means the boundary is documented rather than proven.

goose is the only shortlisted repo publishing both GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md alongside Scorecard, cargo-deny and MCP/model-tool-call conformance CI, and ships a dedicated goose-local-inference crate.

Cline is the only shortlisted repo computing pass^k alongside pass@k with an automated failure classifier, while its own README documents the smoke-test layer and regression workflow as disabled - and its regression baselines directory does not actually exist in the tree.

better_alternatives_found.name: mini-SWE-agent
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Directly beats the #1-ranked OpenHands on the benchmark the judge used to rank it: mini-SWE-agent is the highest-placed open-source harness on Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 76.2% (Muse Spark 1.1) while OpenHands has no TB2.1 entry at all. MIT, 7,850 stars, pushed 2026-09-21, ~100-line Python core with no monorepo or config sprawl - a far better fit for Linux/Python 3.12 local-first reproducibility than a 90k-star web platform, and trivially auditable for agent-run reproducibility.

better_alternatives_found.name: oh-my-pi
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Absent from both rankings despite 32,364 stars, MIT licence and commits on 2026-09-22. Rust core (~80k lines) plus TypeScript, Bazel build with MODULE.bazel.lock, deny.toml, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt, Nix flake, its own python/ tree, 60+ providers, 31 built-in tools, 14 LSP and 28 DAP operations - a deeper tool surface than goose or cline on the same hygiene dimensions the engineering judge scored, with a documented governance risk (a vouch requirement for PRs, currently suspended) that deserves scoring rather than omission.

better_alternatives_found.name: container-use
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The sub-layer explicitly covers worktree/sandbox isolation, yet both rankings scored isolation only as a side feature of monolithic coding clients. container-use (Dagger, Apache-2.0, 4,046 stars, pushed 2026-09-21) is purpose-built for it: isolated containerised dev environments plus a git branch per agent, agent-agnostic so it isolates Codex, Claude Code or goose alike instead of tying isolation to one client's sandbox implementation.

better_alternatives_found.name: OpenSandbox
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Apache-2.0, 15,450 stars, pushed 2026-09-21: a dedicated extensible sandbox runtime for AI agents, larger and more focused than any isolation component inside the ranked clients. Given Codex's own high-severity sandbox-bypass advisory, a standalone audited sandbox runtime is a stronger control for unattended quant runs than trusting a coding client's in-tree sandbox crate.

better_alternatives_found.name: OpenShell
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Apache-2.0, 8,739 stars, pushed 2026-09-22, vendor-backed by NVIDIA and described as a safe private runtime for autonomous AI agents - a local-first execution-isolation layer with organisational backing that neither ranking considered, despite both lenses treating execution isolation as decisive.

better_alternatives_found.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Both judges wrote off AutoGen but neither scored its maintainer-designated successor. AutoGen's own README redirects users here, and the repo is MIT, 13,708 stars, pushed 2026-09-21 with a stated production/stable-API posture - so the orchestration slot the second ranking filled with LangGraph has an unexamined direct competitor that carries the migration path from the entry both judges declared dead.

No rate limits hit; all 120 gh api calls succeeded on first try (gh authenticated, 5000/h core quota was not exhausted).

tvly/WebSearch were not needed: all 39 candidates in the computed-task list already carried a GitHub repository_url, so GitHub's API alone provided complete mechanical metadata for every candidate; no additional discovery modality was required to reach full coverage of the given candidate set.

license=NOASSERTION (serena, pgvector, weaviate, sourcebot-dev/sourcebot, and the archived sourcegraph snapshot) is GitHub's own license-detector output, not a legal finding that no OSI license exists -- some of these repos plausibly do carry a recognizable license file whose text GitHub's detector didn't match to a known SPDX id. The mechanical rule as given only allows spdx_id evidence, so these were dropped on that basis; a human or a second detector pass could overturn this for any one of them.

Mechanical rules alone (not archived, pushed<=12mo or release<=18mo, OSI/spdx license, relevance) left 33 of 40 candidates passing, not <=12. To cut to the requested cap without a subjective merit call, a second purely mechanical tiebreak (GitHub star count, already used as the discovery-modality proxy in the candidate list itself) was applied to select the top 12 by stars. This is a materiality/adoption-count filter, not a quality judgment, but it is a real synthesis choice this task made and should be named as such if the shortlist is used downstream.
BLINDNESS RULE followed: no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> was opened; all data came from `gh api` against the given candidate URLs.
