sota_claims.claim: Docling is the only document-ingestion candidate in this shortlist that combines a permissive MIT licence, hosting by a neutral foundation (LF AI & Data) rather than a single vendor, and a published technical report describing the specific layout and table-structure models it ships.

Faiss is the only repository in this shortlist that runs a dedicated index-serialization backward-compatibility CI job, making it the strongest documented guarantee of durable on-disk format stability in the retrieval layer.

An independent, non-vendor 2026 benchmark of long-term-memory frameworks placed mem0 in a 77-81% LoCoMo accuracy cluster with RAG and full-context baselines while Graphiti and cognee reached only 55-56%, a ranking that contradicts both Mem0's and Zep's own published evaluations and makes mem0 the only agent-memory project here with favourable third-party evidence.

Qdrant is the only shortlisted vector store that deploys as a single self-contained Rust binary with no external database, queue or object-store dependency, giving it the lowest single-machine operational footprint of the three stores under a Linux/WSL2 local-first constraint.

Graphiti no longer has a maintained embedded graph backend: its own pyproject marks the Kuzu extra deprecated because the upstream project is unmaintained and states it will be removed, leaving an external Neo4j or FalkorDB as the practical requirement as of v0.30.x.

limits: COVERAGE IS NOT COMPREHENSIVE FOR THIS SUB-LAYER. The sub-layer definition explicitly names 'code navigation and retrieval (LSP/symbol tools, structural search, code RAG)', and the supplied shortlist contains zero candidates of that kind — no LSP/symbol server, no ast-grep/zoekt/Sourcegraph-class structural search, no code-graph indexer. Roughly a third of the stated scope went unjudged. Any ranking built only on these 12 rows cannot support a claim of full SOTA coverage for F-retrieval-memory.

The shortlist looks star-ranked rather than capability-ranked: all 12 entries exceed 30,000 stars. That selection rule systematically excludes exactly the small, focused, high-engineering-quality tools that the code-navigation slot requires, and it is itself a popularity bias — the thing the request asked to avoid. Serena, ast-grep, zoekt and codegraph-class MCP tools all surfaced in open web search for this slot and none reached the shortlist.

Two of the twelve (vLLM, PaddleOCR) sit only at the edge of this sub-layer — GPU inference serving and OCR respectively — and occupy slots that closer-fitting candidates could have used. I scored them on their actual fit rather than excluding them, but their presence inflates apparent coverage.

Nothing was installed, executed, indexed or benchmarked. Every score is documentary, derived from GitHub API metadata, repository files (pyproject.toml, LICENSE, workflow and directory listings), official docs and papers, as of 2026-09-21. All performance and accuracy figures are cited from sources, not measured here.

Vector-database performance evidence is weak across the board. The '2026 vector DB benchmark' pages returned by search (lushbinary, digitalapplied, salttechno, iternal, dev.to) are SEO/affiliate content with no published method or reproducible harness, and their numbers mutually contradict; I declined to score on them. The remaining figures are vendor-published. No ANN-benchmarks or VectorDBBench run at the current versions was located.

Agent-memory accuracy evidence rests substantially on a single independent paper (arXiv:2601.07978). It is the best non-vendor evidence available and it explicitly documents the vendor-evaluation bias problem, but it is one testbed, at unstated framework versions, on one dataset (LoCoMo). It should not be treated as settled: it disagrees sharply with both Mem0's and Zep's own published numbers, and the version drift since publication is unknown.

The supplied mechanical metadata contained at least two errors I had to correct by inspection: llama_index was flagged has_tests 'unknown' but llama-index-core/tests/ holds 45 entries, and cognee's root tests/ holds a single file while the real suite lives at cognee/tests/. I verified directory listings and workflow names directly, but I did not verify that any test suite passes, that CI gates merges, or that the named jobs are required checks.

Star counts and contributor-page counts were used only as weak signals. For OpenViking in particular (repository created 2026-01-05, ~38,400 stars by 2026-09-21, no independent evaluation found) the growth provenance is unverified and I did not treat its popularity as quality evidence.

Security posture was assessed only by the presence and content of a disclosure policy. Qdrant, Milvus and Faiss have no SECURITY.md in the repository or .github/; I did not audit any codebase, dependency tree or supply chain, and no CVE history or OpenSSF Scorecard result was retrieved (cognee runs a scorecard job but I did not read its output).

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for sub-layer F-retrieval-memory, judged for a US-equities R&D program. Because none of the twelve shortlisted repositories is a trading-domain tool, "correctness for US equities" was operationalised as the four properties an equities research stack actually needs from its retrieval/memory substrate: (1) point-in-time reconstructability — can the store answer "what was knowable as of date T" via an as-of filter or explicit bi-temporal fact validity, which is the direct analogue of lookahead/survivorship safety; (2) determinism and reproducibility — does the same corpus plus the same pin yield the same retrieval, or does an LLM sit in the ingest/extract path making the index irreproducible across runs; (3) self-hosted portability — can it run offline on a pinned revision with proprietary signal data never leaving the desk, and is the license compatible with a closed trading stack; (4) evidence class — peer-reviewed paper or reproducible in-repo harness, versus vendor blog numbers or contested self-benchmarks. Corporate actions, cost modelling and paper/live parity are out of scope for every candidate here and were scored as unknown rather than credited or penalised. Evidence gathered 2026-09-21 from GitHub API primary sources (repo contents, tests/benchmark directory listings, READMEs, open issues ranked by reactions, license metadata, 90-day unique commit authors) and Tavily web search; no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> was opened and no prior project selection informed discovery.

unknowns: No native temporal or as-of semantics; point-in-time slicing must be built by the caller via IDSelector or separate per-asof indexes
No code navigation, symbol or structural search capability
No measured performance on this project's own hardware or corpus
scores.notes: The strongest evidence-to-risk ratio on the shortlist under this lens. It is a library, not a service: it links into a research process, adds no daemon, no network call and no per-query service cost, so an index file is a pinnable, byte-identical artifact — retrieval is fully deterministic given the index and the query vector, which is the property a reproducible backtest needs and which every LLM-in-the-loop candidate here lacks. Evidence is first-class: a dedicated library paper (arXiv 2401.08281) plus an in-repo benchs/ directory carrying roughly fifty distinct benchmark programs (bench_hnsw, bench_ivf_fastscan, bench_gpu_1bn, bench_fw framework, bench_rabitq and more) and a separate perf_tests/ tree, so claims are reproducible rather than asserted. Maintained by Meta FAIR since 2017, v1.15.1 released 2026-09-16, MIT licensed with no copyleft reach into a proprietary stack. Honest limitation: it supplies no metadata filtering worth the name, so as-of-date enforcement is the integrator's job, and it covers only the vector-store slice of this sub-layer.

unknowns: Whether filtered-ANN recall holds on an equities corpus at this project's vector count and filter selectivity
No bi-temporal fact model; as-of correctness depends on the integrator storing and always applying an as-of payload filter
No code navigation or symbol-level retrieval
scores.notes: Best filtered-retrieval correctness on the shortlist, which is the property that maps most directly onto point-in-time discipline: payload indexes are integrated into HNSW graph traversal rather than applied as a post-filter, so an 'as_of <= T' filter stays both fast and recall-correct instead of silently returning fewer true neighbours. Multiple independent 2026 comparisons put it at the lowest p50 latency among purpose-built engines and 2-4x faster than Milvus on high-selectivity filtered queries. Evidence quality is above vendor-blog grade because Qdrant publishes its benchmark harness as a separate open repository (qdrant/vector-db-benchmark) that competitors can rerun. In-repo tests/ is substantive and operational rather than cosmetic: consensus_tests, e2e_tests, shard-snapshot API tests, OpenAPI and gRPC consistency checks. Deploys as one self-hosted Rust binary with on-disk storage and snapshots, Apache-2.0, no service fee. Documented failure mode to carry forward: a third-party report measures 41 QPS at 99% recall on 50M vectors against pgvectorscale's 471 QPS, so scale beyond roughly 10M vectors should be measured on this project's own corpus before committing.

unknowns: No published accuracy number specifically on SEC filings, 10-K/10-Q tables or earnings transcripts
Table and formula accuracy varies by selected backend; no single headline OmniDocBench figure verified in this session
No retrieval, vector store or memory function — ingestion only
scores.notes: The best-evidenced and most portable ingestion path for the document half of this sub-layer. It carries a published technical report (arXiv 2408.09869) and stands on two prior peer-reviewed artifacts, the DocLayNet layout dataset and TableFormer, whose published table-structure numbers (93.6 vs Acrobat Pro's 65.3 on the same comparison) are the kind of third-party-checkable evidence RAGFlow's DeepDoc lacks. The DoclingDocument representation preserves structure and provenance, so a retrieved passage can be traced back to a page and region — the difference between a citable filing extract and an unattributable chunk. Runs fully local and CPU-capable, MIT licensed, now a Linux Foundation AI & Data project rather than a single-vendor release, v2.129.0 on 2026-09-18 with tests/ and a perfs/ tree. Scored 3 on lifecycle_portability specifically because it is a plain PyTorch-ecosystem Python library: no Docker-compose fleet, no framework fork, nothing to keep running between research sessions.

unknowns: No measurement of LLM ingestion cost or latency at market-data volume; all published numbers are conversational-memory benchmarks
Graph construction is LLM-driven, so the same corpus is not guaranteed to produce the same graph across runs — no published reproducibility study
Whether bi-temporal invalidation behaves correctly under restatements and corporate actions is untested and unclaimed
scores.notes: The only candidate on this shortlist whose core data model matches the lens requirement directly: explicit bi-temporal tracking separates when a fact became true from when it was ingested, with automatic invalidation that preserves the superseded fact rather than overwriting it. That is precisely the machinery needed to reconstruct what was knowable as of date T, and it is the structural answer to lookahead bias — every other memory candidate here either timestamps only ingestion or, in mem0's new algorithm, explicitly accumulates without invalidation. Evidence is peer-review grade and specific: the Zep paper (arXiv 2501.13956) reports 94.8% vs 93.4% on DMR and up to 18.5% improvement on LongMemEval, and the repo carries lint, unit-test and mypy CI badges over tests/, signatures/ and spec/ trees. 27 unique commit authors in 90 days. Two real discounts: quality_cost is 1 because every ingested episode costs an LLM call, which does not scale to tick or filing-volume ingestion; lifecycle_portability is 2 because it requires a graph database backend and issue #1132 records that Kuzu, one of those backends, is archived, while a Postgres/pgvector backend (#779) is still only a feature request.

unknowns: Operational cost of a standalone deployment on this project's hardware is unmeasured
No bi-temporal model; as-of correctness is the integrator's responsibility via scalar filters
1468 open issues; no triage-rate measurement taken
scores.notes: The strongest peer-reviewed provenance among the shortlisted vector databases, with a SIGMOD 2021 system paper the repo itself cites and a follow-up VLDB-track system description, so its design claims have been through review rather than only through a vendor blog. Two properties matter for this lens: scalar indexes built alongside the vector index give correct filtered retrieval at billion scale under high QPS, and an independent 2026 benchmark measures read-after-write freshness — a newly written row is searchable at 12ms p50 via a strong-consistency scan of the unsealed growing segment — which is what prevents a research run from silently querying a stale snapshot mid-ingest. The tests/ tree is the most comprehensive on the shortlist: integration, go_client, java_client, python_client, restful_client and restful_client_v2, plus _helm and docker fixtures. Apache-2.0 under the Linux Foundation, v3.0.2 on 2026-09-20. Discounted twice on fit rather than quality: it is Kubernetes-native and distributed by design, so lifecycle_portability and quality_cost are both below Qdrant's for a single-desk research stack that does not need billion-scale.

unknowns: No published accuracy on US filings specifically; OmniDocBench is a general document corpus
GPU requirement and PaddlePaddle runtime footprint on this project's WSL environment unmeasured
No retrieval, vector store or memory function — ingestion only
scores.notes: The highest published document-parsing accuracy on the shortlist: PP-StructureV3 (arXiv 2507.05595) reports state-of-the-art OmniDocBench results with an English edit distance of 0.145 against MinerU's 0.166 and Marker's 0.331, and third-party coverage puts PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 at 94.5% on OmniDocBench v1.5. It is also the only candidate here that handles scanned and image-only documents, which matters for older filings and exhibits that Docling's PDF path cannot reach. Ships TEST_REPORT.md, a tests/ tree covering pipelines, models and ppstructure, and a separate test_tipc harness, plus a benchmark/ directory — evidence is reproducible, not asserted. Two documented discounts. First, a published third-party head-to-head reports that PP-StructureV3 misses footnotes, author contribution notes and equation numbers where Marker captures them — for financial filings, where the material caveat is frequently in the footnote, that is a correctness failure mode and not a cosmetic one. Second, lifecycle_portability is 2 because it binds the stack to the PaddlePaddle framework rather than the PyTorch ecosystem everything else here uses, which is a real pinning and environment cost.

unknowns: The PagedAttention paper was not fetched in this session, so evidence is scored on verified in-repo artifacts only
No embedding-model-specific quality benchmark verified; vLLM serves the model, it does not establish retrieval quality
GPU memory and throughput for the embedding models this project would actually serve are unmeasured
scores.notes: Fits this sub-layer only at its serving edge, and that placement should be stated plainly rather than scored as if it were a retrieval system: vLLM carries a documented pooling-models path (docs/models/pooling_models) that serves embedding and reranker models locally, which is the substrate under a code-RAG or document-RAG index, not the index itself. For an equities program the real argument is not throughput but containment and cost: embedding proprietary signal text and filings on local hardware keeps alpha-bearing content off third-party APIs and turns a recurring per-token embedding bill into fixed hardware, while pinning the model plus the serving revision makes an embedding run reproducible. Evidence scored 2 rather than 3 because I verified the in-repo benchmarks/ tree, the pooling documentation and active CI in-session but did not fetch the underlying systems paper, and no verified benchmark isolates embedding-serving performance. Discounted on lifecycle_portability and cost: practical throughput needs a GPU, the dependency surface is large (CUDA, custom kernels, a Rust build path), and 8273 open issues indicate a fast-moving surface that requires disciplined version pinning.

unknowns: No peer-reviewed paper and no independent third-party benchmark found; all published numbers are self-run
No track record beyond 8.5 months (created 2026-01-05), so no evidence on long-run API stability or data-format migration
Whether AGPL-3.0 network-copyleft reaches a private trading system that queries it over a socket is a legal question this review cannot settle
scores.notes: Conceptually the best-designed candidate for auditability, which is an underrated equities requirement: organising agent context as an inspectable viking:// virtual filesystem navigated with ls, tree, read, write and grep means a human can open a directory and see exactly what the system believes, instead of auditing an opaque embedding blob — that is a genuine advantage when a research conclusion has to be defended. It also spans this sub-layer more completely than anything else here, unifying structural navigation, semantic retrieval, memory and skills. The in-repo benchmark/ tree is real and unusually broad (locomo, longmemeval, retrieval, vectordb_perf, memory_organization, skillsbench, tau2, cuvs), and 37 unique commit authors in 90 days is the highest activity measured. Evidence is capped at 2 because every number is self-run with no external replication. The decisive marks against it are structural, not quality: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft is the single largest deployment constraint on this shortlist for a closed trading stack, and issue #2357 shows that support for self-hosted external vector backends such as Postgres+pgvector is still only a feature request, so data currently lives in its own young storage layer with no proven exit path. Keep-but-compare, not adopt.

unknowns: No published benchmark or paper establishing retrieval quality was found — adoption is not evidence of correctness
Breaking-change rate across 0.x minor releases not measured
Which of the hundreds of integration packages are actually maintained versus nominally present is unestablished
scores.notes: The broadest ingestion-and-retrieval orchestration layer on the shortlist, and genuinely capable for this sub-layer: node-level metadata filters make as-of-date enforcement expressible, and it fronts essentially every store and reader a research pipeline would want, so it lowers integration cost against Qdrant, Milvus or Faiss rather than competing with them. Evidence is the weak point and is scored 1 deliberately: I found extensive documentation and very large adoption but no published benchmark, paper or reproducible harness establishing that its retrieval pipelines are correct or competitive, and popularity is the exact bias this review is meant to resist. A tests/ tree does exist under llama-index-core, which is why has_tests was flagged unknown by the mechanical pass — that flag is resolved as yes. Discounted on lifecycle_portability because it is a monorepo of hundreds of separately versioned integration packages on a near-daily release cadence (v0.14.25 shipped 2026-09-21), and on quality_cost because several of its higher-level pipelines insert additional LLM calls whose cost is not obvious at the call site. Best treated as convenience glue whose specific pipelines are validated locally, never as a component trusted on reputation.

unknowns: No open-source-only benchmark number is published; the README states the headline scores reflect the managed platform
Per-operation LLM token cost is not exposed by the API (open feature request), so cost cannot be measured from the outside
No temporal validity model documented that would support as-of reconstruction
scores.notes: The contested-evidence case on this shortlist, and the scores reflect the contest rather than the headline. Three independent challenges are on the public record: Zep's published rebuttal argues the Mem0 paper's SOTA claim rests on a flawed LoCoMo benchmark plus a demonstrably incorrect implementation of the competitor it was measured against; Letta, the team behind MemGPT, states it could not determine how Mem0's MemGPT numbers were computed and received no clarification; and Mem0's own README concedes the 92.5 LoCoMo and 94.4 LongMemEval figures 'reflect Mem0's managed platform, which includes proprietary optimizations not available in the open-source SDK'. That last admission is decisive for a self-hosted equities stack — the published numbers do not describe the artifact one would actually deploy. On design, the April 2026 single-pass ADD-only algorithm explicitly accumulates memories and overwrites nothing, which in a market context means a superseded fact and its replacement coexist with no invalidation — the opposite of what point-in-time discipline requires, and the exact axis on which Graphiti is stronger. Maintenance is genuinely healthy (23 authors in 90 days, tests/ and evaluation/ trees, Apache-2.0), and the open evaluation framework is a real transparency gesture. quality_cost is 1 because an LLM call fires on both add and retrieve while issue #2820 shows token usage is still not reported, so spend is unobservable. Also noted: hardcoded English-only BM25 and entity extraction (#4884), a stale OSS Docker image (#5090) and a client/server host mismatch (#4777) all point to the open-source path trailing the managed one.

unknowns: The evals/ directory contains only README.md and an 'old' subdirectory, so the current state of the evaluation suite could not be established from the repo
Unique-author count over 90 days measured at 6, but the commits API page cap means this may undercount — treat as indicative only
No independent replication of the paper's results found
scores.notes: A credible knowledge-graph memory platform with a genuine research artifact behind it (arXiv 2505.24478, Markovic et al.) and an honest local-first stance — it documents starting without any OpenAI or Anthropic key using local extraction and embedding models, which matters for keeping proprietary research text on-premises. Apache-2.0, broad connector surface, MCP server included. It is ranked low here on lifecycle_portability for a specific and checkable reason: the open issue list contains correctness bugs of the kind that quietly corrupt a research index rather than fail loudly. Issue #4491 reports that index_data_points uses pydantic model_copy(), which shallow-copies the metadata dict and corrupts multi-field index buckets; #4364 reports a LanceError spill that reproduces out-of-process and across 384/512/1024 dimensions, so it is not a deployment artifact; #4159 reports that MCP cognify does not hold a strong reference to its background tasks, meaning ingestion work can be garbage-collected away without notice. Any one of those produces a silently wrong retrieval set, which is worse than an outage in a backtest. Evidence scored 2 rather than 3 because the paper exists but the in-repo evaluation suite appears to have been retired to evals/old, weakening reproducibility exactly where it is most needed.

unknowns: No independent or peer-reviewed benchmark of DeepDoc parsing accuracy was found
Full resource footprint of the docker-compose stack unmeasured
No temporal or as-of model documented
scores.notes: A capable end-to-end RAG product, but the weakest fit on this shortlist for a composable research stack, and the reasons are structural rather than a judgement on its engineering. It is an application, not a library: the deployment is a docker-compose fleet with a search engine (Elasticsearch or Infinity), MySQL, Redis and MinIO alongside the Go and Python services, which is a large surface to pin, reproduce and keep running for a single research desk, and it cannot be dropped inside a backtest process the way Faiss or Docling can. Evidence is scored 1 because everything published about DeepDoc accuracy is vendor blog material, with no peer-reviewed or third-party benchmark found; notably, RAGFlow's own v0.15.0 engineering post concedes that 'even if DeepDoc works perfectly, it still cannot resolve the issue of recall accuracy alone' — an honest statement, and one that undercuts using DeepDoc as the evidence for choosing the platform. Maintenance and licensing are genuinely strong (Apache-2.0, v0.27.2 on 2026-09-10, substantial test/ tree with api, integration, playwright, unit_test and benchmark subtrees, plus run_tests.py and run_go_tests.sh). Reasonable as a standalone document-QA appliance beside the research stack; not as the retrieval substrate inside it.

sota_claims.claim: Faiss is the reference open-source similarity-search and vector-clustering library, the only shortlisted vector component with a dedicated peer-reviewed library paper backed by an in-repo suite of roughly fifty reproducible benchmark programs, and it is fully deterministic and dependency-light enough to link directly into a reproducible backtest.

Graphiti is the only shortlisted agent-memory system with explicit bi-temporal fact tracking and automatic invalidation that preserves superseded facts, giving it the one property on this list that maps directly onto point-in-time reconstruction and lookahead-bias avoidance.

PP-StructureV3 reports state-of-the-art document-parsing accuracy on OmniDocBench for both English and Chinese, at an English edit distance of 0.145 against MinerU's 0.166 and Marker's 0.331, making PaddleOCR the highest-measured ingestion path on this shortlist for scanned and image-only filings.

Milvus has the strongest peer-reviewed provenance of any shortlisted vector database, with a SIGMOD 2021 system paper the repository itself designates as the canonical citation, and independent 2026 benchmarking measures it holding 0.984 recall at up to 732 filtered QPS.

Mem0's headline agent-memory SOTA claim should not be treated as established: a published competitor rebuttal argues it rests on a flawed LoCoMo benchmark and an incorrect implementation of the system it was compared against, the MemGPT team says it could not reproduce how its own numbers were computed, and Mem0's own README states the figures reflect a managed platform containing proprietary optimizations absent from the open-source SDK.

limits: COVERAGE IS NOT COMPREHENSIVE FOR THIS SUB-LAYER, and the gap is systematic rather than random. The sub-layer definition names LSP/symbol tools and structural search first, yet not one of the twelve shortlisted repositories provides code navigation at all — the entire first half of the stated scope is unrepresented. A star-count-ordered shortlist selects for general-purpose consumer-facing AI infrastructure and against precisely the focused developer tooling this sub-layer needs. Absent and worth a dedicated pass: Serena, ast-grep, zoekt, tree-sitter, Sourcebot and Sourcegraph (symbol and structural search); Text Embeddings Inference and Infinity (local embedding serving, lighter than vLLM); LanceDB, sqlite-vec, Chroma, Weaviate and pgvector/pgvectorscale (embedded and Postgres-native stores — pgvectorscale is specifically relevant given the 50M-vector benchmark cited against Qdrant); Letta/MemGPT and Zep server (memory); LightRAG, R2R, txtai and Haystack (retrieval frameworks); MinerU, Marker and unstructured (ingestion, and Marker beat PP-StructureV3 on footnote capture in the one head-to-head found). A judgment built only on these twelve should not be described as full SOTA coverage.

NO CANDIDATE IS A TRADING-DOMAIN TOOL, so the lens was applied by analogy and that substitution should be visible in any downstream use. None of the twelve ships point-in-time correctness, survivorship-bias safeguards, corporate-action handling, transaction-cost modelling or paper/live parity; those are properties of the layer built above this one. Every score on this axis therefore measures whether the tool makes such safeguards expressible and enforceable (as-of filters, bi-temporal validity, deterministic replay), never whether it provides them. Any claim that one of these repositories is 'correct for US equities' would be a category error.

EVIDENCE CLASSES ARE MIXED AND WERE NOT WEIGHTED EQUALLY, but the shortlist forces some reliance on weak sources. Peer-reviewed papers (Faiss, Milvus, Zep/Graphiti, Docling, PP-StructureV3, cognee) and reproducible in-repo harnesses (Faiss benchs/, Qdrant's separately published benchmark repo, OpenViking's benchmark/ tree) are primary. Vector-database latency and recall figures, by contrast, come substantially from 2026 SEO-grade comparison blogs with undisclosed or unverifiable methodology; those were used only to corroborate a direction already supported by a primary source, never as the basis for a score. No number in this review was measured on this project's hardware or corpus, so every performance figure is a claim to be re-measured before it is relied upon.

SEVERAL MECHANICAL AND DERIVED METADATA POINTS ARE UNRELIABLE. The 90-day unique-commit-author counts (OpenViking 37, Graphiti 27, mem0 23, cognee 6) come from a commits API call capped at 100 results, so a high-velocity repository's author count is truncated and cognee's 6 in particular may substantially undercount — it is indicative, not measured, and should not alone support a maintenance conclusion. Open-issue counts were read as raw totals with no triage-rate or staleness analysis, so vLLM's 8273 and Milvus's 1468 reflect project scale as much as project health. Issue selection was ranked by reaction count, which surfaces what users vote on rather than what is most severe — the cognee correctness bugs cited carry zero reactions and were found only by reading titles.

TWO SPECIFIC ITEMS WERE NOT VERIFIED IN-SESSION AND ARE SCORED CONSERVATIVELY AS A RESULT. The vLLM PagedAttention systems paper was not fetched, so vLLM's evidence score of 2 rests only on the in-repo pooling documentation and benchmarks tree that I did confirm; a reader who fetches that paper may justifiably raise it. Separately, whether AGPL-3.0 network copyleft reaches a proprietary trading system that queries OpenViking over a socket is a legal question outside this review's competence — it is flagged as the dominant constraint on that candidate and scored as a 1 on license fit, but the flag is a prompt for counsel, not a determination. Finally, the blindness rule was honoured: no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> was opened, and no candidate was privileged or excluded on the basis of the tooling or trading destination named in the injected project instructions.

verdicts.claim: Docling is the only document-ingestion candidate in this shortlist that combines a permissive MIT licence, hosting by a neutral foundation (LF AI & Data) rather than a single vendor, and a published technical report describing the specific layout and table-structure models it ships.
verdicts.reason: All three legs check out against primary sources and I could not find a shortlisted ingestion candidate that matches. GitHub API returns license.spdx_id=MIT and owner=docling-project; LF AI & Data lists Docling as a hosted project donated by IBM in April 2025; arXiv 2408.09869 is the technical report naming the DocLayNet layout model and TableFormer table-structure model. The nearest competitor, PaddleOCR, is permissively licensed (Apache-2.0) and has a technical report but is owned by a single vendor (Baidu/PaddlePaddle org); MinerU is AGPL-3.0 and Marker is GPL-family, both failing the permissive leg. Caveats that bound but do not refute it: only 8 of the 12 shortlisted repos were named to me, and LF AI & Data hosting is governance, not maintainer diversity (commits remain concentrated in IBM Research Zurich).

verdicts.claim: Faiss is the only repository in this shortlist that runs a dedicated index-serialization backward-compatibility CI job, making it the strongest documented guarantee of durable on-disk format stability in the retrieval layer.
verdicts.reason: The workflow exists (.github/workflows/index-io-backward-compatibility.yml, jobs 'CMake Write -> Conda Read' and 'Conda Write -> CMake Read'), but both the exclusivity and the 'strongest guarantee' conclusion fail. Milvus ships a dedicated data-compatibility suite at tests/python_client/deploy whose README specifies exactly this: 'upgrade milvus to check data compatibility -- Deploy Milvus (Previous Release), Insert data, Search, Stop Milvus, Deploy Milvus (Latest Release/Build), Build index, Search', plus tests/python_client/rolling_upgrade. It is dispatched from Milvus's Jenkins pipeline rather than a .github/workflows file, so the claim is only true if you silently restrict 'CI job' to GitHub Actions YAML. On strength: the Faiss job pins one released version (conda faiss-cpu=1.15.1) and exercises a single version pair, whereas the Milvus suite reads data written by the previous release with the new binary -- a stronger statement about durable cross-release on-disk stability, not one in Faiss's favour.

verdicts.claim: An independent, non-vendor 2026 benchmark of long-term-memory frameworks placed mem0 in a 77-81% LoCoMo accuracy cluster with RAG and full-context baselines while Graphiti and cognee reached only 55-56%, a ranking that contradicts both Mem0's and Zep's own published evaluations and makes mem0 the only agent-memory project here with favourable third-party evidence.
verdicts.reason: The numeric half verifies: arXiv 2601.07978 ('Cost and Accuracy of Long-Term Memory in Distributed Multi-Agent Systems Based on Large Language Models', Jan 2026) does report two clusters, mem0/RAG/full-context at 77-81% and Graphiti/cognee at 55-56% on LoCoMo. The load-bearing conclusion -- 'the only agent-memory project here with favourable third-party evidence' -- is refuted. An independent June 2026 evaluation by Particula, using LongMemEval rather than LoCoMo, puts Zep/Graphiti at 63.8% against Mem0's 49.0%, a 15-point gap in the opposite direction on the benchmark that weights temporal fact validity. Graphiti therefore also has favourable third-party evidence and the ranking inverts with benchmark choice. Two further problems: the arXiv study ran resource-constrained distributed multi-agent configurations rather than the vendors' tuned single-agent setups, and it evaluated only three frameworks, so 'contradicts' overstates what is largely a methodology difference.

verdicts.claim: Qdrant is the only shortlisted vector store that deploys as a single self-contained Rust binary with no external database, queue or object-store dependency, giving it the lowest single-machine operational footprint of the three stores under a Linux/WSL2 local-first constraint.
verdicts.reason: Refuted twice over. (1) Milvus Lite is an in-process embedded build shipped as a pymilvus extra: MilvusClient('./milvus_demo.db') persists to a single local file with no etcd, MinIO, queue or object store, and Milvus MEP-26 removed the MinIO and etcd dependencies from standalone as of the 2.1 release by substituting local disk storage and embedded etcd. 'No external database, queue or object-store dependency' is therefore not unique to Qdrant. (2) The claim scopes itself to 'the three stores', which includes Faiss -- an in-process C++/Python library with no server process, no port, no daemon and no service state, so strictly lower single-machine operational footprint than any Qdrant binary. The underlying facts about Qdrant (Apache-2.0, single Rust binary, 34.7k stars, pushed 2026-09-22) are correct; the 'only' and 'lowest' superlatives are not.

verdicts.claim: Graphiti no longer has a maintained embedded graph backend: its own pyproject marks the Kuzu extra deprecated because the upstream project is unmaintained and states it will be removed, leaving an external Neo4j or FalkorDB as the practical requirement as of v0.30.x.
verdicts.reason: The Kuzu half is exactly right -- I read pyproject.toml at graphiti-core 0.30.2 and the comment reads 'Deprecated: the upstream Kuzu project is unmaintained; this extra will be removed in a future release.' But the conclusion is contradicted by the next two lines of the same file. Graphiti ships a `falkordblite` extra (falkordblite>=0.5.0 for python_version>='3.12'), and the adjacent pin comment reads 'redis<9 pin: redis-py 8.x breaks falkordblite's embedded server startup' -- an actively maintained embedded FalkorDB backend whose startup path the maintainers are still pinning dependencies around in the current release. Graphiti does still have a maintained embedded graph backend on Python 3.12+, and an external Neo4j/FalkorDB server is not the practical requirement the claim asserts. Same file, same release, directly below the quoted line.

verdicts.claim: Faiss is the reference open-source similarity-search and vector-clustering library, the only shortlisted vector component with a dedicated peer-reviewed library paper backed by an in-repo suite of roughly fifty reproducible benchmark programs, and it is fully deterministic and dependency-light enough to link directly into a reproducible backtest.
verdicts.reason: 'Only shortlisted vector component with a dedicated peer-reviewed library paper' is false, and the paper cited is not peer-reviewed. arXiv:2401.08281 'The Faiss library' lists no journal or conference venue, and the repository's own citation block records it as @article{douze2024faiss, ... journal={arXiv preprint}}. Milvus, on the same shortlist, has a genuinely peer-reviewed system paper in ACM SIGMOD 2021 proceedings (DOI 10.1145/3448016.3457550) -- which the other judge correctly identified, so the two judges' claims are mutually inconsistent and this one loses. The remaining legs (reference status, in-repo benchmark programs, C++ core with no external dependencies) hold. 'Fully deterministic' is also overstated for a library whose IVF/PQ training uses randomised k-means initialisation and whose multithreaded and GPU reductions can reorder tie-breaks.

verdicts.claim: Graphiti is the only shortlisted agent-memory system with explicit bi-temporal fact tracking and automatic invalidation that preserves superseded facts, giving it the one property on this list that maps directly onto point-in-time reconstruction and lookahead-bias avoidance.
verdicts.reason: Supported, and by a non-vendor source rather than only the Zep paper: an independent 2026 comparison describes the mechanism concretely -- every entity and relationship is time-stamped, facts carry validity windows, and when a new episode contradicts an existing fact the old fact receives an `invalid_at` marker while the new one takes over with its own `valid_from`, producing a layered history rather than an overwrite. I found no equivalent documented mechanism in mem0 or cognee (cognee has 'temporal awareness' over an ECL pipeline but no documented automatic invalidation preserving superseded facts). Two caveats that bound its value without refuting it: the primary citation arXiv 2501.13956 is vendor-authored, and Graphiti's ingest path is LLM-driven entity/relationship extraction, which violates the same judge's own criterion (2) determinism -- the same corpus at the same pin does not necessarily produce the same graph, so the bi-temporal property is reproducible in schema but not in content.

verdicts.claim: PP-StructureV3 reports state-of-the-art document-parsing accuracy on OmniDocBench for both English and Chinese, at an English edit distance of 0.145 against MinerU's 0.166 and Marker's 0.331, making PaddleOCR the highest-measured ingestion path on this shortlist for scanned and image-only filings.
verdicts.reason: The cited figures are self-reported by the PaddleOCR team in their own 3.0 technical report against OmniDocBench v1.0, a benchmark version superseded three times before the 2026-09-21 cutoff (v1.5 on 2025-09-25, v1.6 on 2026-04-09, v1.7 on 2026-04-30). On the current OmniDocBench leaderboard PP-StructureV3 scores 86.73 overall with a text edit distance of 0.073, ranking roughly 23rd, behind Logics-Parsing-v2 (93.33), FireRed-OCR (93.26), MinerU-2.5 (93.04, text edit 0.045), PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 (92.05) and dots.ocr (90.77). It has also been superseded inside its own repository: Baidu's own PaddleOCR-VL / VL-1.5 line now posts materially better numbers than PP-StructureV3. 'State-of-the-art' and 'highest-measured ingestion path' were true in mid-2025 and are not true as of the cutoff date.

verdicts.claim: Milvus has the strongest peer-reviewed provenance of any shortlisted vector database, with a SIGMOD 2021 system paper the repository itself designates as the canonical citation, and independent 2026 benchmarking measures it holding 0.984 recall at up to 732 filtered QPS.
verdicts.reason: The peer-review half survives (ACM SIGMOD '21, DOI 10.1145/3448016.3457550). The benchmark half is refuted by its own source. The 0.984 / 268-732 QPS pair traces to AIMultiple's open-source vector database benchmark -- a commercial comparison-content site, not an independent research venue -- and that page's own table shows Weaviate, pgvector and LanceDB all at 1.00 worst-case filtered recall against Milvus's 0.984, with Weaviate at 58-861 filtered QPS and Redis at 183-1374, so Milvus leads on neither the recall nor the throughput axis it was quoted for. The same benchmark also puts Weaviate at 8330 sustained QPS against Milvus's 5063. The number is quoted accurately; the comparative implication is contradicted by the table it was taken from.

verdicts.claim: Mem0's headline agent-memory SOTA claim should not be treated as established: a published competitor rebuttal argues it rests on a flawed LoCoMo benchmark and an incorrect implementation of the system it was compared against, the MemGPT team says it could not reproduce how its own numbers were computed, and Mem0's own README states the figures reflect a managed platform containing proprietary optimizations absent from the open-source SDK.
verdicts.reason: I tried to refute this and the strongest leg verifies verbatim in primary source. Mem0's own README, line 54, reads: 'Scores reflect Mem0's managed platform, which includes proprietary optimizations not available in the open-source SDK; open-source users should expect directionally similar gains but not identical numbers.' That alone establishes the caution: the headline 92.5 LoCoMo / 7.0K tokens / 0.88s p50 figures are not what a self-hosted open-source deployment gets, which is the only deployment shape relevant to a local-first stack. The rebuttal source is explicitly self-labelled as a competitor (Zep) inside the claim, so it is not passed off as neutral, and the independent arXiv 2601.07978 study measuring mem0 at 77-81% rather than 92.5% on the same benchmark corroborates the gap in the same direction. Mitigating fact found but not overturning: mem0 open-sources its evaluation harness at github.com/mem0ai/memory-benchmarks.

survivors: Docling combines an MIT licence, LF AI & Data (neutral foundation) hosting and a published technical report naming its DocLayNet layout and TableFormer table-structure models -- unique among the named ingestion candidates (https://github.com/docling-project/docling)

Graphiti is the only shortlisted agent-memory system with explicit bi-temporal fact tracking and automatic invalidation preserving superseded facts via valid_from/invalid_at, the one property mapping onto point-in-time reconstruction -- though its LLM-driven ingest breaks the determinism criterion the same judge set (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti)

Mem0's headline SOTA numbers should not be treated as established: mem0's own README states the scores reflect the managed platform with proprietary optimizations absent from the open-source SDK (https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0)

better_alternatives_found.name: LanceDB / Lance
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Apache-2.0, 11.5k stars, pushed 2026-09-21, and absent from both rankings. It beats the ranked stores on two of the criteria the research judge himself defined. (1) Point-in-time reconstructability: the Lance columnar format has built-in zero-copy dataset versioning and time-travel, so 'what was knowable as of version/date T' is a native table property rather than something you must hand-model as a metadata filter -- neither Qdrant nor Milvus offers this. (2) Operational footprint: it is embedded and zero-process (a filesystem directory, no server, no port), strictly below the Qdrant single-binary footprint the engineering judge called lowest. It also recorded 1.00 worst-case filtered recall in the very benchmark cited to favour Milvus's 0.984. This is the clearest single omission in the shortlist under a local-first, reproducible-backtest constraint.

better_alternatives_found.name: text-embeddings-inference
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The sub-layer definition explicitly includes 'local embedding serving' and not one of the twelve shortlisted repositories covers it -- a whole named component of the layer has zero candidates, which is a coverage gap rather than a ranking error. TEI is the reference option: Apache-2.0, a dependency-light Rust server with a token-budget batcher, 5.1k stars, pushed 2026-09-17, self-hosted with no data egress (relevant to the judge's criterion 3, proprietary signal data never leaving the desk). Its main competitor, michaelfeil/infinity, is a Python server with three swappable engines that also serves rerankers and ColBERT; one of the two belongs in the candidate set before any ranking of this sub-layer is complete.

better_alternatives_found.name: ast-grep
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The sub-layer definition opens with 'code navigation and retrieval (LSP/symbol tools, structural search, code RAG)' and none of the twelve shortlisted repositories is a code-navigation or structural-search tool -- the shortlist is entirely document ingestion, vector stores and agent memory. ast-grep is the strongest single candidate for the missing structural-search slot: MIT, 16.0k stars, pushed 2026-09-21, AST-aware search and rewrite across 25 languages via tree-sitter, a single Rust binary with no service dependency, and fully deterministic (a pattern match, not an embedding), which satisfies the reproducibility criterion every vector-based candidate on the shortlist fails. sourcegraph/zoekt (Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-09-16) is the adjacent candidate for indexed repository-scale search.

better_alternatives_found.name: Letta (ex-MemGPT)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Apache-2.0, 24.8k stars, pushed 2026-09-10, self-hostable server, and omitted from both rankings despite being one of the four systems in the independent June 2026 Particula comparison alongside mem0, Zep and cognee -- it was inside the evidence frame the judges drew from and still never entered the candidate set. It occupies a distinct architectural position from every shortlisted memory system (the agent runtime is the memory, with self-editing context management, rather than a memory layer bolted onto an external agent), so excluding it narrows the design space rather than filtering it on merit. It is also the system whose team is reported to have disputed Mem0's comparison numbers, making its absence from a shortlist that includes that dispute notable.

better_alternatives_found.name: MinerU
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Included as the measured counterweight to the refuted PaddleOCR SOTA claim rather than as a recommendation. MinerU2.5 scores 93.04 overall / 0.045 text edit distance on current OmniDocBench against PP-StructureV3's 86.73 / 0.073, so on the benchmark the research judge selected, the ranked candidate is beaten by roughly seven points by a repository that was never shortlisted. Load-bearing caveat that must travel with it: MinerU is AGPL-3.0, a genuine blocker for a closed proprietary trading stack under the judge's own criterion (3) license compatibility. So it plausibly beats PaddleOCR on accuracy and plausibly loses to Docling (MIT) on license fit -- the correct conclusion being that the accuracy claim and the licence claim point at different winners, which neither judge surfaced.

judges.lens: Engineering quality: code/test/CI health, release discipline, API stability, documentation depth, dependency and platform hygiene, security/provenance, community and maintainer organisation, operational fit (Linux/WSL2, Python 3.12+, local-first). Scored from public GitHub API metadata, repository file listings, primary docs and dated third-party write-ups only (evidence window to 2026-09-21). Nothing was installed, executed or benchmarked locally; no project file was read.

scores.notes: Strongest engineering-quality profile on the shortlist. Test matrix is genuinely broad: tests/ holds android, bidi, electron, extension, image_tools, installation, library, mcp, page, playwright-test, stress, webview subtrees, and the 35 active workflows include 'tests 1', 'tests 2', 'tests others', 'tests BiDi', 'tests docker', 'tests Fedora', 'tests WebView (iOS Simulator)', 'tests WebDriver (Safari)', 'tests WebView (WebKitGTK)', plus 'Publish Test Results' and 'Update test results DB'. Release discipline: monthly-cadence minor tags (v1.63.0 2026-09-04, v1.62.1 2026-07-30, v1.62.0 2026-07-24, v1.61.1 2026-06-23) on a stable v1.x API. Microsoft org with SECURITY.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, SUPPORT.md, FILING_ISSUES.md. 637 commits in the 90 days to 2026-09-21; 187 PRs merged in the last month; open issues 202 against 96,477 stars, an unusually low backlog ratio for this size. Apache-2.0, no deployment restriction, first-party Linux/Docker images and a Python binding, so it fits a Linux/WSL2 + Python 3.12 local-first target. Also carries an in-repo MCP CI workflow, so the agent-facing surface is maintained in the same tree as the core.

unknowns: Whether the 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha' classifier still reflects the maintainers' stability intent now that the project is on a 3.x line
scores.notes: The clearest fit for the quality/evaluation-framework part of this sub-layer: tests/ contains dedicated evaluate/, teleprompt/, reliability/, adapters/, streaming/, propose/ and predict/ suites, and CI includes a 'Paired CI Performance Benchmarks' workflow alongside 'Lint, Test, and Build' and pre-commit checks. Peer-reviewed lineage rather than blog-only evidence: DSPy's optimizer line is academic, and GEPA is described by an independent write-up as an ICLR 2026 Oral that beats GRPO by ~10% with 35x fewer rollouts and beats MIPROv2 by +14% with 9.2x shorter prompts. Stanford NLP org; 153 commits/90d and 63 merged PRs in the last month (steady rather than frantic); releases 3.3.0 (2026-08-03), 3.3.1 (2026-08-21), 3.4.0b1 (2026-09-11) with beta tags used properly; versioned documentation build ('Bootstrap versioned documentation', 'Update DSPy Docs') and SECURITY.md. MIT. requires-python '>=3.10, <3.15' covers 3.12+, and the POSIX::Linux classifier plus a LiteLLM backend means it runs fully against a local vLLM endpoint with no vendor dependency. Portability marked down one step: hard litellm dependency is a large moving transitive surface, and the packaging metadata still declares Alpha status while the API is on a 3.x line.

unknowns: Whether any first-party or well-maintained Python binding exists; none is in-repo
scores.notes: Best supply-chain and release hygiene of the twelve. Workflows include scorecards-analysis.yml (OpenSSF Scorecards), release-please.yml, convetional-commit.yml (conventional-commit enforcement), deflake.yml (explicit flake management), daily.yml and bisect.yml (Chrome-for-Testing bisection), plus CodeQL and update-browser-pins.yml for pinned browser builds. Tests are real and typed: test/ and test-d/ (type-level tests), .mocharc.js. Release discipline is the strongest here: paired puppeteer / puppeteer-core tags roughly every 1-2 weeks (v25.11.0 2026-09-14, v25.10.0 2026-09-03) under release-please automation with a maintained CHANGELOG.md and versions.json. Chrome DevTools team provenance, 1,204 subscribers (highest watch count on the shortlist), 195 commits/90d, SECURITY.md. Apache-2.0, Docker support in-repo, long-stable major-version API. Capability_fit held at 2 rather than 3: it is Chrome/Firefox driving only, with no assertion/test-runner layer and no Python surface, so for a Python-3.12 local-first agent stack it is a lower-level substrate than Playwright rather than a peer.

unknowns: Whether the 89.1% WebVoyager figure has ever been independently reproduced rather than repeated
Whether PostHog telemetry is opt-in or opt-out by default
scores.notes: Best-evidenced agentic-browser layer. tests/ci contains 70 entries plus agent_tasks/ and mind2web_data/, and CI runs eval-on-pr.yml (per-PR evaluation), test.yaml, lint.yml, CodeQL, security-check, install-script.yml and docker.yml (15 workflows). The 89.1% WebVoyager success rate over 586 tasks is quoted consistently by several independent 2026 roundups, which makes it the most widely cited open-source browser-agent number, though those roundups repeat the project's figure rather than re-running it. Maintenance is strong: 561 commits/90d, 100+ contributors, 0.13.10 released 2026-09-04. MIT. The serious engineering-quality deduction is dependency hygiene: pyproject.toml pins roughly twenty runtime dependencies with exact '==' constraints (pydantic==2.13.5, openai==2.26.0, anthropic==0.76.0, aiohttp==3.14.3, mcp==2.1.1, httpx==0.28.1), which is an anti-pattern for a library and will conflict with any co-installed agent stack; combined with a 0.x version line this makes lifecycle_portability a 1. requires-python '>=3.11,<4.0' is otherwise fine for 3.12+. quality_cost held at 2: a posthog telemetry dependency ships in the base install, and the agent loop is inherently token-expensive per step.

unknowns: Actual test coverage per package; the monorepo keeps tests inside libs/*/tests so a root-level scan misses them
scores.notes: Deepest CI of any Python repo on the shortlist: 37 workflows covering unit testing, linting, compile-integration tests, scheduled integration tests, '📼 VCR Cassette Tests' (recorded-provider regression testing), '⚡ CodSpeed' performance regression, CodeQL, Pydantic version-matrix testing, PR title lint, version-equality checks and package release automation. It also ships libs/standard-tests, a reusable conformance suite that third-party integrations run against, which is itself a quality framework and the reason capability_fit is not 1. Release discipline is per-package and continuous (langchain-core==1.6.4 and langchain-openai==1.6.3 both on 2026-09-21; langchain==1.4.2 on 2026-09-18). LangChain Inc backing, 502 commits/90d, 173 merged PRs in the last month, 923 subscribers, CITATION.cff. MIT, requires-python '>=3.10.0,<4.0.0'. Marked down on lifecycle_portability for the well-known cost of its major-version transitions and the very large partner-integration surface (libs/partners) whose quality varies by package, and on quality_cost for dependency weight relative to the retrieval work actually needed in this sub-layer. Capability fit is indirect: it is an agent platform that contains research/retrieval pieces, not a research tool.

Index-time token cost on a realistic corpus; not published in a form I could verify
scores.notes: The only shortlist entry whose core method is peer-reviewed: EMNLP 2025 Findings, arXiv 2410.05779, with the repo description carrying the [EMNLP2025] tag. CI is unusually honest for a research repo: 21 workflows including 'E2E Tests (Real Databases)', 'Integration Tests', 'Offline Unit Tests', 'PostgreSQL Smoke Tests', 'WebUI Unit Tests', 'Windows Storage Tests' and 'Windows Vector Drop', and tests/ is organised by subsystem (api, chunker, evaluation, extraction, kg, llm, parser, pipeline, sidecar) alongside many named regression tests. Very active: 2,266 commits/90d, 184 merged PRs in the last month, v1.5.7 on 2026-09-02 with rc tags used before the final. MIT. Deployment fit is excellent for local-first: Dockerfile + Dockerfile.lite + Dockerfile.postgres, three compose files, a podman compose, k8s-deploy/, a systemd unit example, and requirements-offline*.txt files for air-gapped installs. requires-python '>=3.10'. Held at 2 on portability for storage-backend churn and frequent rc cycles, and at 2 on quality_cost because graph construction is LLM-token-expensive at index time by design. Capability fit is 2: it is document/graph retrieval, not web research or token-efficiency tooling.

unknowns: Whether the AGPL-3.0 network-use clause would bind an internal agent service that calls a self-hosted instance; not resolvable from repo text
Self-hosted quality delta versus cloud on anti-bot sites; the docs state a gap without quantifying it
scores.notes: Capability is squarely on target (scrape/crawl/map/search for LLM-ready content, MCP server, CLI, and SDKs in seven languages) and the engineering is serious despite the mechanical scan reporting has_tests=no: apps/api/src/__tests__ contains e2e_extract, e2e_map, e2e_noAuth, e2e_full_withAuth, e2e_v1_withAuth_all_params, deep-research, controllers, routes and snips, and the 42 workflows include per-SDK test suites (JS, Python, Rust, Java, Ruby, PHP, Go), 'Server Test Suite', 'Server Test Suite (k8s)', 'Unit Tests', 'Type Check & Lint', 'Audit NPM Packages', 'Validate Lockfiles', 'Run Eval Benchmark Prod' and 'Scrape Evals'. 593 commits/90d, 167 merged PRs in the last month, company-backed. The decisive deduction under this lens is deployment fit: AGPL-3.0 plus an explicitly non-parity self-host — the project's own docs state /agent and /browser are unsupported self-hosted and that self-hosted instances do not get the same Fire-engine anti-bot capability, and SELF_HOST.md confirms the open baseline is 'bundled Playwright with basic fetch fallback'. That makes the open artifact a degraded subset of the product, which is a different risk class from Apache/MIT peers. Portability 2: Docker Compose plus Helm/k8s manifests exist, but the baseline needs NuQ-Postgres, Redis and a Playwright service. Note also that the main repo tag v2.11.0 is from 2026-06-19 while main is pushed daily, so the tagged release does not track the deployed code.

unknowns: Whether Vercel Labs offers any support or longevity commitment; the README's own badge marks it a LABS PRODUCT
Rust test depth in cli/tests; directory exists but contents not enumerated
Why 797 open issues accumulated in ~8 months relative to 90 commits in the last quarter
scores.notes: Purpose-built for exactly this sub-layer: a native Rust browser-automation CLI for agents, with a deliberate context-footprint design (skills served via 'agent-browser skills get' instead of a fat MCP tool surface) and an evals/ harness that measures CLI-vs-MCP context footprint deterministically (evals/context-footprint.ts) plus benchmarks/bench.ts. Apache-2.0, installable via npm, brew and cargo, with documented Linux deps ('agent-browser install --with-deps') and a downloaded Chrome-for-Testing binary — good local-first fit. Evidence held at 2: CI is thin relative to peers (5 workflows, of which 3 are Copilot; only ci.yml and release.yml are substantive), the JS-side test/ directory contains a single file (launcher.test.mjs), and the evals require an external AI-Gateway API key so they cannot run in a closed CI. Maintenance/provenance 2: real Vercel Labs org and fast releases (v0.38.1 2026-09-16), but the repo is ~8 months old, two authors account for 80 of the last 100 commits (ctate 54, Railly 26), and 'Labs' is self-declared experimental. Building from source needs Node 24+, pnpm 11+ and Rust, which is a heavier toolchain than the npm install suggests.
