scores.notes: Fits the literature/document-retrieval slice, not web research or token efficiency. Tests exist per package (llama-index-core/tests) despite the root scan reporting none, and CI covers Linting, Unit Testing, Core Typecheck, Build Package, CodeQL and llama-dev tests (19 workflows). MIT, requires-python '>=3.10,<4.0', CHANGELOG.md, SECURITY.md, CITATION.cff, readthedocs config — documentation and release hygiene are solid, with v0.14.25 on 2026-09-21. Maintenance is the notable soft spot relative to peers of similar size: 110 commits in 90 days and 40 merged PRs in the last month, an order of magnitude below RAGFlow or LightRAG and well below LangChain, on 815 open issues; the presence of a 'Close new integration PRs' workflow plus STALE.md indicates the project is actively narrowing what it accepts. Evidence 2 rather than 3 because quality assurance for the large integration surface is not visible in the main tree, and the core has no benchmark or performance-regression CI comparable to LangChain's CodSpeed job.

unknowns: Whether the Go rewrite is complete, partial or dual-track; the repo carries both go.mod/run_go_tests.sh and a Python pyproject with no in-repo migration statement I could verify
Actual test coverage; codecov.yml exists but no coverage figure was retrievable
scores.notes: Maintenance velocity is the highest on the shortlist (2,669 commits/90d, 978 merged PRs in the last month, monthly releases to v0.27.2 on 2026-09-10, InfiniFlow org, SECURITY.md, .trivyignore, twelve translated READMEs). Apache-2.0 and genuinely self-hostable (docker/, helm/, admin/). Deep-document-understanding (deepdoc/) is a real differentiator for literature retrieval. But under an engineering-quality lens the operational and stability picture is poor for this sub-layer: requires-python is pinned to '>=3.13,<3.14', a single minor version, which is a hard constraint for a Python 3.12 target; the codebase is mid-rewrite with Go now the dominant language by bytes (27.7 MB Go vs 16.7 MB Python vs 8.7 MB TypeScript) alongside a C++ component; the version line is still 0.x; and there are 1,475 open issues. CI is comparatively thin for the size (12 workflows: deepdoc-drift, entrypoint-loop-test, release, sep-tests, serenedb, web-lint plus CodeQL/Dependabot/Copilot), even though test/ does contain unit_test, integration, playwright, benchmark and testcases. quality_cost 1: the deployment needs a full server stack, which is out of proportion to a research-retrieval role.

unknowns: Star authenticity: the GitHub stargazers endpoint returned HTTP 404 for every repository tried in this environment, so neither star-history nor bot detection could be run; the 73,425 figure is therefore unverified for authenticity in either direction
Whether any third party has independently reproduced the 60-95% token-reduction claim; I found none
Accuracy/information-loss profile on non-repetitive payloads (prose, diffs, novel code) as opposed to repeated JSON
Net latency and failure cost of inserting a proxy in the agent's critical path
scores.notes: Capability is exactly the token-efficiency slot (library, proxy, MCP server, agent wrap, CCR reversible cache) and the license/security posture is good: Apache-2.0, SECURITY.md (5.2 KB), sbom/, deny.toml, .gitleaks.toml, .gitguardian.yaml, and a stated local-only compression model. The test and benchmark surface is large and real — tests/ holds hundreds of files including e2e_cortex_* and e2e_real_compression.py, benchmarks/ holds comprehensive_eval.py, headroom_adversarial_benchmark.py, headroom_worst_case_benchmark.py and compression_benchmark.py, and 33 workflows include an Evaluation Suite, Security, several E2E jobs and Release Please. Evidence is nonetheless capped at 2 because every headline savings number is project-published; the one substantive independent write-up states explicitly that these should be treated as 'project-published benchmark claims, not independent lab results'. Provenance scores 1: the repo was created 2026-01-07, was transferred from the personal account chopratejas/headroom into an org created 2026-06-16, is ~9 months old, and the last 100 commits are concentrated in two accounts (gglucass 16, chopratejas 14) — a single-vendor, young project. Portability scores 1: v0.38.0 pre-1.0 with 100 releases already published, a maturin Rust+Python hybrid build, and a release cadence that implies ongoing API churn. quality_cost 1: it adds a compression/proxy layer to the critical path (tests include repro_unsendable_panic.py and test_5xx_accounting_all_providers.py, i.e. real failure modes in that path) while the benefit remains unreplicated.

unknowns: Whether the slowdown is a deliberate pause, a pivot to the hosted product, or abandonment; no in-repo statement found
When or whether the 2.0.0 beta line will reach a stable release
scores.notes: Capability (self-hostable research agent with web + document retrieval, deep research, automations) is a reasonable fit, and the engineering basics are present: tests/, pytest.ini, a dedicated 'eval' workflow, CodeQL, pre-commit, codespell and 16 workflows overall. The disqualifying signals under this lens are maintenance and lifecycle. Activity has collapsed relative to every peer: 12 commits in the 90 days to 2026-09-21, zero PRs merged in the last month, last push 2026-08-02, and the two most recent commits before that are from 2026-06-24 — a ~6-week gap inside an already thin quarter. The latest release is 2.0.0-beta.28 from 2026-03-26, so the project has been in an unreleased beta line for roughly six months. requires-python is '>=3.10, <3.13', which excludes Python 3.13 and 3.14 outright and makes it the worst forward-compatibility fit on the shortlist for a Python 3.12+ target that expects to move. AGPL-3.0 is workable for purely internal self-hosting but constrains redistribution and hosted derivatives, hence 2 rather than 3. Contributor count is 73, the only shortlist entry below the 100-per-page API cap.

sota_claims.claim: Playwright is the most broadly CI-verified open-source cross-browser automation framework, running its own test matrix in-repo across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit plus BiDi, WebDriver (including Safari), Electron, Android, WebView (iOS Simulator and WebKitGTK), Docker and Fedora.

browser-use is the most widely cited open-source LLM-driven browser agent for WebVoyager, reported at an 89.1% success rate across 586 tasks in multiple independent 2026 roundups — though those roundups repeat the project's own figure rather than independently reproducing it.

DSPy is the leading peer-reviewed open-source framework for programmatic prompt and pipeline optimisation, with its GEPA optimiser accepted as an ICLR 2026 Oral and reported to beat GRPO by ~10% with 35x fewer rollouts and MIPROv2 by +14% with 9.2x shorter prompts.

LightRAG is the only shortlisted retrieval framework whose core method is peer-reviewed (EMNLP 2025 Findings, arXiv 2410.05779) and whose CI also runs end-to-end tests against real database backends rather than mocks.

Puppeteer has the strongest supply-chain and release discipline of the shortlist, combining OpenSSF Scorecards analysis, release-please automated versioning, conventional-commit enforcement, pinned browser updates and a dedicated de-flaking workflow in the same CI.

limits: Star authenticity could not be tested: the GitHub stargazers endpoint returned HTTP 404 for every repository attempted in this environment (verified against stanfordnlp/dspy and vercel-labs/agent-browser as controls, not only headroomlabs-ai/headroom), so no star-history or bot-detection check was run and the headroom star-inflation concern remains neither confirmed nor refuted. Independent evidence does show the count rising from ~49k in June 2026 to 73.4k by the cutoff, and a transfer from the personal account chopratejas/headroom into an org created 2026-06-16.

Nothing was installed, executed, built or benchmarked. Test and CI quality was inferred from directory listings, workflow names and packaging metadata via the GitHub API — not from coverage reports, green-run history or reproduced results. A workflow named 'Integration Tests' is evidence that a job exists, not that it passes or is meaningful.

All headline performance numbers cited (browser-use 89.1% WebVoyager, Headroom 60-95% token reduction) are project-published. Third-party pages repeat them; I found no independent reproduction of either. One independent write-up explicitly cautions that Headroom's figures are 'project-published benchmark claims, not independent lab results'.

Several comparison pages surfaced by web search are vendor blogs with a commercial interest in the ranking (Firecrawl, Bright Data, TinyFish, Spider, Respan). They were used only to corroborate that a figure is widely circulated, never as primary evidence for a score.

Contributor counts are floored at the 100-per-page API limit for eleven of twelve repositories, so contributor breadth is a lower bound, not a measurement; only khoj-ai/khoj (73) is an actual count. Commit-author concentration was measured over the last 100 commits only.

Scores are per-repository and per-criterion by design; no averages, totals or cross-repository aggregates were computed, and criteria marked 0 would have been listed as unknowns (none reached 0 — the weakest scores here are 1, meaning established but poor, not unknown).

The shortlist was supplied, not discovered by me. I did not run an independent discovery sweep, so coverage gaps in the shortlist itself (for example dedicated LLM-eval harnesses, literature-retrieval APIs, or static-review tooling, which are named in the sub-layer definition but thinly represented) are not corrected by this judgment.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for US-equities R&D: does the tool correctly solve the F-layer requirement (web/document retrieval, context efficiency, evaluation) in a way that preserves research validity — reproducible/auditable retrieval, no silent lossy transforms on numeric evidence, deterministic replay, citable provenance — and what independent published evidence or documented failure modes exist. Scope note: this sub-layer is retrieval/context/eval plumbing, not a market-data layer; point-in-time correctness, survivorship-free universes, corporate actions and paper/live parity are supplied by the data and execution layers, so for these 12 candidates those criteria are scored as not-established (0, listed in unknowns) rather than as failures. Where a tool's design actively threatens research validity (live-only retrieval with no as-of snapshot, lossy numeric summarisation, nondeterministic LLM-driven extraction as the data path), that is charged against capability_fit or quality_cost and stated. All facts below are from public GitHub API reads and public web sources as of 2026-09-21/22 UTC; no candidate was executed locally.

unknowns: No independent (non-vendor) benchmark of extraction fidelity on financial documents was located
No as-of / point-in-time snapshot or archival semantics documented — retrieval returns the live page only
AGPL-3.0 obligations for internal, non-user-facing commercial use are unresolved in the project's own issue tracker (#1964)
Which capabilities are cloud-only vs self-host is documented as differing but was not enumerated in this run
scores.notes: Strongest general retrieval capability in the set: search + scrape + crawl to LLM-ready markdown, 183,013 stars, 9,881 forks, ~166 contributors, pushed 2026-09-22, releases through v2.11.0 (2026-06-19), SDKs in 8 languages under apps/. Real test evidence exists but is nested: apps/api ships vitest.config.ts and apps/test-suite ships jest config, an index-benchmark and load-test harness — the shortlist's has_tests=no was a shallow-scan artifact. Lens hazards: (1) it returns the page as it is now, with no as-of snapshot, so using it for historical equities research imports revision and lookahead risk unless the caller stores and timestamps raw captures itself; (2) the vendor's own finance-research-agent post is marketing, not an independent accuracy measurement; (3) AGPL-3.0 plus documented open-source-vs-cloud capability differences is the weakest licence/deployment position among the high-capability candidates. Credit billing (roughly one credit per page, billed even on error status per a third-party guide) makes large historical sweeps costly on the hosted path.

unknowns: No published benchmark of research validity, citation fidelity or retrieval correctness for this framework
Per-workload token/latency overhead of the abstraction layer is not measured in any source located
No point-in-time or lookahead safeguards of any kind in the framework
scores.notes: Generic agent/retrieval framework, not a research-validity tool in itself; capability_fit is 2 because it supplies the plumbing (citations, reasoning traces and tool-call content types were added as typed interfaces in the v1.0 line) but no correctness guarantees. Evidence is better than average for a framework because libs/standard-tests is a published, importable contract-test package that every integration must pass — genuine upstream test evidence — plus a CITATION.cff; but nothing measures research outcomes. Maintenance is exceptional: 146,825 stars, ~467 contributors, per-package releases the same day as the read (langchain-core==1.6.4, langchain-openai==1.6.3, both 2026-09-21). MIT and self-hostable, so licence fit is clean. Lifecycle is the weak point: multiple independent 2026 write-ups document the 1.0 migration cost and abstraction churn, and several report teams moving to raw provider SDKs; pinning a research pipeline to these abstractions means re-verifying results after each major bump. The monorepo layout (libs/core/tests, libs/standard-tests/tests) again contradicts the shortlist's has_tests=no.

unknowns: Per-task cost and token consumption on long research sweeps is not published in any source located
Run-to-run determinism / variance of extracted values is not measured in any source located
No point-in-time or as-of retrieval semantics
scores.notes: The most-adopted open-source LLM-driven browser agent (115,798 stars, ~361 contributors, MIT, 0.13.10 on 2026-09-04) and the one candidate with genuinely independent published evaluation in both directions. The vendor reports 89.1% on WebVoyager as state of the art; the COLM 2025 paper 'An Illusion of Progress? Assessing the Current State of Web Agents' (arXiv:2504.01382) and the associated Online-Mind2Web benchmark measure Browser Use materially lower under a harder, human-verified protocol, and a Google-DeepMind-collaborating third party ran ~4,000 browser hours across OnlineMind2Web and WebVoyager. In-repo tests/ contains agent_tasks, ci, mind2web_data and scripts, so the benchmark data path is committed. That published record is exactly why quality_cost is 1 under this lens: a nondeterministic LLM agent is a legitimate tool for reaching login- or JS-walled sources, but it is the wrong component to put on the numeric data path for equities research, because its own benchmark literature shows a large gap between headline success rates and verified real-world success, and each retrieval costs model calls. Rapid 0.x versioning plus a parallel cloud product caps lifecycle_portability.

unknowns: No published evidence about use as a research-data ingestion path specifically (it is a testing/automation substrate)
No point-in-time, corporate-action or survivorship semantics — entirely out of its scope
scores.notes: Scores lowest-risk of the twelve under this lens and highest on the criteria that this lens actually cares about. Apache-2.0, Microsoft-maintained, 96,477 stars, ~472 contributors, v1.63.0 (2026-09-04), pushed the day of the read, with a first-party tests/ tree and browser_patches. Its decisive property here is deterministic, auditable replay: the Trace Viewer records DOM snapshots, network calls, console logs and per-action screenshots for every run, so a retrieval step can be re-inspected months later and a disputed extracted value traced to the exact page state that produced it — no other candidate in this sub-layer offers that. Official best-practice docs direct CI failures to traces rather than screenshots. capability_fit is 2, not 3, because it solves the browser-test and deterministic-fetch half of the sub-layer but supplies no retrieval intelligence, search, ranking or context compression; it is the substrate under several of the other candidates (Firecrawl ships a playwright-service-ts app). Multi-language bindings and stable semver give it the best lifecycle position in the set.

unknowns: No trace-replay artefact comparable to Playwright's Trace Viewer was located in the docs read
No published evidence of use as a research-data ingestion path
No point-in-time / market-data semantics — out of scope
scores.notes: Chrome-team-maintained, Apache-2.0, 95,607 stars, 9,580 forks, ~445 contributors, 1,204 watchers, puppeteer-v25.11.0 (2026-09-14), pushed 2026-09-21. Evidence quality is high and structural: committed test/ and test-d/ (type tests), .mocharc.js, docker/, website/ and versions.json pinning browser revisions — browser-revision pinning matters under this lens because it is what makes a scrape reproducible across machines and months. Deterministic and LLM-free, so quality_cost is 3. Marked one below Playwright on lifecycle_portability because it is JavaScript/TypeScript only (no Python/Java/.NET bindings) and Chrome-centric with Firefox as a secondary target, which constrains where a research pipeline can run it; and because no equivalent of Playwright's post-hoc trace artefact surfaced in this read. Same capability_fit ceiling as Playwright: it is substrate, not research tooling.

unknowns: No independent, peer-reviewed benchmark of DeepDoc layout/table extraction accuracy was located — the layout-model accuracy claims are on the vendor's own blog
Table-extraction fidelity on SEC-style filings (10-K/10-Q footnotes, multi-page tables) is not measured in any source located
Full infrastructure footprint and steady-state cost of a self-hosted deployment were not measured in this run
Open-issue count of 1,475 was not triaged into bug vs feature
scores.notes: The strongest document-understanding fit in the set for equities research, because the binding constraint on filings research is layout-aware parsing of PDFs with multi-page tables, not vector search: RAGFlow's DeepDoc component is a purpose-built layout/OCR stack (YOLO-trained layout model, upgraded across releases) rather than a naive text splitter. Apache-2.0, 91,119 stars, ~454 contributors, v0.27.2 (2026-09-10), pushed 2026-09-22, with committed test/ trees, run_tests.py, run_go_tests.sh and codecov.yml. Evidence is 2 rather than 3 because every accuracy claim traced back to ragflow.io's own blog; no third-party or peer-reviewed measurement of DeepDoc was found. Deployment is heavy — a docker/helm stack with search, object-store and cache dependencies — which is the main lifecycle_portability and quality_cost drag; 1,475 open issues is the highest in the set and was not triaged here.

unknowns: Star-count authenticity is UNVERIFIED: the GitHub stargazers endpoint returned HTTP 404 for this repo on both probes in this run, so star provenance could not be audited, and no star-history or bot-detection tooling was run
No independent replication of any compression or accuracy figure was located — every benchmark table traced to the project's own docs or to blog posts restating them
Accuracy impact of the ~97% numeric-array 'statistical summary' path on downstream numeric reasoning is not measured anywhere located
Whether CCR original-retention is guaranteed outside proxy flows (i.e. whether a given transform is recoverable) was not established
scores.notes: Directly on-sub-layer (context/token efficiency) and unusually honest about itself, which is why the evidence score is low rather than the integrity score: docs/content/docs/limitations.mdx states in its own words that the compression figures 'are not from a published, repeatable benchmark suite -- we could not trace a prior version of this table to one', and that each row is a 'directional single-sample measurement' against a synthetic payload. Committed harnesses exist (benchmarks/ holds ~30 scripts incl. compression_benchmark.py, index_proof_table.py with a seed, comprehensive_eval.py), but all published results are self-run. The decisive lens hazard is in that same table: JSON arrays of numbers are compressed ~97% by 'statistical summary', i.e. a lossy transform that replaces per-observation values with aggregates — applied to a price, volume or fundamentals series that silently destroys the data a quantitative result depends on, and the docs note that only marker-bearing compression in CCR proxy flows retains originals. Code and RAG document contexts pass through unchanged, which limits the upside for a filings-research workload. Apache-2.0 and self-hostable (licence fit 3). Maintenance 2, not 3: activity is intense (v0.38.0 on 2026-09-21, ~268 contributors) but the repo was created 2026-01-07 and its 73,425 stars in ~8.5 months remain unverified for authenticity per the unknown above; a blog post also records a rename/move from chopratejas/headroom, so historical provenance is split across identities.

unknowns: No published benchmark of retrieval or extraction correctness for this framework was located
Quality of the specific readers/integrations relevant to filings and market news is untested in any source located
No point-in-time or lookahead safeguards
scores.notes: Document-processing and retrieval framework, MIT, 52,270 stars, ~476 contributors, v0.14.25 released 2026-09-21 (same day as the read). Test evidence is real but per-package (llama-index-core/tests, llama-dev, llama-index-instrumentation), again contradicting the shortlist's has_tests=no; CITATION.cff, SECURITY.md and a docs site are present. The llama-index-instrumentation package and observability integrations are the parts that matter most under this lens, because they are what would let a research run be traced and re-audited. capability_fit is 2: it is a broad integration surface rather than a correctness mechanism, and its value for equities work depends entirely on which reader/parser is plugged in underneath it. Lifecycle is the concern — a very large integrations/ tree on 0.x versioning with frequent minor releases means integration behaviour can shift under a pinned pipeline.

unknowns: Published benchmark and eval RESULTS were not located — the repo ships the harnesses, not committed result sets, and reproducing them requires Vercel Sandbox credentials and an AI Gateway key
No third-party replication of the CLI-vs-MCP context-footprint claim was located
Long-run stability is unestablished: repo created 2026-01-11 (~8 months old) with 797 open issues
No point-in-time / as-of retrieval semantics
scores.notes: The best-instrumented candidate for the token-efficiency half of this sub-layer, and the one whose own methodology I could read and check. benchmarks/README.md documents per-scenario latency with warmup, multiple iterations and stddev, isolates daemon RSS from Chrome RSS, and explicitly cautions that 'command latency is dominated by Chrome (CDP round-trips), not the daemon' — i.e. it argues against its own headline rather than for it, which is the mark of a usable measurement. evals/ adds skill-loading, skill-selection, command-usage and a deterministic context-footprint.ts that measures CLI vs MCP context cost, with an optional LLM judge. Apache-2.0, ~115 contributors, v0.38.1 (2026-09-16), pushed 2026-09-21. quality_cost 3: the CLI issues deterministic commands, so unlike browser-use it can sit on a data path without model nondeterminism. Held at maintenance 2 and evidence 2 because the project is eight months old, carries 797 open issues, publishes no result sets, and both harnesses are bound to Vercel infrastructure (Sandbox microVMs, AI Gateway), so independent reproduction has a paywall-shaped prerequisite.

unknowns: The paper's evaluation is LLM-judged win-rate on comprehensiveness/diversity/empowerment across agriculture, CS, legal and mixed corpora — no factual-accuracy, numeric-extraction or finance-domain metric was located
Determinism of the LLM-driven entity/relation graph construction across re-indexing runs is not measured in any source located
Incremental-update correctness when the underlying corpus is revised (the filings-restatement case) is not established
scores.notes: The only candidate in this sub-layer with a peer-reviewed venue publication: 'LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation', Findings of EMNLP 2025, pp. 10746-10761 (aclanthology 2025.findings-emnlp.568), and it backs it with a committed reproduce/ harness (Step_0 through Step_3 plus batch_eval.py) and docs/Reproduce.md — published evidence plus a replication path is the strongest combination in the set. MIT, 39,805 stars, ~310 contributors, v1.5.7 (2026-09-02), pushed 2026-09-22, with Docker/Podman/k8s deployment and a web UI. capability_fit is held at 2 under this lens for two reasons: the graph index is built by LLM entity/relation extraction, so the index itself is a nondeterministic artefact that may not rebuild identically; and the paper's quality metrics are LLM-judged qualitative win-rates, not the factual-accuracy measure a filings pipeline needs. The paper's cost analysis (token and API-call counts vs GraphRAG, with a lower incremental-update cost because it skips community summarisation) is a genuine quality_cost positive, corroborated independently by an AWS engineering write-up running both on one stack.

unknowns: No finance- or equities-specific evaluation of DSPy optimizers was located
Cross-version reproducibility of a compiled program (whether an artefact optimized under 3.3.x reproduces under 3.4.x) is not established in any source located
Absolute optimizer cost in model calls for a realistic research pipeline is not published — the GEPA claims are relative (vs MIPROv2 and GRPO)
scores.notes: The clearest fit for the evaluation/quality-framework third of this sub-layer, and the one whose design directly serves research validity: DSPy forces an explicit metric and an explicit dev/eval set, then compiles prompts against them, so an evaluation becomes a versionable artefact rather than a prompt someone edited. Evidence is the strongest in the set after LightRAG and is multi-generational: the original DSPy work, MIPROv2, and GEPA — reported by multiple independent write-ups as an ICLR 2026 oral beating MIPROv2 by ~13-14% aggregate and GRPO by ~10% (up to 20%) with up to 35x fewer rollouts. In-repo tests/ is segmented by concern including tests/evaluate, tests/reliability and tests/teleprompt. MIT, 38,189 stars, ~407 contributors, 3.4.0b1 (2026-09-11). Two lens caveats that keep this off a perfect card: the framework will optimize against whatever devset it is given and provides no point-in-time or lookahead safeguard, so a devset built from forward-looking data produces a confidently overfit program; and optimizer semantics change across the 3.x line, so a recorded result is only reproducible against a pinned version.

unknowns: No published benchmark of its research or retrieval quality was located, despite a committed tests/evals directory
Whether the project is still actively developed as a product or superseded by the vendor's newer offerings could not be confirmed from the repo alone
AGPL-3.0 implications for embedding it in a commercial research stack were not analysed
No point-in-time / market-data semantics
scores.notes: Self-hostable research agent combining web and document retrieval — a reasonable capability shape for the sub-layer, with genuine test evidence (pytest.ini, tests/ with ~20 test modules plus a tests/evals directory, docker-compose and devcontainer). The disqualifying dimension here is maintenance, and it is the only candidate in the set that fails it: last commit 2026-08-02, ~1.7 months before the cutoff, with the two commits before that dated 2026-06-24 — i.e. roughly five commits across three months; the newest release is 2.0.0-beta.28 from 2026-03-26, six months stale and still pre-release; and it has ~73 contributors, the smallest in the set by a factor of four. The vendor's own site now foregrounds different products (Open Paper, Pipali Beta), which is consistent with attention having moved off this repo. Combined with AGPL-3.0 (licence fit 1, same class as Firecrawl but without Firecrawl's capability or momentum to justify the cost), this is the weakest candidate on the list under any lens, and it is a poor foundation for a multi-year research stack.

sota_claims.claim: LightRAG is the only candidate in this sub-layer with a peer-reviewed venue publication (Findings of EMNLP 2025, pp. 10746-10761) paired with a committed in-repo reproduction harness, making it the best-evidenced open-source graph-RAG engine on the shortlist.

DSPy's GEPA optimizer is the current state of the art in reflective prompt optimization, reported as an ICLR 2026 oral that beats MIPROv2 by roughly 13-14% aggregate and the GRPO reinforcement-learning baseline by about 10% on average with up to 35x fewer rollouts.

browser-use's self-reported 89.1% WebVoyager state-of-the-art result should not be taken at face value for research-grade use, because the COLM 2025 paper 'An Illusion of Progress?' and its Online-Mind2Web benchmark measure web agents including Browser Use substantially lower under a harder human-verified protocol.

Playwright is the only candidate whose retrieval steps are deterministically replayable after the fact, because its Trace Viewer records DOM snapshots, network calls, console logs and per-action screenshots as a portable artefact — the single most valuable property in this sub-layer for auditable equities research.

Headroom's headline compression figures are explicitly disclaimed by Headroom's own documentation as not coming from a published, repeatable benchmark suite but from directional single-sample measurements on synthetic payloads, so no state-of-the-art compression claim for it is currently supportable.

limits: None of the twelve candidates provides point-in-time/as-of retrieval, survivorship-free universes, corporate-action handling or paper/live parity; those belong to the data and execution layers, so I scored them as not-established (listed in each repo's unknowns) rather than penalising every repo for the same out-of-scope gap. The one place I did charge it is where a tool's design actively creates the hazard: Firecrawl and the browser agents return only the live page with no as-of snapshot, so a caller must timestamp and store raw captures itself or import revision/lookahead risk.

Headroom's 73,425-star count is UNVERIFIED for authenticity. The GitHub stargazers endpoint returned HTTP 404 for headroomlabs-ai/headroom on both probes in this run, so I could not sample starred_at dates, and I ran no star-history or bot-detection tooling. The caution carried in the input shortlist is neither confirmed nor refuted; I scored maintenance_provenance 2 on repo age and the documented chopratejas->headroomlabs-ai rename rather than on the star concern.

The evidence base is unevenly independent. Only LightRAG (EMNLP 2025 Findings), DSPy/GEPA (ICLR 2026 reports) and the web-agent critique (arXiv:2504.01382, COLM 2025) rest on peer review or third-party evaluation. Firecrawl's finance accuracy claim, RAGFlow's DeepDoc accuracy claims, Headroom's compression tables and agent-browser's latency/context-footprint numbers are all vendor-self-published; agent-browser and Headroom at least commit runnable harnesses, but agent-browser's require Vercel Sandbox credentials plus an AI Gateway key to reproduce.

The has_tests flags in the supplied shortlist metadata are unreliable and I did not rely on them. The shallow top-level scan reported has_tests=no for langchain, llama_index and firecrawl, all three of which actually carry substantial test trees one level down (libs/core/tests and libs/standard-tests; llama-index-core/tests; apps/api/vitest.config.ts and apps/test-suite with jest plus an index-benchmark). I verified test locations per repo via the GitHub contents API.

No candidate was executed, installed or measured locally in this run, and I opened no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> per the blindness rule. Every score derives from GitHub API metadata and public documentation read on 2026-09-21/22 UTC, so all figures are as-of that date; star counts, release tags and issue counts move. Cross-repo scores are deliberately not averaged or aggregated, and criteria I could not establish are left at 0 with the gap named rather than inferred.

verdicts.claim: Playwright is the most broadly CI-verified open-source cross-browser automation framework, running its own test matrix in-repo across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit plus BiDi, WebDriver (including Safari), Electron, Android, WebView (iOS Simulator and WebKitGTK), Docker and Fedora.
verdicts.reason: Two enumerated items are factually absent from the repository. GitHub code search over microsoft/playwright returns total_count=0 for 'fedora' and total_count=0 for 'safaridriver'; the single file matching 'webdriver in:path' is tests/mcp/webdriver.spec.ts (an MCP test, not a browser-driver matrix). .github/workflows/tests_bidi.yml runs only channels [bidi-chromium, moz-firefox-nightly] — no WebDriver and no Safari. tests_webview_simulator.yml drives an iOS Simulator WebView via ios-webkit-debug-proxy, which is WebKit, not Safari. By contrast SeleniumHQ/selenium does exercise Safari in CI (code search 'safari path:.github/workflows' -> 3 files: bazel.yml, ci-ruby.yml, ci-python.yml), so the 'most broadly CI-verified' superlative fails on precisely the axis the claim asserts. The uncontested part (chromium/firefox/webkit x ubuntu/macos/windows, tracing, Android, Electron, installation, driver, Chrome/Edge channels, Docker) is real, but the claim as written overstates the matrix.

verdicts.claim: browser-use is the most widely cited open-source LLM-driven browser agent for WebVoyager, reported at an 89.1% success rate across 586 tasks in multiple independent 2026 roundups — though those roundups repeat the project's own figure rather than independently reproducing it.
verdicts.reason: The '89.1% / 586 tasks' figure does appear in 2026 roundups, but those roundups are not independent: brightdata.com is a commercial proxy/scraping vendor and firecrawl.dev is a direct competitor that is itself a candidate in this same sub-layer shortlist (ranked 3rd by judge 2). No primary or academic source reproduces the number. More decisively, the project itself has retired the figure: the current browser-use README (read via the GitHub readme API on 2026-09-21) contains no 'WebVoyager' or '89.1' string at all — it now presents a self-authored 'Browser Use Benchmark v2' on a 60-task subset, and browser-use's own engineering blog now headlines Online-Mind2Web instead. So the claim rests on stale third-party marketing copy that the upstream project no longer stands behind, and 'most widely cited' is not supportable from any primary source.

verdicts.claim: DSPy is the leading peer-reviewed open-source framework for programmatic prompt and pipeline optimisation, with its GEPA optimiser accepted as an ICLR 2026 Oral and reported to beat GRPO by ~10% with 35x fewer rollouts and MIPROv2 by +14% with 9.2x shorter prompts.
verdicts.reason: The venue is correct (arXiv 2507.19457 comments field reads 'Accepted to ICLR 2026 (Oral)'), but the headline numbers are contradicted by the current primary source. The arXiv abstract as last revised 14 Feb 2026 (the ICLR camera-ready revision) states: 'Across six tasks, GEPA outperforms GRPO by 6% on average and by up to 20%, while using up to 35x fewer rollouts. GEPA also outperforms the leading prompt optimizer, MIPROv2, by over 10% (e.g., +12% accuracy on AIME-2025)'. It says 6%, not ~10%, over GRPO; it says 'over 10% / +12%', not +14%, over MIPROv2; and it contains no '9.2x shorter prompts' figure at all. Those numbers come from the superseded v1 abstract and from vendor blog restatements (morphllm.com), not from the accepted paper. Also note the attribution slip: GEPA is not 'DSPy's optimiser' — it is a separate MIT-licensed project, gepa-ai/gepa (6,694 stars), which dspy.GEPA wraps.

verdicts.claim: LightRAG is the only shortlisted retrieval framework whose core method is peer-reviewed (EMNLP 2025 Findings, arXiv 2410.05779) and whose CI also runs end-to-end tests against real database backends rather than mocks.
verdicts.reason: The peer-review half checks out (aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.568 is 'LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation'). The CI half misdescribes the workflows. The primary suite .github/workflows/tests.yml is literally named 'Offline Unit Tests' and its own comments say 'Run only tests marked as offline (no external dependencies); integration tests requiring databases/APIs are skipped by default' and that it installs 'the mock-target libraries (qdrant-client, pymongo, anthropic, boto3, ...) the offline suite constructs data classes from' — i.e. mocks ARE the default path. The only real-backend job is .github/workflows/pg-smoke.yml, titled 'PostgreSQL Smoke Tests', covering a single backend (postgres:18) as a smoke test, not 'end-to-end tests against real database backends' plural. Qdrant, MongoDB, Neo4j, Redis and Milvus storage paths are exercised only against mocks in public CI.

verdicts.claim: Puppeteer has the strongest supply-chain and release discipline of the shortlist, combining OpenSSF Scorecards analysis, release-please automated versioning, conventional-commit enforcement, pinned browser updates and a dedicated de-flaking workflow in the same CI.
verdicts.reason: Every enumerated element is verifiable in the live .github/workflows listing: scorecards-analysis.yml, release-please.yml, convetional-commit.yml (sic), update-browser-pins.yml and deflake.yml, alongside ci.yml, daily.yml, bisect.yml and pre-release.yml. publish.yml goes further than the claim: it publishes with 'npm publish --provenance --access public' under OIDC (id-token: write) and pins every action by commit SHA. The comparative superlative also holds against what is measurable: api.scorecard.dev returns Puppeteer 7.8 on a fresh 2026-09-21 scan, versus langchain-ai/langchain 5.8 (2026-09-14) and SeleniumHQ/selenium 3.0 (2026-09-21); microsoft/playwright has no Scorecards workflow and its only public Scorecard record is 6.5 from 2022-08-15; dspy, LightRAG, firecrawl and browser-use have no Scorecard record at all. I found no counter-evidence. Caveat worth carrying forward, not a refutation: 7.8/10 is good but not exemplary, and the deprecation step still uses a long-lived NPM_TOKEN via wombat-dressing-room.

verdicts.claim: LightRAG is the only candidate in this sub-layer with a peer-reviewed venue publication (Findings of EMNLP 2025, pp. 10746-10761) paired with a committed in-repo reproduction harness, making it the best-evidenced open-source graph-RAG engine on the shortlist.
verdicts.reason: The 'only' quantifier is false. DSPy carries an OpenReview venue field of 'ICLR 2024 spotlight' for 'DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into State-of-the-Art Pipelines' (forum sY5N0zY5Od), and dspy.GEPA's underlying paper (arXiv 2507.19457) is 'Accepted to ICLR 2026 (Oral)' — an oral at a top-tier venue outranks a Findings track paper on selectivity. Both LightRAG (reproduce/Step_0..Step_3.py, batch_eval.py) and DSPy ship committed reproduction/eval code. Headroom likewise ships ~30 committed benchmark scripts under benchmarks/. So LightRAG is not the only peer-reviewed candidate, and on venue tier it is not the best-evidenced.

verdicts.claim: DSPy's GEPA optimizer is the current state of the art in reflective prompt optimization, reported as an ICLR 2026 oral that beats MIPROv2 by roughly 13-14% aggregate and the GRPO reinforcement-learning baseline by about 10% on average with up to 35x fewer rollouts.
verdicts.reason: Refuted twice over. (1) Numbers: the camera-ready arXiv abstract (2507.19457, last revised 14 Feb 2026) says 6% average over GRPO (up to 20%) and 'over 10% (e.g., +12% on AIME-2025)' over MIPROv2 — not ~10% and not 13-14%. (2) Currency: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering, arXiv 2510.04618), also published at ICLR 2026, reports outperforming ReAct + GEPA by 11.9% on AppWorld, and on offline adaptation took 9,517 seconds / 357 rollouts versus GEPA's 53,898 seconds / 1,434 rollouts — an 82.3% latency reduction. Independently, Arize's published benchmark across HotpotQA, HoVer, PUPA and IFBench reports its Prompt Learning approach 'performs comparably to or better than GEPA with far fewer rollouts'. 'Current state of the art' is therefore not supportable as of 2026-09-21. (Caveat for the catalog: ACE has no credible upstream repository — GitHub search returns only third-party reimplementations with <5 stars — so it is counter-evidence, not an adoptable alternative.)

verdicts.claim: browser-use's self-reported 89.1% WebVoyager state-of-the-art result should not be taken at face value for research-grade use, because the COLM 2025 paper 'An Illusion of Progress?' and its Online-Mind2Web benchmark measure web agents including Browser Use substantially lower under a harder human-verified protocol.
verdicts.reason: I tried to refute this and could not; it is the best-evidenced claim in the set. The Online-Mind2Web repository README confirms COLM 2025 acceptance ('07/08/2025 Online-Mind2Web has been accepted to COLM 2025!') and the 300-task/136-site design. The official human-evaluated leaderboard CSV in the OSU-NLP HuggingFace space lists 'Browser Use, gpt-4o-2024-08-06, Browser Use, OSU NLP, Easy 55.4, Medium 26.6, Hard 8.1, Average SR 30.0, 2025-3-22' — a ~59-point gap against the 89.1% WebVoyager self-report, from an independent evaluator under human verification. Two further points strengthen rather than weaken the claim: browser-use's own 2026 blog now advertises '97% on Online-Mind2Web ... the highest score ever', yet no Browser Use entry appears anywhere in the official leaderboard CSV (current top rows are Hark 97.7, Navigator/n1.5 97.3, ACT-2 92.7, all third-party-evaluated by Careerflow.ai), so the newer self-report is likewise unverified; and the leaderboard's own top scores having moved from 61.3 to 97.7 in 18 months is itself a reason to distrust vendor-reported figures.

verdicts.claim: Playwright is the only candidate whose retrieval steps are deterministically replayable after the fact, because its Trace Viewer records DOM snapshots, network calls, console logs and per-action screenshots as a portable artefact — the single most valuable property in this sub-layer for auditable equities research.
verdicts.reason: Both the property and the exclusivity fail. Playwright's own documentation defines Trace Viewer as 'a GUI tool that helps you explore recorded Playwright traces after the script has run' — post-hoc inspection of a recording, not deterministic replay (nothing is re-executed, and the DOM snapshots are re-rendered approximations). For 'only': puppeteer/replay (active, last push 2026-09-20) is an actual replay library — 'provides an API to replay and stringify recordings created using Chrome DevTools Recorder' — i.e. it literally re-executes a recorded flow, which Trace Viewer does not. And the purpose-built answer for citable, auditable web provenance is WARC/WACZ archiving (webrecorder/browsertrix-crawler, AGPL-3.0, pushed 2026-09-21), which replays the recorded HTTP responses themselves and is the accepted standard in the web-archiving literature. Neither was considered by either judge.

verdicts.claim: Headroom's headline compression figures are explicitly disclaimed by Headroom's own documentation as not coming from a published, repeatable benchmark suite but from directional single-sample measurements on synthetic payloads, so no state-of-the-art compression claim for it is currently supportable.
verdicts.reason: The first half is verbatim accurate — docs/content/docs/limitations.mdx carries a Methodology callout reading 'The compression figures below are not from a published, repeatable benchmark suite -- we could not trace a prior version of this table to one. Instead ... each row is a directional single-sample measurement taken with compress() against a synthetic payload of that shape.' But the conclusion is over-broad, and the refuting evidence is in the same paragraph: it continues 'For a seeded, committed harness that reproduces figures of this kind exactly, run uv run python benchmarks/index_proof_table.py --seed 20260902.' The repository does contain that harness plus ~30 further committed benchmark scripts (compression_benchmark.py, comprehensive_eval.py, real_world_agent_benchmark.py, headroom_adversarial_benchmark.py, headroom_worst_case_benchmark.py, bench_latency.py, bench_relevance.py, a scenarios/ and a results/ directory) and a separate docs/content/docs/benchmarks.mdx page. The disclaimer scopes one documentation table, not the project's evidence base. The correct skeptical position is that Headroom's numbers are self-generated and not third-party-reproduced — not that no claim is supportable.

survivors: Puppeteer has the strongest supply-chain and release discipline of the shortlist, combining OpenSSF Scorecards analysis, release-please automated versioning, conventional-commit enforcement, pinned browser updates and a dedicated de-flaking workflow in the same CI. (https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer)

browser-use's self-reported 89.1% WebVoyager state-of-the-art result should not be taken at face value for research-grade use, because the COLM 2025 paper 'An Illusion of Progress?' and its Online-Mind2Web benchmark measure web agents including Browser Use substantially lower under a harder human-verified protocol. (https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use)

better_alternatives_found.name: browsertrix-crawler (Webrecorder)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Directly beats the property judge 2 attributed to Playwright Trace Viewer (claim 9). Browsertrix drives a real browser and emits WARC/WACZ archives that replay the actual recorded HTTP responses, which is the archival-science standard for citable, as-of-date web provenance — exactly the 'no silent lossy transform, deterministic replay, citable provenance' criterion judge 2 named as most valuable for equities research. Playwright traces are a debugging viewer, not a replayable archive of the retrieval. Active (pushed 2026-09-21), 1,143 stars. Caveat to carry: AGPL-3.0, single-container Docker deployment, and the web-archiving literature documents replay fidelity failures for ad-heavy/dynamic pages (doi 10.1002/asi.70039).

better_alternatives_found.name: Inspect AI (UK AI Security Institute)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The sub-layer definition explicitly covers 'quality/evaluation frameworks (LLM eval)', yet neither judge ranked a single dedicated eval framework — both rankings are browser automation, prompt optimisation and retrieval only. Inspect is a government-maintained (UK AISI), MIT-licensed Python eval framework built around durable, replayable .eval log files with full sample/message/score provenance, which is the eval-side analogue of the auditability criterion judge 2 applied elsewhere. Active (pushed 2026-09-22), 2,829 stars. It is a stronger fit than the eval tools that did surface: vibrantlabsai/ragas has not been pushed since 2026-02-24 (~7 months stale), and Arize-ai/phoenix carries a NOASSERTION license.

better_alternatives_found.name: Crawl4AI
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: Plausibly beats firecrawl/firecrawl, which judge 2 ranked 3rd in this sub-layer. Crawl4AI has 84,043 stars against Firecrawl's 183,019 but ships under Apache-2.0 where Firecrawl's self-hosted core is AGPL-3.0 — a documented licensing constraint for embedding a retrieval layer in a proprietary research stack, repeatedly flagged in 2026 comparisons. Both are actively maintained (Crawl4AI pushed 2026-09-22). Neither judge recorded Firecrawl's AGPL obligation.

better_alternatives_found.name: LLMLingua (Microsoft)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: The context-efficiency slot in the shortlist is occupied by headroomlabs-ai/headroom, whose compression figures are self-generated and, per its own limitations page, partly single-sample on synthetic payloads. LLMLingua is the peer-reviewed alternative for the same function: prompt compression published at EMNLP 2023 and ACL 2024, MIT-licensed, 6,689 stars. Its published numbers are third-party-reviewable in a way Headroom's are not. Caveat: it is research-grade and less actively developed (pushed 2026-09-10) and solves a narrower problem than Headroom's proxy/runtime integration, so this is a complement-or-benchmark candidate, not a drop-in replacement.

better_alternatives_found.name: Stagehand (Browserbase)
better_alternatives_found.discovery_reason: A credible browser-agent alternative to browser-use, absent from both rankings. MIT-licensed, 24,750 stars, pushed 2026-09-21. Its design point is directly relevant to judge 2's research-validity lens: it keeps deterministic Playwright primitives as the default data path and invokes the LLM only for the steps that need understanding, which limits nondeterministic LLM-driven extraction — the exact failure mode judge 2 said should be charged against capability_fit. Multiple 2026 comparisons describe this Playwright-plus-selective-AI split as the production pattern.

better_alternatives_found.name: GEPA (gepa-ai)

Anything depending on the optimiser should pin this repository rather than inherit it transitively through DSPy's much larger dependency surface. Listing it corrects a provenance error rather than proposing a new capability.

Direct github.com URLs were sparse in raw snippets for several queries (backup, observability, CI-alternatives, supply-chain, local-inference topics returned mostly vendor blog/listicle URLs rather than repo links), so candidate repo names were extracted from article text/tool-name mentions and then independently verified against the GitHub API (gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>) rather than taken from a raw URL match.

All 55 gh api repos/<owner>/<repo> lookups succeeded (200) and returned full_name + stargazers_count, confirming existence and giving a live popularity signal used to prioritize candidates; none errored or required retry.

Discovery did not open any file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> and did not use prior knowledge of the project's already-selected tools; candidate selection was driven purely by what appeared across independent public web searches and was cross-checked for repeat appearance across multiple queries (e.g. Cronicle, LocalStack, Restic/Borg, OTel/Prometheus/Grafana family, Ollama/vLLM/llama.cpp) as a bias check, plus inclusion of org-backed repos (sigstore, in-toto, ossf, CNCF grafana/jaeger, OpenTelemetry, argoproj, Netflix, llm-d/Red Hat) per the goal's explicit call for organisation repos.

No gh API rate-limit (5000/h) or search rate-limit (30/min) was hit; all repo lookups used the direct repos/<owner>/<repo> endpoint, not the search endpoint, so the 30/min search cap was not exercised.

Coverage per requested sub-topic is uneven: supply-chain security and observability each got 8-11 candidates, backup/recovery got 6, local-service-fixtures got 5, and local-inference/gateways got 9 — collectively 55 verified candidates rather than a strict 12-25, reflecting the six distinct sub-topics folded into one 'F-ops' layer; a narrower per-sub-topic cap of 12-25 was not separately enforced.

GitHub's license API returns spdx_id=NOASSERTION with license.key="other"/license.name="Other" for several well-known repos (in-toto, slsa, gitsign, Cronicle, windmill, n8n, localstack, borg, duplicati, SigNoz, litellm, open-webui, sigstore-python, awesome-prometheus-alerts, tyk) — GitHub does not resolve a named SPDX license for these even though several are known to ship real license terms (e.g. borg=BSD-3-derived, n8n=Sustainable Use License, windmill=AGPL/Elastic dual); this is a detection gap in GitHub's API, not a determination that no license exists, but per the stated mechanical rule (recognised OSI or explicitly noted commercial/source-available terms) these were dropped since the API-observable fact is NOASSERTION/"Other" with no explicit terms string to record without going beyond gh api output

judges.lens: Engineering quality for sub-layer F-ops (CI/supply-chain security for agent repos, scheduling/workflow supervision, local service hosting, backup/recovery, observability, optional local inference/gateways). Judged on: code/test/CI health, release discipline, API stability, documentation depth, dependency and platform hygiene, security/provenance, community and maintainer organisation, and operational fit for a local-first Linux/WSL2, Python 3.12+ single-box stack. All scores are documentary: every repo was assessed from GitHub API metadata, primary repository files (README, contents listing, release assets, security advisories), and the OpenSSF Scorecard API as of 2026-09-21. Nothing was built, installed or executed, and no file under <PROJECTS_ROOT> was opened.

scores.notes: Strongest overall engineering posture in the shortlist. OpenSSF Scorecard 8.1 (2026-09-21) with CI-Tests=10, SAST=10, Fuzzing=10, Code-Review=10, Branch-Protection=8, Pinned-Dependencies=8 - the only shortlisted repo where CI-Tests and SAST are both independently confirmed at 10. Repo root carries MAINTAINERS.md, CODEOWNERS, RELEASE.md, SECURITY.md, SECURITY-INSIGHTS.yml, docs/stability.md and a compliance/ directory, which is unusually explicit API-stability and governance documentation. 2,506 commits and 441 merged PRs in the trailing 52 weeks / 90 days; release train runs proper rc tags (v3.15.0-rc.0 on 2026-09-14) ahead of GA. Native OTLP ingestion is in-tree (storage/remote/write_otlp_handler.go plus a full otlptranslator package) and documented on prometheus.io, which covers the OTel metrics requirement of this sub-layer without a separate collector. Apache-2.0, single static Go binary, agent mode available - lowest operational cost of any serious metrics backend for one box.

scores.notes: Directly covers the 'CI/supply-chain security for agent repos' requirement: `trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret,misconfig` over a working tree, plus SBOM, license and IaC scanning, with a maintained GitHub Action (aquasecurity/trivy-action). Best provenance in the shortlist by a wide margin: every single artifact of v0.74.0 ships a matching .sigstore.json attestation (24 bundles observed, including checksums.txt.sigstore.json) - no other shortlisted repo does this. Root contains SECURITY.md, a .vex directory, release-please-config.json/manifest (automated, auditable release cadence), CHANGELOG.md, and notably zizmor.yml, i.e. the project lints its own Actions workflows for supply-chain issues. Real test estate rather than a placeholder: integration/ holds client_server_test.go, k8s_test.go, sbom_test.go, registry_test.go, module_test.go and a testdata tree, alongside a separate e2e/ directory and 27 Actions workflows. 517 commits/52w, 118 merged PRs/90d, only 171 open issues for a 38k-star project - healthy triage. Apache-2.0, single Go binary, offline DB mode makes it viable air-gapped.

Evidence scored 2 rather than 3 because the test story is directory-level (fstest/, cmdtest/, 13 workflows) with no independently confirmed CI-Tests signal. MIT, single Go binary, trivially portable to WSL2.

scores.notes: Strongest engineering evidence of the local-inference candidates: 77 Actions workflows, a tests/ directory with 66 entries, a separate ci/ harness (ci/run.sh), CODEOWNERS, SECURITY.md, .clang-tidy/.clang-format/.pre-commit-config.yaml/mypy.ini/pyrightconfig.json - multi-language lint and type gates are all configured in-tree. Activity is very high and broadly distributed: 4,541 commits/52w and 1,349 merged PRs/90d. MIT and CMake-based with CPU-only operation viable, so it is the cheapest path to local inference on hardware without a GPU, and the most portable to WSL2. The single severe defect under this lens is release lifecycle: the tag stream is per-build prereleases (b11095, b11094, b11093, b11090, b11081, b11080, b11078, b11077 were all published within 2026-09-21/22), with prerelease=true on every one. There is no stable channel to pin, no semantic version to reason about compatibility from, and consequently no way to express a supported-version policy in a downstream runtime - which is why lifecycle_portability is 1 despite otherwise excellent engineering.

scores.notes: The most rigorously governed project in the shortlist. Apache Software Foundation process is visible in-tree: GOVERNANCE.md, COMMITTERS.rst, COMMUNITY_ESCALATION.md, ISSUE_TRIAGE_PROCESS.rst, .asf.yaml, plus reproducible_build.yaml and a constraints/ directory for reproducible installs. Scorecard 7.3 (2026-09-21) with Code-Review=10, Maintained=10, Security-Policy=10, Fuzzing=10 and Signed-Releases=8 - the highest Signed-Releases score of any shortlisted repo, reflecting ASF's mandatory release signing. Test estate is exceptional and explicitly layered: airflow-e2e-tests, kubernetes-tests, docker-tests, task-sdk-integration-tests, airflow-ctl-tests, devel-common, across 69 workflows. Version support is documented as a matrix (Python 3.10-3.14, Kubernetes 1.30-1.35), which is exactly the API-stability discipline this lens rewards, and 8,189 commits / 2,846 merged PRs show no slowdown. Scored down on two axes for this sub-layer specifically: capability_fit 2 because Airflow is a data-pipeline orchestrator whose unit of work is an idempotent DAG task, which is an awkward shape for supervising long-running agent processes; quality_cost 1 because the README itself states SQLite is for tests and must not be used in production, so a real deployment means a database plus scheduler plus API server plus workers - disproportionate for a single-box local-first stack.

scores.notes: Capability is the broadest gateway story in the shortlist: drop-in OpenAI, Anthropic and ElevenLabs API compatibility across every backend, all modalities behind one API, API-key auth with user quotas and role-based access, and explicitly no GPU required - which suits a local-first box better than vLLM. Test and verification evidence is genuinely unusual for a project this size: separate e2e, e2e-aio, e2e-backends, e2e-ui and integration test trees, plus a formal-verification/ directory containing FizzBee models (compaction.fizz, conn_lifecycle.fizz, model_loader_shutdown.fizz, response_lifecycle.fizz, session_lifecycle.fizz, tts_pipeline.fizz) with a checked-in fizzbee.sha256 - formal specification of concurrency lifecycles is a quality signal no other shortlisted repo shows. Release cadence is clean semver (v4.10.0, v4.9.0, v4.8.x monthly) and open issues are only 179 against 49k stars. The decisive markdown is provenance: of roughly 96 commits in the 90 days to 2026-09-21, 83 were authored by `localai-org-maint-bot` and a further 4 by `mudler-agent`, with named humans contributing single digits. Authorship is therefore overwhelmingly automated around a single principal maintainer, which makes the review chain and bus factor the main engineering risk, independent of how good the artefacts look.
