scores.notes: The capability is exactly right for this sub-layer - running GitHub Actions workflows locally is the cheapest way to validate an agent repo's CI before pushing - and the packaging is ideal (MIT, single Go binary, 72k stars). Everything else fails. OpenSSF Scorecard scores it 3.9 (2026-09-14) with Maintained=0, Security-Policy=0, Signed-Releases=0, SAST=0, Fuzzing=0. The activity data is unambiguous: 20 commits in the trailing 52 weeks, and zero commits and zero merged PRs in the 90 days to 2026-09-21, against 115 open PRs and 268 open issues. The five most recent commits are three version bumps and two Dependabot dependency bumps; the last substantive change observed is 2026-05-13 and the last release is v0.2.89 on 2026-06-01. This intersects badly with security: CISA's bulletin for the week of 2026-08-24 records an advisory against nektos/act for an HTTP Artifacts V4 backend whose control-plane RPCs (CreateArtifact, GetSignedArtifactURL, ListArtifacts, FinalizeArtifact, DeleteArtifact) accept caller-supplied input, and the repo's own advisory list already carries three high-severity entries including GHSA-xmgr-9pqc-h5vw and GHSA-x34h-54cw-9825 (both patched only in 0.2.86, March 2026). A tool whose job is to execute untrusted workflow definitions on a developer machine, with an unpatched-as-of-this-review artifact-server advisory and no active maintainer, is the highest-risk item in the shortlist. Evidence is 1 because main_test.go and pkg tests exist but nothing confirms they gate anything.

sota_claims.claim: Prometheus is the most independently assured repository in this sub-layer, holding the highest OpenSSF Scorecard of the twelve (8.1 as of 2026-09-21) and the only one where CI-Tests, SAST, Fuzzing and Code-Review are all scored 10/10, while also carrying native in-tree OTLP metrics ingestion so a single Apache-2.0 Go binary covers both the Prometheus and OpenTelemetry metrics paths.

Trivy is the only repository in this shortlist that publishes a Sigstore attestation bundle for every release artifact - all 24 assets of v0.74.0, including the checksums file, ship a matching .sigstore.json - making it the strongest supply-chain-provenance exemplar as well as the scanner that would enforce that standard on agent repos.

nektos/act is effectively unmaintained as of 2026-09-21 - zero commits and zero merged pull requests in the preceding 90 days, 115 open PRs, OpenSSF Scorecard Maintained=0 and Security-Policy=0, and no release since v0.2.89 on 2026-06-01 - which is disqualifying given CISA's 2026-08-24 bulletin recording an advisory against its unauthenticated Artifacts V4 control-plane RPCs in a tool whose function is executing untrusted workflow definitions locally.

Apache Airflow has the strongest release and governance discipline of the shortlist - Apache Software Foundation process artifacts in-tree, the highest Signed-Releases score observed (8/10), reproducible builds with pinned constraints, and a published Python 3.10-3.14 support matrix - but pairs it with the highest operational cost, since its own README rules out SQLite outside tests and therefore mandates a database plus scheduler plus workers.

llama.cpp has the deepest CI and test apparatus of the local-inference candidates (77 Actions workflows, a 66-entry tests/ tree, a separate ci/ harness, and clang-tidy/mypy/pyright gates) yet offers no stable release channel at all - eight tags published on 2026-09-21/22 alone, every one marked prerelease - so nothing downstream can pin a supported version.

limits: The shortlist was supplied pre-filtered; I ran no independent discovery pass, so absent categories are unexamined rather than rejected. Notably missing from this sub-layer's coverage: OpenTelemetry Collector, Grafana Alloy, Loki, Tempo, Jaeger, VictoriaMetrics and SigNoz for the OTel/traces/logs lane; restic and borgbackup for local-first backup with deduplication; Dagster, Prefect, Temporal and plain systemd timers for lighter scheduling/supervision than Airflow; zizmor, semgrep, grype, syft, the OpenSSF scorecard-action and Sigstore/cosign for the supply-chain lane; and LiteLLM for the gateway slot. No conclusion here should be read as 'these twelve are the best available'.

The OpenSSF Scorecard API returned HTTP 404 for five of the twelve repositories (uptime-kuma, ollama, vllm, llama.cpp, LocalAI), so their security posture is unknown, not clean. Comparisons on provenance are therefore only valid among the seven repositories that have a Scorecard record.

Scorecard snapshot dates are not uniform: Trivy's is 2026-03-16 while the others are 2026-09-14 or 2026-09-21, so Trivy's 6.4 is roughly six months stale relative to its peers and its SAST=1/Fuzzing=0 may have moved.

The input metadata listed has_tests as 'unknown' for six repositories. I resolved this only to the level of confirming that test directories and test files exist; I measured no coverage percentage, ran no test suite, and in most cases could not confirm that CI actually gates merges on those tests. Evidence scores of 2 reflect exactly this gap.

Nothing was built, installed, executed or benchmarked. Every score is documentary, derived from GitHub API metadata, repository file listings, README text, release assets, security advisories and the Scorecard API. No claim here constitutes runtime or performance evidence.

Release-signing conclusions are based on release asset filenames only. Projects that sign or attest through a separate channel (package repositories, container registry attestations, detached signatures on a project website) would be undercounted; I marked these as unknowns for Prometheus, rclone and Grafana rather than asserting absence of signing.

Commit-authorship concentration was computed from at most 100 commits in a 90-day window per repository via the GitHub commits API, which is a sample rather than a census for the highest-volume repos (Grafana, Airflow, vLLM), and it attributes by commit author, so squash-merge policies can understate reviewer and contributor breadth.

judges.lens: Research validity and task fit for US-equities operations (F-ops sub-layer: CI/supply-chain security, scheduling/workflow supervision, local service hosting, backup/recovery, observability, optional local inference/gateways). Scored on whether each tool correctly solves its ops requirement and whether it carries any property that bears on point-in-time correctness, lookahead safeguards, paper/live parity or reproducibility — plus what published evidence, upstream tests and documented failure modes support it. Blind discovery: no file under <OPERATOR_HOME> was opened; all evidence is public web/GitHub dated to 2026-09-21.

unknowns: Long-term retention / remote-storage strategy for multi-year trading telemetry is unmeasured
Handling of OpenTelemetry exponential (native) histograms from Airflow requires specific configuration per upstream guidance; not verified
No measured scrape-to-alert latency for an intraday execution loop
scores.notes: Correctly and completely solves the ops-metrics requirement, and is the only repo in the shortlist that publishes its own correctness boundary: the overview states 'If you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough.' Under this lens that is a feature, not a defect — it cleanly separates ops telemetry from the fill/position/P&L system of record, which must never be Prometheus. Architecture is stateless and standalone ('Each Prometheus server is standalone, not depending on network storage or other remote services'), so it stays observable when the trading stack itself degrades. Evidence: in-repo compliance/ directory with remote_write_sender_test.go (an interop conformance suite, rare in this shortlist), 29 CI workflows, SECURITY.md present. Prometheus 3.x added a stable OTLP metrics ingestion endpoint, so it satisfies the OTel half of the sub-layer natively — metrics only, not traces or logs. Apache-2.0, single binary, local TSDB: lowest operational cost in the shortlist. Maintenance: v3.14.0 2026-08-18 plus v3.15.0-rc.0 2026-09-14, 100+ commits in the 90 days to 2026-09-21, 1158 watchers.

unknowns: Scheduler latency / jitter under an equities EOD deadline is unbenchmarked
Migration cost from 2.x to 3.x for an existing deployment not assessed
Contributes nothing to corporate-action handling, survivorship or cost modelling — those must live in the pipeline code, not the orchestrator
scores.notes: The single most lens-relevant property in this shortlist: Airflow's data-interval model binds a run to the interval of data it processes, not to wall-clock execution — 'The "logical date" ... of a Dag run, for example, denotes the start of the data interval, not when the Dag is actually executed.' That is a structural guard against lookahead in scheduled ingest and backtest pipelines, and backfill is a first-class documented mechanism with explicit control over data reprocessing, which is what reproducing a historical run requires. Hard boundary from its own README: 'Airflow is not a streaming solution, but it is often used to process real-time data, pulling data off streams in batches' — corroborated by vendor docs advising against schedules more frequent than once a minute. So it fits daily/EOD equities supervision and cannot supervise sub-minute intraday execution. Evidence is unusually deep: separate airflow-e2e-tests, docker-tests, kubernetes-tests and task-sdk-integration-tests trees, 69 CI workflows. Native OpenTelemetry metrics export (apache-airflow[otel]) feeds the observability requirement directly, and upstream notes OTel labels metrics with resource info while 'StatsD has no resource concept, so metrics cannot be attributed to the process that produced them' — material for HA. ASF governance, 3.3.2 released 2026-09-17. Portability and cost are the weak points: metadata DB + scheduler + workers is heavy for a single-operator stack and 2119 open issues reflect that surface area.

unknowns: Which unified-alerting features in v13 are Enterprise-only was not determined
AGPL-3.0 network-copyleft applicability to a private trading deployment is a legal question I did not resolve
No measured dashboard query load against a Prometheus TSDB of trading size
scores.notes: Covers the dashboards + alerting half of the observability requirement and is the natural consumer of the Prometheus/OTel layer. Strongest visible test evidence after Airflow: an e2e-playwright tree with named suites including alerting-suite, smoke-tests-suite, dashboards-suite and plugin-e2e, plus 132 CI workflows. Maintenance signal is notable — v13.2.2, v13.1.6, v13.0.9 and v12.4.11 were all published on 2026-09-15, i.e. coordinated backports across four supported majors, which is what you want for a component sitting in an operational alert path. Deployment fit is the deduction: Grafana Labs moved the core from Apache-2.0 to AGPLv3 on 2026-04-20 (first affected release Grafana 8.0), so anything 8.x+ carries network copyleft; self-hosting unmodified for internal use is fine, but modifying and exposing it as a service is a constraint, and Enterprise/Cloud gating creates a second pull. Portability is mid: dashboard JSON exports cleanly, but the plugin ecosystem and Enterprise-only features are not portable. 3331 open issues and a Go+Node build make it the heaviest observability component here.

unknowns: Which models beyond the few explicitly validated work under batch invariance is not enumerated upstream
No independent third-party verification that the beta batch-invariance mode actually achieves bitwise determinism
GPU cost and the throughput penalty of batch invariance are documented as real but unquantified upstream
Whether determinism holds across vLLM version upgrades (it almost certainly does not) is unaddressed
scores.notes: Under a research-validity lens this is the most defensible local-inference choice, for one specific reason: it ships a documented determinism mode. Upstream states 'Batch invariance ensures that the output of a model is deterministic and independent of the batch size or the order of requests in a batch' via VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1, with the honest caveat 'Enabling batch invariance may impact performance compared to the default non-deterministic mode. This trade-off is intentional to guarantee reproducibility.' If any LLM-assisted step enters a research or signal pipeline, that is the difference between a reproducible experiment and an unreproducible one. It is explicitly beta (tracking issue #27433), so the guarantee is not yet dependable. Evidence is the strongest in the shortlist: a peer-reviewed SOSP 2023 paper (PagedAttention, arXiv:2309.06180) plus a tests/ tree with basic_correctness, evals, kernels, spec_decode, distributed, quantization and models suites, Buildkite CI alongside 25 GH workflows. Apache-2.0; OpenAI-compatible server API makes it swappable. The deduction is cost: 8273 open issues — by far the highest here — a demanding CUDA/ROCm build, a required capable GPU, and determinism bought with throughput.

unknowns: False-positive rate against this stack's actual Python/Go dependency set is unmeasured
No peer-reviewed or vendor-neutral accuracy study located; 2026 comparisons found are SEO/vendor blogs
Offline/air-gapped DB refresh cadence and staleness risk not assessed
scores.notes: Covers the whole stated CI/supply-chain requirement in one Apache-2.0 binary: dependency vulnerabilities, IaC/misconfiguration, secrets, SBOM generation and VEX (the repo carries a .vex/ directory). Portability is a genuine strength for evidence durability — it emits SPDX/CycloneDX SBOMs and SARIF, so findings and bills of material outlive the scanner. In-repo evidence is solid: an integration/ suite with client_server_test.go, k8s_test.go, sbom_test.go, registry_test.go, vm_test.go and standalone_tar_test.go, a separate e2e/ tree, 27 CI workflows and a substantial SECURITY.md. Evidence scored 2 rather than 3 because the accuracy claim is contested, not established: independent 2026 comparisons report Grype running roughly 30-40% faster on image-only scans with a reputation for lower false positives, and OSV-Scanner producing fewer false positives for language ecosystems where NVD CPE matching over-matches — but every one of those sources is a commercial blog, not a controlled study. Trivy's real differentiator is breadth (IaC, Kubernetes and secrets, which Grype does not touch), not per-CVE precision. Maintenance is healthy: v0.74.0 2026-08-14, 100+ commits in 90 days.

unknowns: Restore-time verification for a large historical parquet/tick catalog is unmeasured
crypt key-management and key-loss recovery story not assessed
Whether bucket-side versioning at the chosen provider gives true point-in-time restore was not verified
scores.notes: Best-in-class object-store sync, mount and crypt across 70+ backends, and the evidence quality is high: the repo ships fstest/test_all, a per-backend integration matrix driven by fstest/test_all/config.yaml and documented in CONTRIBUTING, and upstream states that releases (unlike betas) go through 'the full integration test suite'. Data portability is a real strength — it writes plain objects in native formats, so a catalog stays readable without rclone. The capability deduction is squarely on the lens: multiple independent sources confirm rclone has 'no native versioning or incremental snapshots' and that 'if you sync and a file is deleted locally' the deletion propagates — a mirror, not an archive. For US-equities research validity you need to restore the catalog exactly as it stood on a past date (to re-run a backtest and get the same answer); rclone alone cannot do that, and needs either provider-side bucket versioning or a snapshotting layer such as restic on top. Documented operational burden: provider rate limits require tuning (--tpslimit), and 1270 open issues. MIT, v1.75.1 2026-09-04, 100+ commits in 90 days, 12-year history.

unknowns: No documented determinism or batch-invariance guarantee found — reproducibility of outputs is unestablished
Quantization quality loss for any specific model on this hardware is unmeasured
No stable-release contract: releases are per-build tags, so the support window for any pin is unknown
scores.notes: CPU-first local inference with an OpenAI-compatible server. The lens-relevant capability is constrained decoding: GBNF grammars and JSON-schema-to-grammar conversion force structurally valid output, which is a genuine correctness lever for structured extraction (the repo carries test-grammar-integration, test-json-schema-to-grammar, test-json-schema and test-gbnf-validator). Evidence is excellent — a very large tests/ tree covering backend ops, samplers, quantization, gguf and optimization, 77 CI workflows, and in-repo measurement tools (llama-bench, perplexity) that let you quantify quality/perf yourself rather than trusting a claim. GGUF is the de-facto local weight format and the server speaks the OpenAI API, so nothing locks in. Two deductions. Capability: unlike vLLM there is no documented determinism mode, so output reproducibility is unestablished under this lens. Cost: release cadence is multiple tagged builds per day (b11090, b11093, b11094, b11095 all on 2026-09-21/22), which means there is no stable-version contract — you must pin a build number and own the upgrade risk yourself — plus 2540 open issues. MIT.

unknowns: Per-backend maturity varies widely and is unmeasured
The scope of the repo's formal-verification/ directory was not verified
No published benchmark, paper or independent evaluation located
Determinism/reproducibility is not addressed upstream
scores.notes: The best fit in this shortlist for the 'gateway' half of the optional inference requirement rather than the 'engine' half: an OpenAI-compatible drop-in spanning text, embeddings, rerank, TTS, image generation and object detection, plus MCP support, over multiple swappable backends. If the stack needs one local endpoint for several modalities (e.g. embeddings for document retrieval alongside chat), that breadth is the differentiator; if it needs maximum throughput or determinism on one model, vLLM or llama.cpp is the better answer. Evidence is mid: a tests/ tree with e2e, e2e-aio, e2e-backends, e2e-ui and integration suites plus a formal-verification/ directory and 43 CI workflows — real upstream testing, but no paper, no benchmark and no third-party evaluation. Maintenance is a positive outlier: v4.10.0 released 2026-09-17, 100+ commits in 90 days, and only 179 open issues against 49k stars — the lowest issue-to-star ratio in the shortlist. MIT, and its whole value proposition is the OpenAI API shape, so it is trivially replaceable. Cost deduction: it wraps other engines, inheriting their failure modes and adding a layer, on a smaller contributor base than the engines it wraps.

unknowns: Whether a commercial trading operation qualifies under the free tier was not resolved — upstream states the free Community tier is 5 nodes, personal use only
Measured agent CPU/disk overhead at per-second resolution is unbenchmarked
No published validation of its ML anomaly-detection accuracy located
Behaviour of the CDN-delivered closed UI in an air-gapped or offline deployment is unverified
scores.notes: Strong per-second host and service telemetry with built-in ML anomaly detection and alerting, and a large tests/ tree (health/alarm tests, api, k6 load tests, run-unit-tests.sh) with 39 CI workflows — genuinely capable for the local-service-hosting-health part of the sub-layer. But it is agent-centric infrastructure monitoring, not an application-metric store with a query language you would express trading KPIs in, so it complements rather than replaces Prometheus. The two heavy deductions are licensing and portability, and they are linked. Upstream is explicit that the Agent is GPLv3+ while 'Netdata UI – Closed-source but free to use with Netdata Agent and Cloud. Delivered via CDN', and that 'The free Community tier supports 5 nodes (personal use only). Larger deployments and commercial use require paid plans.' For a commercial equities operation that is a material open-core boundary, not a footnote. Portability scores 1 because DBENGINE is a proprietary-shaped local store and the dashboard/alert layer does not travel — you can export metrics to Prometheus, but you cannot take the thing you actually built with you. Maintenance itself is excellent: v2.11.1 2026-09-16, 100+ commits in 90 days, only 405 open issues.

unknowns: No HA/failover story verified upstream; single-instance by design
Probe scheduling jitter and timing accuracy are unmeasured and unpublished
Bus factor: development appears concentrated in one primary maintainer; no governance document located
Durability of the default SQLite store relies on community patterns (e.g. Litestream), not an upstream mechanism
scores.notes: Cheap, MIT, fully self-hosted liveness monitoring with a wide notification-channel set — a reasonable fit for 'is the broker endpoint, the market-data feed and my paper session reachable' supervision, and 2.x added MariaDB alongside the default SQLite for deployments that outgrow a single file. Maintenance is genuinely strong: 2.5.5 on 2026-09-16 after 2.5.4, 2.5.3, 2.5.2 and 2.5.1 in the preceding month, with 100+ commits in 90 days. Evidence scores 1, the lowest here: a test/ tree exists (backend-test, e2e, manual-test-grpc/radius) and 29 CI workflows run, but I found no published benchmark, no correctness evidence for probe timing, and no third-party evaluation — for an alerting component whose value is entirely 'did it notice in time', that is an unfilled gap. The capability limit matters under this lens: it probes reachability, so it cannot detect the failure mode that actually costs money in equities — a feed that returns HTTP 200 with stale or wrong data. It must sit alongside a freshness/staleness metric in Prometheus, never instead of one. 816 open issues, single-instance, no documented HA.

unknowns: I did not reproduce the temperature-0 nondeterminism on the current version; the reports are third-party summaries of upstream issue #586
Provenance and integrity verification of weights pulled from the ollama.com registry was not assessed
No published paper or benchmark located
scores.notes: Lowest-friction local model runtime with a registry and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and the in-repo integration/ suite is better than its reputation suggests — Go tests covering concurrency, max_queue, structured_output, tools_stress and a set of reg_* regression groups, across 16 CI workflows. Maintenance is strong (v0.34.2 2026-09-15 plus an rc four days later, 100+ commits in 90 days). The quality_cost score of 1 is driven specifically by this lens: third-party analysis of upstream issue #586 reports that 'with the same seed, same temperature=0, and same num_ctx, the output still differed slightly between the first and second run', and that the same code produced different output on Ubuntu versus Windows. If an LLM step feeds a research or signal pipeline, that is unreproducible by default and Ollama offers no documented mode to fix it — vLLM does. Portability scores 2 rather than 3 because the Modelfile/model-store and the ollama.com registry pull toward its own ecosystem, though GGUF import and the OpenAI-compatible API provide exits. 4053 open issues. Best read as a convenience layer over engines that give you more control.

unknowns: No public maintainer statement on project status located — dormancy is inferred from commit and release data, not announced
No published fidelity benchmark quantifying the gap between act's default images and GitHub-hosted runners
Whether a maintained downstream fork (e.g. the actions-oss/act-cli lineage) is the correct pin was not evaluated
scores.notes: Genuinely useful for shortening the push-to-test loop on workflow changes, MIT, and zero lock-in — it consumes standard .github/workflows YAML, so dropping it costs nothing. But it fails this lens on the property that matters most, parity, and it fails it by the project's own admission: the user guide directs anyone who 'need[s] an environment that works just like the corresponding GitHub runner' to alternative nektos/act-environments images, warning that such an image is '>18GB'. The default experience is therefore an approximation of CI, not a reproduction of it, so a green act run does not establish that the real pipeline passes. Maintenance is the decisive finding and it is mechanical, not impressionistic: the GitHub API returns zero commits on the default branch for the 90 days to 2026-09-21; the most recent commit is 2026-06-01 ('chore: bump VERSION to 0.2.89'), the one before it a Dependabot bump on 2026-05-13; the last release is v0.2.89 on 2026-06-01. 383 open issues include long-standing, heavily-upvoted requests (podman support with 61 reactions, Ubuntu 24.04 with 42). Meanwhile the ecosystem is routing around upstream: github-act-runner now tracks actions-oss/act-cli rather than nektos/act, and gitea's fork was archived 2026-04-23. Evidence scores 1: 11 CI workflows and a `make test` unit target, nothing published.

sota_claims.claim: Prometheus is the only tool in this shortlist that publishes its own correctness boundary — its overview states that if you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice because the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough — which makes it correct as the ops-telemetry layer and disqualifying as the system of record for fills, positions or P&L.

Airflow's logical-date/data-interval model is the only scheduling primitive in this shortlist that binds a run to the interval of data it processes rather than to wall-clock execution time, making it the strongest available structural guard against lookahead in scheduled US-equities ingest and backtest pipelines.

vLLM is the only local-inference engine in this shortlist shipping a documented determinism mode — batch invariance via VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1, which upstream says makes output independent of batch size and request order — and it is still beta with an explicitly intentional throughput cost.

rclone is a mirroring tool rather than a backup system — it has no native versioning or incremental snapshots, so it cannot on its own restore a research catalog to its exact state on a past date and must be paired with provider-side bucket versioning or a snapshotting layer such as restic to support reproducible historical backtests.

nektos/act is effectively dormant as of 2026-09-21 — zero commits on the default branch in the preceding 90 days, last commit 2026-06-01 (a version bump) and no release since v0.2.89 — while downstream consumers such as github-act-runner have retargeted to the actions-oss/act-cli fork and gitea's fork was archived on 2026-04-23.

limits: Blindness rule honoured: no file under <OPERATOR_HOME> was opened and no prior project selection was consulted. All evidence is public GitHub API data and public web pages retrieved on 2026-09-21; every repository has at least two cited public URLs.

None of the twelve repositories addresses US-equities research validity directly. Point-in-time correctness, survivorship and lookahead safeguards, corporate actions, transaction costs and paper/live parity are out of scope for every F-ops tool here. capability_fit was therefore scored against the ops requirement, with the few lens-relevant correctness properties called out individually (Airflow data intervals, vLLM batch invariance, Prometheus's accuracy disclaimer, llama.cpp grammar-constrained decoding, rclone's missing versioning).

Several decision-relevant third-party comparisons — Trivy-versus-Grype timings and false-positive reputation, Ollama temperature-0 nondeterminism — come from SEO/vendor blogs, forum posts and a secondary summary of an upstream issue, not from peer-reviewed or vendor-neutral studies. I did not reproduce any of them, so those points are scored as contested rather than established and are listed in the relevant unknowns.

has_tests and has_ci were verified only by listing test directories and counting CI workflows through the GitHub API. No upstream test suite was executed for any repository, so no quality score here is execution-verified; the shortlist's 'has_tests: unknown' entries for trivy, airflow, act, rclone, prometheus and ollama were resolved to directory evidence only.

quality_cost reflects documented operational weight, open-issue load and release-contract stability, not measured resource or dollar cost. Nothing was benchmarked on this machine, and GPU/retention/storage costs for vLLM, Netdata per-second retention and Airflow's metadata database remain unquantified.

verdicts.claim: Prometheus is the most independently assured repo in the sub-layer: highest OpenSSF Scorecard of the twelve (8.1), the only one with CI-Tests, SAST, Fuzzing and Code-Review all 10/10, plus in-tree OTLP metrics ingestion.
verdicts.reason: The 8.1 score and in-tree OTLP ingestion are confirmed (storage/remote/write_otlp_handler.go and storage/remote/otlptranslator/ exist in-tree). But the uniqueness claim is a measurement artifact, not a property: Prometheus was scanned with Scorecard v5.5.0, which emits CI-Tests/Contributors/Vulnerabilities/Dependency-Update-Tool, while airflow, trivy, rclone, grafana and netdata were scanned with v5.5.1-0.20260908181711, which emits none of them. Those five have NO CI-Tests score at all, so 'the only one where CI-Tests ... is 10/10' cannot be established by comparison. Worse, 'most independently assured' is contradicted by Prometheus's own report: Signed-Releases 0 ('Project has not signed or included provenance with any releases') and Vulnerabilities 0 ('63 existing vulnerabilities detected'). A non-shortlisted F-ops repo, anchore/grype, scores 8.2 overall with Signed-Releases 8 and Vulnerabilities 7 - higher than any repo the judge ranked.

verdicts.claim: Trivy is the only repo in the shortlist publishing a Sigstore attestation bundle for every release artifact - all 24 assets of v0.74.0, including the checksums file, ship a matching .sigstore.json - making it the strongest supply-chain-provenance exemplar.
verdicts.reason: The arithmetic is wrong and the superlative is false. v0.74.0 has 47 assets, not 48: 24 artifacts plus 23 .sigstore.json bundles. Programmatic pairing shows exactly one unsigned artifact - bom.json, the SBOM - so 'every release artifact' is untrue, and it is the provenance document itself that is unattested. The checksums file IS signed, so that sub-detail holds. Independently, Trivy's own Scorecard rates Signed-Releases 3/10 (overall 6.4, SAST 1, Token-Permissions 0, CII-Best-Practices 0), while apache/airflow scores 8/10 and anchore/grype 8/10 on the same check - so on the only independent provenance metric available Trivy is the weakest of the three, not 'the strongest supply-chain-provenance exemplar'.

verdicts.claim: nektos/act is effectively unmaintained as of 2026-09-21 - zero commits and zero merged PRs in the preceding 90 days, 115 open PRs, Scorecard Maintained=0 and Security-Policy=0, no release since v0.2.89 on 2026-06-01 - disqualifying given the CISA 2026-08-24 bulletin recording an advisory against its unauthenticated Artifacts V4 control-plane RPCs.
verdicts.reason: Every element verified against primary sources. Default-branch (master) HEAD is 4f411281 'chore: bump VERSION to 0.2.89' dated 2026-06-01, i.e. zero commits in the 90 days to 2026-09-21. GitHub search returns total_count=0 for merged PRs since 2026-06-23 and 115 open PRs. Latest release is v0.2.89 (2026-06-01). Scorecard (2026-09-14) gives overall 3.9 with Maintained 0 ('0 commit(s) and 0 issue activity found in the last 90 days'), Security-Policy 0, SAST 0, Fuzzing 0, Token-Permissions 0, Signed-Releases 0. CISA bulletin SB26-243 does contain the 'nektos--act' entry describing CreateArtifact/GetSignedArtifactURL/ListArtifacts/FinalizeArtifact/DeleteArtifact accepting a caller-supplied workflow_run_backend_id that validateRunIDV4 never checks. I found no counter-evidence of resumed maintenance.

verdicts.claim: Airflow has the strongest release and governance discipline of the shortlist - ASF process artifacts in-tree, the highest Signed-Releases score observed (8/10), reproducible builds with pinned constraints, and a published Python 3.10-3.14 support matrix - but the highest operational cost, since its README rules out SQLite outside tests.
verdicts.reason: The supporting facts check out: Signed-Releases 8/10 ('5 out of the last 5 releases have a total of 5 signed artifacts') is indeed the highest observed; README line 106 shows the Python 3.10/3.11/3.12/3.13/3.14 matrix; lines 117-118 state 'SQLite is used in Airflow tests. Do not use it in production'; lines 157-185 document the constraints-<version> branches. The superlative does not. Airflow's own Scorecard is 7.3, below Prometheus's 8.1, and it scores CII-Best-Practices 0 ('no effort to earn an OpenSSF best practices badge detected') against Prometheus's 'badge detected: Passing', SAST 0, and Pinned-Dependencies 0 ('dependency not pinned by hash detected') - which undercuts the 'reproducible builds with pinned constraints' framing at the hash level. Its report also returns 'no workflows found' for Dangerous-Workflow and 'No tokens found' for Token-Permissions, so the 7.3 is computed over a reduced check set and is not comparable to Prometheus's full one.

verdicts.claim: llama.cpp has the deepest CI/test apparatus of the local-inference candidates (77 Actions workflows, 66-entry tests/ tree, separate ci/ harness, clang-tidy/mypy/pyright gates) yet offers no stable release channel at all - eight tags published on 2026-09-21/22, every one prerelease - so nothing downstream can pin a supported version.
verdicts.reason: Refuted on the load-bearing conclusion. GET /repos/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/latest returns tag v0.4.1, prerelease=false, published 2026-09-14. Paginating the releases list shows a semver stable line running v0.1.0, v0.1.1, v0.1.2, v0.2.0 (2026-08-21), v0.3.0 (2026-08-25), v0.4.0 (2026-09-04), v0.4.1 (2026-09-14), all with prerelease=false, published alongside the nightly bNNNNN tags. The judge evidently read only the first page of the releases feed, which is saturated by nightlies, and missed the stable channel introduced on 2026-08-21. Downstream consumers can pin v0.4.1. The workflow count is also wrong: .github/workflows contains 58 entries, not 77 (tests/ = 66 is correct).

verdicts.claim: Prometheus is the only tool in the shortlist that publishes its own correctness boundary - its overview states that if you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice because the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough - making it correct as ops telemetry and disqualifying as the system of record for fills, positions or P&L.
verdicts.reason: The quotation is verbatim and current at the cited primary source, under the heading 'When does it not fit?': 'If you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a case, you would be best off using some other system to collect and analyze the data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring.' The inference to fills/positions/P&L is a sound reading of that boundary. The only soft element is the superlative 'the only tool in this shortlist' - I could not disprove it, but it is an absence-of-evidence assertion across eleven other doc sets and should not be relied on as a discriminator.

verdicts.claim: Airflow's logical-date/data-interval model is the only scheduling primitive in the shortlist that binds a run to the interval of data it processes rather than to wall-clock execution time, making it the strongest available structural guard against lookahead in scheduled US-equities ingest and backtest pipelines.
verdicts.reason: The cited page itself documents the exception that breaks the guard. Under 'Manual Triggering and Data Intervals' it states: 'When you manually trigger a Dag (for example from the UI, CLI, REST API, or TriggerDagRunOperator), do not assume the run's data_interval is derived from, or equal to, the supplied logical_date. For scheduled runs, the timetable defines the data interval directly. For manually triggered runs, the resulting data_interval depends on the timetable and the trigger path, and may differ from the run's logical_date.' Manual triggers, backfills and reruns are precisely the backtest/research path where a lookahead guard matters, so the binding is a scheduled-run convention rather than a structural safeguard. The superlative is also vacuous: Airflow is the only scheduler in either ranking, so 'only in this shortlist' asserts nothing about merit, and the judge did not consider dagster-io/dagster, whose partition/asset model expresses the same binding declaratively.

verdicts.claim: vLLM is the only local-inference engine in the shortlist shipping a documented determinism mode - batch invariance via VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1, which upstream says makes output independent of batch size and request order - and it is still beta with an explicitly intentional throughput cost.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed at the cited primary doc. It carries the note 'Batch invariance is currently in beta. Some features are still under active development' linking tracking issue #27433; states that the feature 'ensures that the output of a model is deterministic and independent of the batch size or the order of requests in a batch'; shows 'export VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1'; and under Implementation Details states 'Enabling batch invariance may impact performance compared to the default non-deterministic mode. This trade-off is intentional to guarantee reproducibility.' Two precision defects short of refutation: the doc says 'performance', not specifically 'throughput', and the claim omits a hard gate the same page imposes - 'Batch invariance requires NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or higher' - which is material for a single-box local-first stack, and validation is limited to a 22-model tested list.

verdicts.claim: rclone is a mirroring tool rather than a backup system - it has no native versioning or incremental snapshots, so it cannot on its own restore a research catalog to its exact state on a past date and must be paired with provider-side bucket versioning or a snapshotting layer such as restic.
verdicts.reason: The cited source is a third-party dev.to opinion post, not a primary source, and rclone's own documentation contradicts the absolute premise. rclone.org/docs documents --backup-dir: 'When using sync, copy or move, any files which would have been overwritten or deleted are moved in their original hierarchy into this directory', combined with --suffix to timestamp them - a native retention mechanism for prior versions. The S3 backend further ships --s3-versions ('Include old versions in directory listings'), --s3-version-at ('Show file versions as they were at the specified time', accepting '2006-01-02' or a duration) and --s3-version-deleted, which is native point-in-time reading rather than something the user must bolt on. The claim's practical conclusion (pair with restic or bucket versioning for a real deduplicated snapshot history) is defensible, but 'no native versioning' as stated is false and the evidence offered is not primary.

verdicts.claim: nektos/act is effectively dormant as of 2026-09-21 - zero commits on the default branch in 90 days, last commit 2026-06-01 (a version bump), no release since v0.2.89 - while downstream consumers such as github-act-runner have retargeted to the actions-oss/act-cli fork and gitea's fork was archived on 2026-04-23.
verdicts.reason: All four downstream assertions verified independently. master HEAD is 4f411281 'chore: bump VERSION to 0.2.89', 2026-06-01, i.e. a version bump and zero commits in the trailing 90 days; latest release v0.2.89 (2026-06-01). The go.mod of ChristopherHX/github-act-runner requires 'github.com/actions-oss/act-cli v0.4.0' and also replaces actionlint with actions-oss/act-cli-actionlint, confirming the retarget. The Gitea fork lives on gitea.com, not GitHub; its API returns archived=true, archived_at 2026-04-23T18:55:53Z, description 'Fork of https://github.com/nektos/act, Merged into act_runner' - date exact. One caveat that does not refute but weakens the implied remedy: actions-oss/act-cli is itself thin (7 stars, last push 2026-03-01, latest release v0.4.1 on 2026-02-14), so the retarget shows abandonment of upstream rather than arrival at a healthier successor.
